sections.title: socketley.storage
sections.html:
Any runtime's script may use a storage runtime by name, in this daemon or in another process. The daemon does not stop while the script waits:

socketley.storage.put(runtime, bucket, key, data [, {content_type=, metadata={}}] [, callback])
socketley.storage.get(runtime, bucket, key [, callback])
socketley.storage.head(runtime, bucket, key [, callback])
socketley.storage.delete(runtime, bucket, key [, callback])
socketley.storage.list(runtime, bucket [, prefix] [, {delimiter=, max_keys=, start_after=}] [, callback])

Some callbacks can pause: on_message, on_client_message and the storage hooks above. In these, a call without a callback waits and returns the answer. The connection that a server handler is answering is kept open while it waits, as it is for a linked cache. Anywhere else (an on_tick, a cache's on_write, a proxy's filter), pass a function as the last argument. The call then returns true at once, and the function is called with the answer on a later turn. A call that must wait, made where waiting is not possible and without a function, returns nil and a message saying so.

The answers are:

  • put and head return a table with size, etag, content_type, mtime_ms and metadata.

  • get returns the data and that table.

  • delete returns true, also for a key that was not there, as S3 does.

  • list returns a table with objects (each with key, size, etag, content_type, mtime_ms), prefixes, truncated and, when truncated, next (pass it as start_after for the following page).

A failure returns nil and the S3 error code and message (NoSuchKey, NoSuchBucket, InvalidBucketName, EntityTooLarge). When the request did not reach the runtime, the call returns nil and a reason (no such runtime, the request channel is full). Metadata names are lowercased and stored as x-amz-meta-*. Buckets are created with the S3 API. An object moves whole in memory, and the request crosses a process boundary in a frame that waits in a 4 MiB queue. A script may therefore put or get at most 1 MiB per call, and at most 1024 calls may be waiting on one runtime. Use the S3 port for larger objects.

sections.title: DNS FLAGS
sections.html:
A dns runtime is an authoritative name server. It answers queries over UDP and TCP on one port, and only for the zones in the files it is given.

socketley create dns ns --zone example.com --publish 203.0.113.7 -s
dig @127.0.0.1 example.com SOA

When a zone is given by its name, the runtime writes it with this machine's public address for its name servers. --publish gives that address. It may be left out only where a network interface has a public address, and behind NAT none has one. create also makes an entrance: a proxy of the runtime's own (see --proxy). As soon as the entrance starts, it asks Let's Encrypt for a certificate for each zone and its wildcard. It does so for every name except those reserved for examples and tests, such as example.com, .test and .internal, because no public CA issues certificates for them. For a lab or a test that uses real names, give --proxy none. The runtime also answers one client network at most 100 times a second (--rrl). A load test from a single host therefore sees most answers dropped unless it gives --rrl 0.

The runtime asks no other server and caches nothing. A name that is in none of its zones is answered REFUSED and is never looked up. So the runtime cannot be used as an open resolver, and every answer it gives is its own. Like every other runtime, it runs in a worker process of its own. It may run as --shards processes that share the port. Each UDP query goes to a shard drawn at random, so a resolver that asks from one port, or with one ID, is still spread over every shard. It binds IPv4, and also IPv6 when the host has it and no --bind address is given. The default port is 53. A port below 1024 needs root or CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE, which the packaged service grants. -p, --bind, --cpus, --max-connections (TCP connections; default 256) and the common flags apply as documented under COMMON FLAGS. --listen and --tls are refused.

--zone name|file#

A zone to serve, given by its name or as a zone file. Required. Give the flag once for each zone, or give several zones separated by commas.

Details

A name, such as example.com, needs no file. The first time, the runtime writes one under state-dir/zones/name.zone and serves it from then on. The file has an SOA record and names ns1 and ns2 as the zone's name servers. The addresses of --publish (or this machine's public addresses) become the addresses of ns1 and ns2, and of the zone's own name, which is the entrance's. You tell the registrar these two names and addresses as the domain's name servers and their glue. The file is yours to edit; the runtime never writes it again while it exists.

A path is made absolute against the caller's directory. If a file called zone.zone does not exist there, it is written in the same way. A zone file uses the master file format of RFC 1035. The zone's apex is the owner of its one SOA record. Every record must lie at or below the apex, and the apex must name its servers with NS records. A CNAME must be the only record of its name. Below a delegation, only the addresses of the delegated servers may appear. create and start refuse a file that is not such a zone, and name the line that is wrong. $ORIGIN and $TTL are read. $INCLUDE is refused, since it would let a zone file read any file the worker can read. Types A, AAAA, NS, CNAME, SOA, PTR, MX, TXT, SRV, CAA and HINFO are written in their usual form. Any other type is written in RFC 3597's form, TYPEn \# length hex. A TXT string longer than 255 bytes is split into several strings, as a DKIM key needs.

The runtime checks the file once a second, and reads it again when it was edited. The new zone is served once the whole file has been read and checked. If the file no longer parses, the previous zone stays in place and the log gives the reason. A changed zone whose serial did not change is still served. The log then says that its secondaries will not notice the change until the serial is raised.

--transfer list#

The addresses and address blocks that may copy a whole zone by AXFR over TCP (RFC 5936). Give them comma-separated: a secondary's address, such as 192.0.2.53, or a block, such as 2001:db8::/48. Everyone else is answered REFUSED, so the names a zone holds are not handed to whoever asks. An IXFR from these addresses over UDP is answered with the SOA alone. This tells the secondary the serial and that it must come over TCP. Over TCP, an IXFR is answered as an AXFR.

--notify list#

The secondaries that get a NOTIFY (RFC 1996) when the runtime starts and whenever a zone's serial changes. Give them as host[:port], comma-separated. The runtime sends the NOTIFY again after 1, 3, 7, 15 and 31 seconds until the secondary answers it. Only the first shard sends them.

--publish list#

This machine's public IPv4 and IPv6 addresses, comma-separated, used to answer for the names of the daemon's runtimes. A runtime of the daemon is reached by names given with --domain, --acme, or a storage runtime's --domain and --website-domain. Every such name that falls within a zone is answered with these addresses. Without this flag, those names are answered with this machine's public addresses when the runtime has an entrance (below), and not at all with --proxy none.

--proxy name|none#

The entrance through which the names of runtimes are reached, or none for no entrance. An entrance is a proxy without --backend. It routes each HTTP request, by the name the request asks for, to the runtime that has that name (see PROXY FLAGS).

Details

create makes the entrance as this runtime's child. Its name is dns-proxy when the flag is not given. It listens on --proxy-port with --tls and --backend-timeout 5m, because a site may take a while to begin answering, as behind any web server. The entrance asks the CA for its own certificate: each zone with its wildcard, proven over DNS-01 by this runtime's answers. Before that, acme issue waits SOCKETLEY_ACME_DNS_WAIT seconds and asks the resolver of /etc/resolv.conf for a TXT record that exists only in this runtime's answers. It then asks every name server the zone is delegated to for that record directly, since a CA may ask any of them. Some zones are not ready in that time: a zone that the world's DNS does not delegate here yet, or a zone with a secondary that has not taken up the record. Each name of such a zone is proven by itself instead, over TLS-ALPN-01 on 443, without the wildcard. The wildcard is asked for again every six hours until the zone is delegated.

An entrance on 443 comes with dns-proxy-http on port 80, which sends every request to HTTPS (--redirect-https). Behind the entrance, every response over TLS carries Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000 unless the answering runtime set its own. Over TLS, the entrance speaks HTTP/2 to a client that offers it by ALPN, and HTTP/1.1 to a client that does not. Each HTTP/2 stream is routed by the name it asks for, like an HTTP/1.1 request. A stream that asks for a name other than the one its connection's handshake gave is answered 421. A client may have eight streams open at once. SOCKETLEY_PROXY_HTTP2=0 turns HTTP/2 off. Over UDP on the same port, the entrance speaks HTTP/3 (RFC 9114), and every answer over TCP names it in Alt-Svc: h3. An HTTP/3 stream is routed by its own :authority exactly as an HTTP/2 stream is. A browser that cannot reach the UDP port goes on over TCP. SOCKETLEY_PROXY_HTTP3=0 opens no UDP socket.

The entrance stops, starts and is removed with this runtime. If this runtime is removed while another dns runtime also names the entrance, the entrance becomes that runtime's instead. A proxy of that name that already exists is used as it is, provided it is an entrance. none makes no entrance. With an entrance and no --publish, the names are answered with this machine's public addresses. The runtime reads them from the machine's interfaces and checks them again every minute.

socketley create dns ns --zone example.com -s     # and ns-proxy on 443
socketley create server chat --domain --http /srv/chat -s
curl https://chat.example.com/
--proxy-port port#

The port that the entrance made by create listens on. Default: 443.

--rrl n#

Response rate limiting: the most answers a second the runtime gives one client network. A client network is an IPv4 /24 or an IPv6 /56. Past the limit, every second answer is replaced by a truncated one (TC set, no records, as large as the query), and the others are dropped. A resolver in that network then retries over TCP, which is not limited, and is served. A victim whose address a flood forges receives nothing larger than what was sent. Default: 100. 0 means no limit. The limit is for the whole runtime: with --shards, each shard allows its share of n, since each of one network's queries goes to a shard drawn at random.

--dnssec#

Signs every zone as it is loaded (RFC 4033 to 4035). Each zone gets one key of ECDSA P-256 with SHA-256 (algorithm 13). The key is made at the first start and kept in state-dir/dns/name.dnssec/ for every shard. The runtime adds the key's DNSKEY at the apex, an NSEC chain through the names, and an RRSIG over every record set the zone holds. A signature's nonce is derived from the key and what it signs (RFC 6979), so every shard serves one set with the same signature, and a reload signs again only the sets whose bytes changed (the SOA at least, whose serial moves). The signatures last three weeks and are made again a week before they end. A query with the DO bit is answered with the signatures. A name or type that does not exist is answered with the NSEC records that prove it. A zone transfer carries them too. Give the parent zone the DS record that socketley dnssec prints.

sections.title: Names runtimes are reached by
sections.html:
Whenever the names of its runtimes change, the daemon writes them into state-dir/.dns/names. While a CA checks a DNS-01 answer, acme issue writes the answer there as acme-token. A dns runtime checks that directory once a second, as it checks its zone files. It adds to each zone the names that fall within it, with the addresses of --publish and TTL 300. It adds the DNS-01 answers as TXT records of _acme-challenge.name, with TTL 10. What the zone file says about a name wins: a name with addresses of its own, or an alias, keeps them, and nothing is added below a delegation.

socketley create dns ns --zone /etc/zones/example.com.zone \
    --publish 203.0.113.7,2001:db8::7 -s
socketley create storage files -p 9301 --domain files.example.com ...
dig files.example.com            # 203.0.113.7
dig photos.files.example.com     # 203.0.113.7

So that a secondary notices changes, a zone is served with its file's serial plus the seconds from 2023-11-14 to the last change of the published records that fall in that zone. A name published in one zone, an ACME answer or another runtime's records there, reads and signs again that zone alone; every other zone is served on as it was, with its serial and its signatures. A name without a dot falls in every zone. The served serial grows with every change of the file's serial and of the zone's published records. It is the same in every shard and after every restart.

sections.title: What it answers
sections.html:
A name that is found is answered authoritatively with its records. A CNAME is followed, up to eight steps, while its target is in the same zone. A wildcard (*.label) stands for every name below its parent that does not exist. A name below a delegation gets a referral, without the authoritative flag: the NS records of the cut, plus the addresses of those servers where the zone holds them. An absent name is answered NXDOMAIN. A name without the type asked for is answered NODATA. Both answers carry the zone's SOA, with a TTL of the lesser of its own TTL and its MINIMUM (RFC 2308). The addresses of the hosts that an NS, MX or SRV answer names follow in the additional section, when the zone has them and they fit.

ANY is answered with one HINFO record, as RFC 8482 allows, rather than with every record, so that it amplifies nothing. Classes other than IN, such as CHAOS's version.bind, are answered REFUSED. A query with EDNS (RFC 6891) is answered with EDNS. An answer over UDP stays within the size the query offers and never exceeds 1232 bytes, the size that needs no fragments. An answer to a query without EDNS stays within 512 bytes. An answer that does not fit is sent as the question alone with TC set. The client then asks again over TCP, where it gets the whole answer. A response is never answered. A malformed query is answered FORMERR, and opcodes other than QUERY are answered NOTIMP.

sections.title: TCP
sections.html: A connection may carry several queries one after another, and they are answered in order (RFC 7766). A connection that is quiet for 10 seconds, with nothing left to write, is closed. Only a whole query or a write counts as activity, so a query begun and not finished leaves the connection quiet. A shard holds at most --max-connections connections (default 256). One more connection closes the quietest connection that has nothing left to write, to make room. When a peer has not read 64 KiB of answers, its connection's further queries wait unread until it has. A connection whose answers have not moved for 30 seconds is closed.

sections.title: Stats
sections.html: stats adds these figures for each shard: zones, records, udp_queries, tcp_queries, the answers by rcode (noerror, nxdomain, refused, formerr, notimp, other_rcode), truncated, referrals, dropped (packets that were not queries), rrl_dropped and rrl_slipped, send_failed (answers the socket would not take), tcp_conns, tcp_refused, tcp_evicted (connections closed to make room for a new one), transfers, transfers_refused, notify_sent, notify_acked, notify_given_up, zone_reloads, zone_reload_failures and, with --dnssec, signatures_made and signatures_kept (taken unchanged from the signing before).

sections.title: SYNC FLAGS
sections.html:
A sync runtime is one job that carries files between a directory and a storage. Because each job is its own runtime, a job that goes wrong has its own line in socketley ls, its own figures, its own lines in the log and its own alert.

socketley create sync photos --dir /srv/photos --storage ui/photos \
    --credentials /etc/socketley/sync.creds --mode out -s

A sync runtime listens on nothing and takes no -p. --shards is refused, because the shards would share no socket and several processes would write one index.

--dir path#

The directory whose files are carried. Required. The path must be absolute, and the directory must exist when the runtime starts.

--storage target[,target...]#

Where the files go. Required. Each target takes one of three forms, with the bucket last:

Details
ui/photos#

A storage runtime of this daemon, reached on its port at 127.0.0.1. A name with no scheme and no port always names a runtime, even when it contains dots.

10.0.0.5:9000/photos#

A host and a port, over plain HTTP.

https://files.example/photos#

A URL, http or https, with nothing between the host and the bucket.

A storage runtime that serves TLS itself must be named by its URL, since its port does not speak plain HTTP. Naming it by its runtime name is refused, and the error gives the URL to use. A bucket name follows the S3 rules: 3 to 63 characters of a-z, 0-9, . and -. More than one target is accepted only with --mode out. Carrying two targets into one directory could not tell which target a file came from when they differ.

--mode out|in|inout#

Which way files are carried, in the same three words a server and a client take. out sends the directory to the storage, in brings the storage to the directory, and inout does both. Default: out.

--credentials file#

The file the job signs its requests with. Required, since a sync signs every request it makes. The file holds access_key and secret_key as key = value lines, plus session_token and region when they are needed. # begins a comment. A file that other users may read is refused, at create and at every read: chmod 600 it.

--prefix key#

The key that everything is written under, below the bucket. Default: the bucket's root.

--every duration#

How often the job walks the whole directory, and with in or inout also lists the storage. The duration is written as 30s, 10m, 1h or 1d. never walks the directory once, at start. Default: one hour. A job that brings the storage here lists it once a minute when --every is never.

Details

Between walks, inotify reports which files changed. A file is carried once it is written and closed, moved in or touched. It is removed once it is deleted. A directory that appears or disappears, or more events than the kernel keeps, causes a walk. When inotify is not available or its watches run out (fs.inotify.max_user_watches), the log says so once, and the walks alone find changes.

--repositories file#

Makes the job pull the git repositories one user keeps in a storage runtime, instead of carrying a directory. See Git repositories under STORAGE FLAGS. The job is then that user's own, and takes no --dir, --storage or --credentials. The storage runtime makes such a job for each of its users and writes the file; it is not meant to be made by hand.

--exclude pattern[,pattern...]#

Shell patterns for files and directories that are not carried, separated by commas. Spaces around the patterns are ignored: '*.tmp, *.md, node_modules'. A pattern with no slash names a file or directory at any depth, like a .gitignore line. A pattern with a slash is matched against the whole path below --dir, and its * crosses slashes. Nothing that matches is carried, and a matching directory is not walked.

What it remembers. A sync keeps an index of what it last carried, in state-dir/sync/name.index, with mode 0600. Without the index, a file deleted here could not be told apart from a file never carried. With it, the deleted file is removed from the far side and the new file is sent. Every record carries a checksum, and the first record that fails its checksum ends the file. So a crash costs at most carrying again what the last moments carried. A file is never believed carried when it was not. The index belongs to one directory and one prefix. When either changes, the index is started again: everything is carried once more and nothing is removed. socketley remove deletes the index, and a rename carries it along.

How it carries. The job sends up to eight requests at a time per target, each on a connection kept between requests, and never two requests about one file. A file above 512 MiB goes as a multipart upload in parts of 64 MiB, since one request carries at most 5 GiB. If a file changes while its parts are being sent, the upload is given up, and the file is carried again once it is written. Without TLS, a file's bytes go from the disk to the socket by splice. A link to a file is carried as the file it names. The link is removed at the walk that finds it pointing at nothing, since no event reports that a link's target is gone. A link to a directory is not followed. A --dir that holds the directory of a storage runtime it names, or lies inside it, is refused, since every object carried would be carried again.

What it takes away. A file is removed from the storage only when it is provably gone here: deleted, or a link to nothing. Three kinds of file are left where they are: a file the walk could not read, a file below a directory the walk may not enter, and a file that an --exclude names since it was carried. If a directory is empty while the index says files were carried from it, nothing is removed, and last_error says why. A disk that is not mounted looks exactly like that, and a bucket emptied because of it cannot be filled again.

Both ways. With in or inout, the job lists the storage first, at start and then at every --every. It compares each object with the index and with the file here. With inout, the walk follows each listing. A file the storage has and this side does not is brought here. It is fetched in ranges of 8 MiB, written below .socketley-sync in --dir, and given its name once it is whole. A file the storage changed since is brought again. A file the storage removed is removed here, unless it changed here since. At the start, a file that both sides have with the same length is taken to be the same file.

A file that both sides changed is kept twice, on both sides. This side's version stays at its name and is carried out over the storage's. The storage's version is kept beside it as name (conflict date time).ext. With inout, every write and removal sent carries the etag this side last saw. So if the storage made a change meanwhile, it refuses the request, and the next listing keeps both versions, rather than the later write winning. With in, nothing is carried out: a file changed here is put back as the storage has it, and this side's version is kept beside it. A key with an empty, . or .. segment is not brought. A folder that is a link out of --dir is not written through. A listing with nothing in it removes nothing here.

What a failure means. A file the storage refuses, and a target that does not answer, are counted. Each is logged once for as long as the reason stays the same. A walk thirty seconds later tries again, whatever --every says. A target that stops answering holds up only its own queue, not the others. The runtime keeps running. A sync that keeps failing for three readings in a row raises an alert, with last_error as its detail. The alert clears once something is carried again. A named runtime that is not a storage, or does not exist, is a failure of the same kind.

Its figures (socketley stats) are mode, dir, indexed (files the index holds), carried, removed, bytes_carried, waiting (what is queued), failures, failing (failures since the last thing carried), watched (directories inotify watches), brought (files brought from the storage), removed_here (files removed here because the storage removed them), conflicts (files both sides changed), last_run_secs and last_error.

sections.title: IDP FLAGS
sections.html:
An idp runtime is an OpenID Connect provider that keeps its own accounts. A user signs in once. After that, every application that asks the provider knows who they are, and so do every route a proxy puts behind it, a storage's web interface and the dashboard.

socketley create idp auth -p 9400 --domain auth.example.com \
    --clients /etc/socketley/idp.clients --cookie-domain example.com -s
socketley auth user add smiley --password - --groups admins

An account is a fixed random id plus fields with no schema. The provider reads these fields: username, password (a scrypt hash), disabled, groups (comma-separated; members of admins are admins), name, email, picture and reset. It keeps every other field as it is, for the applications. So a field an application adds needs no change here, and an older build keeps the fields it does not know. Data that only one application uses, such as a game's characters or a shop's orders, belongs in that application, under the account's id. Every change is synced to a journal under the state directory before it is answered. Changes are folded into a snapshot that names its format. A build older than that format refuses the snapshot rather than rewriting it. See idp-user under COMMANDS.

The provider serves:

  • the authorization code flow with PKCE, and refresh tokens;

  • discovery at /.well-known/openid-configuration;

  • its key at /jwks;

  • /userinfo, which answers from the account as it is now;

  • /logout;

  • /account, where a user changes their name, address and password, and signs out everywhere.

Turning a second step on or off, and making an app password, ask for the password again. Where a second step is on, they also ask for a code. These checks count as a sign-in's do, so a session alone can change neither. A second step that is on can be replaced only by turning it off. Signing out everywhere, and setting a new password, end the account's app passwords along with its sessions.

Tokens are signed ES256 with a P-256 key. The key is made at the first start and kept in the state directory, so a restart signs nobody out. A refresh token is read back only by the provider, and is signed HS256 under a secret made from that key. A refresh token is good once. A refresh gives the next token of its sign-in, which is kept with the account. A refresh token used a second time ends that sign-in, including its newest token. Passwords are hashed and checked off the event loop. The runtime uses one thread for each core it may use, up to four, shared out among its shards. Each thread computes up to four sign-ins' scrypt at once with AVX2. The provider serves plain HTTP and is reached through the entrance, which terminates TLS for its names as for every other runtime's. --tls is refused.

Guessing. Five failed sign-ins from one address within fifteen minutes refuse that address until the failures age out. An IPv6 address is counted by its /64. Sign-ins that are still being checked count with the failures, so many sign-ins sent at once are all refused. Ten failures at one account, from anywhere, make its next try wait half a minute. Each further failure doubles the wait, up to five minutes. A browser that signed in to the account before keeps a count of its own, through a provider cookie that lasts ninety days. So guesses from elsewhere never hold up the account's user. Three wrong codes end a sign-in's second step, and the password is then asked for again. Five wrong codes at an account hold up its codes, as failed passwords do.

A mail runtime checks passwords for some clients that it does not guard itself: a client on its own machine, or one behind a forwarder there. These checks are counted at the account apart from its sign-ins. Ten failures hold up the next check in the same way. At most 64 password checks wait at a shard. A sign-in past them is told to try again in a moment (503).

On several cores. With --shards N the provider is served by N worker processes on its one port (SO_REUSEPORT). Each shard signs in, gives tokens and answers /userinfo with the same key. Shard 0 writes the accounts, as a provider with one shard does. Every other shard reads shard 0's journal from the same files before it answers. So a change made with idp-user or on the account page holds at every shard once it is answered. A change made at another shard is sent to shard 0. A code is redeemed at the shard that gave it, which the code names, wherever the exchange arrives. It is good once there. A sign-in is counted at every shard while it is being checked. A failed sign-in is answered only once every shard counts it against its address and its account. So guesses sent at once over the shards share one budget. The number of shards may change across a restart.

A sign-in is a cookie of the provider's. Three kinds of runtime verify it themselves: a proxy with --auth idp:, a storage with --idp, and the dashboard with daemon.dashboard_idp. They verify it against the key the provider publishes beside its state, once for each session until it expires. They also check each account's standing, which the provider publishes there too. So a session ended at the provider ends there at once, and at those runtimes within a second. A session ends when the user signs out at /logout, signs out everywhere, or when the account is disabled.

/logout ends the session the browser sends, and any copy of its cookie, and keeps the account's other sessions. If another site sent the browser to it, the user is asked first, unless the application names the account by an id_token_hint it was given. Past 32 sessions signed out this way within their lifetimes, or for a cookie from an earlier build, a sign-out ends all of the account's sessions and its refresh tokens, as signing out everywhere does.

--clients file#

The applications that sign in through the provider, one per line. Each line is id secret redirect [redirect...]. A secret of - marks a public client, which must then send a PKCE challenge. A redirect is an https address, compared whole, or an http address on this machine (localhost, 127.0.0.1). An http address on this machine is taken at any port, since an application on the machine picks its port as it runs.

Details

In place of a redirect, device lets the client sign a person in by the device grant, as socketley login does. One address, or one IPv6 /48, may hold at most twenty grants waiting at a shard. ssh lets the client's access tokens ask for SSH certificates. The file is read again when it changes. If it breaks while the runtime runs, the clients read before stay in use.

--ssh-ca hours#

Runs an SSH certificate authority that gives user certificates lasting hours (1 to 168). Its Ed25519 key is made at the first start and kept in the state directory. The public key is served at /ssh/ca.pub. /ssh/user-cert gives a user certificate for the account whose access token is sent. A certificate is given only to a client marked ssh, never to a disabled account, and never on a sign-in more than twelve hours old, refreshed tokens included. Such a sign-in is told to sign in again. A user certificate permits a terminal, port forwarding and agent forwarding. It permits neither X11 forwarding nor the user's ~/.ssh/rc. Every certificate is logged with its serial, the account, its principals and the key's fingerprint. It is kept until it expires so that it can be revoked (see idp-ssh revoke). See ssh-cert and idp-ssh.

--issuer url#

The https address the provider is reached at, which every token names. Default: https://name for the first --domain.

--resources list#

The resource servers an access token may be given for (RFC 8707), as comma-separated https addresses. An example is https://mcp.example.com/mcp. An application that sends resource with one of them at /authorize gets an access token that names that resource as its audience. A runtime that takes tokens for its own clients does not take such a token; an mcp runtime with --idp does.

Details

With any resource set, an application may also sign in with the https address of its client metadata document as its client id, as MCP clients such as Claude Code do. The document is fetched from public addresses only, and is at most five kilobytes. It is kept as long as its Cache-Control says, within a minute and a day. It is taken only for a public client that sends a PKCE challenge, with redirects that are https or on this machine. Such an application is let in only for one of these resources. It is let in only once the signed-in person allows it, every time it asks. The page that asks names the application, its host, the resource and where the person is sent back to. stats counts consents, client_fetches and client_fetch_failures.

--cookie-domain domain#

The domain whose names share the sign-in cookie. A user signed in here is then signed in for a proxy, a storage or the dashboard on any name below it. Default: the cookie is for the provider's host alone.

--shards N#

The number of worker processes that serve the provider, 1 to 64. Shard 0 writes the accounts, and every shard signs in (see On several cores above). The number can change only while the runtime is stopped.

An address that failed to sign in five times in fifteen minutes is refused until the oldest of those failures is fifteen minutes old. When the request came through a proxy on this machine, the address counted is the last address that X-Forwarded-For names.

sections.title: DB FLAGS
sections.html:
A db runtime keeps JSON documents for applications, such as a game's characters, a shop's orders and addresses, or a user's settings. Each document is owned by an account of an idp runtime. An account never writes another account's documents, and each collection's access in --schema says who reads them. Large things, such as a picture or a model, belong in a storage, with their address kept here.

socketley create db data -p 9500 --domain data --idp auth \
    --schema /etc/socketley/db.schema --keys /etc/socketley/db.keys -s
socketley create db copy -p 9500 --replicate https://data.example.com \
    --replicate-key /etc/socketley/db.replica-key --keys /etc/socketley/db.keys -s

A document lives at /c/collection/id. GET reads it, PUT replaces it, PATCH changes it in place and DELETE removes it. A POST to /c/collection makes a new document under a new id. The answer holds the document's fields plus _id, _v (its version: 1 when made, one more with each change, and also its ETag) and _owner (the account's id). If-Match: "3" writes only at that version, and If-None-Match: * writes only where no document exists. Otherwise the answer is 412. A patch looks like {"set":{"a.b":1},"unset":["c"],"inc":{"n":1},"push":{"tags":"x"},"pull":{"tags":"y"}} and works on dotted paths.

POST /c/collection/_query takes a query such as {"where":{"level":{"gte":5},"name":"x"},"sort":"-level","limit":50,"skip":0}. The conditions are eq, ne, gt, gte, lt, lte, in, prefix and exists. count :true answers the number alone. The answer is {"docs":[...]}, plus next when there are more. A range compares a field's values of one kind only, in the order an index uses: null, false, true, numbers, strings. A condition or a sort on a field the schema does not index is judged by reading the documents. The query reads at most 8 MiB of them, unless a key asks for more. Past that, it is refused with 400 needs_index: index the field. POST /tx takes {"ops":[{"op":"put","c":..,"id":..,"doc":{..}},{"op":"patch",..,"changes":{..},"if":3},{"op":"insert",..},{"op":"delete",..}]} and makes every change or none. GET /me names who is asking.

A request comes from one of three kinds of caller:

  • a key, sent as Authorization: Bearer secret, which reaches everything;

  • an account of the --idp runtime, by its sign-in cookie or by an access token the provider gave one of its clients, sent as Authorization: Bearer;

  • nobody.

A write made with the cookie must be application/json and come from the database's own host or an origin in --origins. A form that another site posts cannot meet that. A document over 1 MiB, or nested deeper than 16 levels, is refused.

The documents live on the disk, in segments under the state directory. Each write is one record, appended to the newest segment. A segment is closed at 64 MiB and another is begun. Memory holds where each document lies, its version, its owner and the values its indexes order it by. Memory also holds a cache of the documents last read (--cache). The rest are read from the disk, so a database holds far more than memory.

A read may need a document that the page cache does not hold. Such a read is first tried without it, the document is brought in through the ring, and the read is answered then. So a slow disk holds up that read and not every other. Past three tries, the read waits in line. stats counts these reads as fetched. Some sealed segments have mostly been written again or deleted. They are merged off the event loop into one segment of their living documents, and the old segments are removed. A record torn by a crash ends the newest segment where the last whole record ends. Damage anywhere else refuses the start, so the database must be restored.

No answer is given before what it rests on is on the disk: a write's own record, or the change a read saw. So nothing is read that a crash could take back. One sync runs at a time, off the event loop. It covers every record written while the previous sync ran. So a burst of writes costs a few syncs rather than one each, and reads go on being answered meanwhile. A read behind a write on one connection is answered after the write. A script of this daemon reaches the documents as socketley.db. The runtime serves plain HTTP behind the entrance.

On several cores. With --shards N the database is served by N worker processes on its one port (SO_REUSEPORT). Shard 0 writes the one log, as a database with one shard does. Every other shard reads that log from the same files, as shard 0 puts it on the disk. Those shards answer reads, queries and streams themselves, and send writes to shard 0. A write is answered once it is on shard 0's disk. Before a shard answers, it takes in what shard 0 has made durable. So a read on any shard sees every write that was answered before the read began. Transactions, unique indexes, streams, replicas and backups hold as they do on one shard. The number of shards may change across a restart, since the documents are one log whatever the number.

Every shard answers reads and queries. Writes wait for one disk, so the shards together take at most as many writes as one shard takes. Writes also cost more cores than on one shard, since each write that reaches another shard is handed on to shard 0, and its answer is handed back. A database that is mostly written is served best by one shard.

Every request a reading shard takes reads the log on first. A shard that holds a stream is also told by shard 0 of each change that reaches the disk, so the stream hears of it before the next request. stats counts these messages in shard 0's nudges.

Changes, as they happen. GET /c/collection/_feed is a stream of Server-Sent Events, which a browser reads with EventSource. Each change is sent once it is on the disk, numbered by the change. A change is an event put with {"collection":..,"id":..,"owner":..,"version":..,"doc":{..}} or an event delete with {"collection":..,"id":..,"deleted":true}. The reader sees only what it may read, as with a query: an account sees its own documents of an owner collection. GET /_feed streams the changes of every collection, to a key. A stream that broke resumes from the last change it read, with Last-Event-ID (or ?since=). While a stream is open on any shard, and for two minutes after the last one closed, the database keeps about 32 MiB of changes on every shard, so a stream that resumes may reach any of them. With no stream near, shard 0 keeps about 1 MiB and a shard reading its log keeps none. A stream resuming from an older change is told reset and should read again what it shows. stats gives each shard's history_bytes. A comment every fifteen seconds keeps a quiet stream from looking dead.

Documents with a time to go. A collection whose schema line names ttl:field loses a document once that field's number, in seconds since 1970, has passed. From that moment the document is answered as absent. Its deletion is written and streamed within the minute.

A copy on another machine. A db runtime with --replicate follows another database's /_replicate stream, with a key of that database. It takes every document once, then every change. It writes them to its own disk with each change's own number, so after a restart of either side it goes on where it was. When the source no longer keeps the changes the replica missed, the source sends everything again. A replica answers reads, queries and streams of its own. It refuses writes with 403, naming where to make them. Removing --replicate (import --restart) makes it a database of its own.

Backups. socketley db-backup db file writes every document into one file, off the event loop, while the database serves. socketley db-restore db file stops the database, keeps its documents aside in dir.before-restore, and starts it again on the backup's documents. With --backup-dir, a backup is taken every --backup-every, and the newest --backup-keep backups are kept. A sync runtime can carry that directory to a storage.

--schema file#

The collections, one per line: a name, who reaches it, and the fields indexed. unique: before a field marks an index whose values no two documents share.

Details
# collection  access   indexes
characters    owner    level unique:name
posts         shared   created
scores        public   score
products      catalog  unique:sku price
sessions      owner    ttl:expires_at

The access is one of these: private (and any collection the file does not name): only a key reaches it. owner: an account reads and writes its own documents, and another account's documents are answered as not there. shared: an account reads every document and writes its own. public: anybody reads, and an account writes its own. catalog: anybody reads, and a key writes. The file is read again when it changes. If the new file does not read, or a unique index is broken by the documents already there, the previous schema stays, and stats says why.

--keys file#

Service keys for backends, one per line: name secret. The secret must be at least 16 characters. The file is read again when it changes. A key may set a document's _owner.

--idp runtime#

The idp runtime whose accounts own documents.

--idp-audience clients#

The ids of the idp's clients whose access tokens the runtime takes, comma-separated. A token the provider gave any other application is refused, since it belongs to that application and is no key to this runtime. Without the flag no access token is taken, while keys and the sign-in cookie reach it as before.

--origins list#

The web origins a browser may call the database from, comma-separated. They are answered with CORS and the browser's sign-in. * allows any page, without the sign-in.

--max-bytes size#

The most the documents may hold. A write past it is refused with 507.

--cache size#

The memory that holds the documents last read. Default: 64M. The rest are read from the disk. With --shards, it is the runtime's: each shard caches its share, the size divided by the shard count, and at least 1 MiB. stats shows each shard's share as cache_limit, and how often a document was found there and not as cache_hits and cache_misses.

--replicate url#

The http or https address of the database this one copies, as its entrance answers it. An https address is verified against the system's roots.

--replicate-key file#

A file holding the secret of a key of that database.

--backup-dir dir#

The directory scheduled backups are written to, each as name-time.dbbackup.

--backup-every duration#

How often a scheduled backup is taken. Default: 1d.

--backup-keep n#

How many scheduled backups are kept. Default: 7.

--shards N#

The number of worker processes that serve the database, 1 to 64. Shard 0 writes, and every shard reads (see On several cores above). The number can change only while the runtime is stopped.

In a script:

local c, err = socketley.db.get("data", "characters", id)
socketley.db.put("data", "characters", id, { name = "Merlin", level = 3 }, { ["if"] = c._v })
socketley.db.patch("data", "characters", id, { inc = { level = 1 } })
local r = socketley.db.query("data", "scores", { sort = "-score", limit = 10 })
socketley.db.insert("data", "orders", { item = "sword" })
socketley.db.delete("data", "orders", id)
socketley.db.tx("data", { { op = "put", c = "a", id = "x", doc = {} }, { op = "delete", c = "b", id = "y" } })

Each function answers the document (or the transaction's results), or nil, an error code and a sentence. Inside a callback that can wait, the call waits. Anywhere else, the last argument is a function that is called with the answer.

sections.title: MQTT FLAGS
sections.html:
An mqtt runtime is an MQTT broker for versions 3.1, 3.1.1 and 5.0, over TCP, TLS and WebSocket. Devices, apps and browsers publish to topics and subscribe to them. A client that goes away keeps its session until it comes back or the session expires. The session holds its subscriptions and the messages sent to them while the client was gone. The broker is a runtime like the others. Its own rules pass messages to a cache, a db, a storage, a server or another broker. A storage's events and a script's messages reach its subscribers.

socketley mqtt passwd /etc/socketley/mqtt.users sensor-17
socketley create mqtt broker --users /etc/socketley/mqtt.users \
    --acl /etc/socketley/mqtt.acl --ws 8083 --persistent on -s
socketley create mqtt devices -p 8883 --tls --cert dev.pem --key dev.key \
    --ca devices-ca.pem --routes /etc/socketley/mqtt.routes -s

The broker listens on 1883, or on 8883 with --tls, unless -p gives another port. --max-connections and --write-buffer work as for a server. When a slow client owes more than the write buffer, its QoS 0 messages are dropped and counted, and its QoS 1 and 2 messages wait in its session.

Over TLS 1.3, the first packet of 256 KiB or more that a client is sent hands its connection's send key to the kernel's TLS layer. From then on the kernel encrypts what the client is sent, and a payload goes from the one copy of the message every subscriber sends from, as it does without TLS (see SOCKETLEY_KERNEL_TLS).

What it implements. The broker implements:

  • QoS 0, 1 and 2. QoS 2 is delivered exactly once, by its packet identifier.

  • Retained messages, cleared by an empty one.

  • Wills. A will is sent when a connection is lost, or when a 5.0 client disconnects and asks for it. It is not sent when the client disconnects cleanly. A 5.0 will delay is waited out if one is given, and the will is not sent at all when the client comes back within it.

  • Sessions, kept by 3.1.1's clean session 0 and by 5.0's session expiry. A client id has one connection. A second connection takes the session over, and the first is told so. A session belongs to its user, so a CONNECT under another user (or none) is refused as not authorized.

  • Keep alive: a client that is silent for one and a half times its keep alive is disconnected.

  • A CONNECT is required within ten seconds; otherwise the connection is closed.

  • From 5.0: session and message expiry, the receive maximum both ways, topic aliases, the maximum packet size, subscription identifiers, no local, retain as published, and retain handling.

  • From 5.0: shared subscriptions ($share/group/filter, each message to one member, in turn), and request and response (the response topic and correlation data are carried).

  • From 5.0: user properties, the content type and the payload format, and reason codes and strings on what it refuses.

The wildcards + and # do not match a topic that begins with $. The broker publishes its own figures, retained, under $SYS/broker/ every ten seconds: version, uptime, clients, messages and subscriptions. It does not take the 5.0 AUTH exchange: a CONNECT that names an authentication method is refused with 0x8C. It does not bridge to brokers outside the daemon.

Who may connect. At least one of --users, --idp, --ca or --anonymous must be given. A client certificate that --ca verified lets its client in under the certificate's common name. A password is checked against the users file, off the event loop. Otherwise, with --idp, the password is taken as an access token that provider gave a client --idp-audience names, and the token account's name is the user. A user name given with the token must be that name. Without credentials, a client is let in only with --anonymous. A refusal is 0x86 (bad user name or password), or 4 to a 3.1.1 client. A script's on_auth has the last word (see Lua below).

What each may do. --acl names rules in Mosquitto's form. The broker reads them again within two seconds of a change:

# before any user line: clients without one
topic read public/#
user alice
topic readwrite home/alice/#
topic write telemetry/#
topic deny telemetry/secret/#
pattern readwrite users/%u/#
pattern write devices/%c/state

topic [read|write|readwrite|deny] filter applies to the user named last. pattern applies to everyone. In a pattern, %u stands for the user and %c for the client id, each as one level. A deny wins over any grant, and what no rule grants is refused. A refused publish is answered 0x87 to a 5.0 client. To a 3.1.1 client, it is acknowledged and dropped. A subscription is refused only when no rule grants all of it. A message that a deny covers is held back from a subscription that the deny covers in part. Without --acl, every client may do everything.

Sessions across a restart. With --persistent, the broker writes a snapshot every --persistent-interval when something changed, off the event loop, and at stop. The snapshot holds the sessions, their queues and messages in flight, the retained messages and the topic rules' queues. A start reads them back. So a stop, a restart of the daemon or a killed worker loses at most one interval. At the start that finds them, a session with no expiry left is ended, and the wills it was owed are sent. Without --persistent, the broker keeps nothing across a restart.

Topic rules. --routes names a file of rules, one per line, each a filter and a target. Every message the filter matches is handed to another runtime of the daemon, besides the broker's own subscribers:

# filter          target
sensor/+/temp     cache://telemetry/stream/temps-%1
alarm/#           cache://events/channel/alarms
device/+/state    db://fleet/devices/%1
log/#             storage://raw/mqtt/%Y/%m/%d/
chat/#            server://chat
share/#           mqtt://other/from-edge/%t
door/#            https://hooks.example.com/door

  • cache://runtime/stream/key adds a stream entry with the fields topic, payload, qos and client.

  • cache://runtime/channel/name publishes the payload on the channel.

  • db://runtime/collection[/id] puts a document under id when given, and as a new document otherwise. The document is the payload when the payload is a JSON object, and otherwise {"topic":..,"payload":..,"client":..,"qos":..}.

  • storage://runtime/bucket[/prefix] gathers the messages as JSON lines, {"at":..,"topic":..,"payload":..,"qos":..,"client":..}, into one .ndjson object a minute (or a megabyte, or at stop) under the prefix.

  • server://runtime sends every client of the server {"topic":..,"payload":..} as a line.

  • mqtt://runtime/topic publishes on that broker, at the message's QoS and retained as it was. A message that has passed eight such rules on its way is passed on by no more of them, so rules that lead to each other end.

  • http:// or https:// URL POSTs {"topic":..,"payload":..,"qos":..,"retain":..,"client":..} to the URL, one at a time and in order, on a connection it keeps. The host is resolved on the broker's loop (see What can stop the event loop). A 2xx counts as delivered. A 400 or another refusal is counted as failed and not sent again. No answer, a 408, a 429 or a 5xx is tried again, as for a stopped runtime.

    %1 to %9 stand for the levels the filter's + matched, %t for the whole topic and %c for the client that published. A storage prefix also takes %Y, %m, %d, %H and %M. A line beginning with # is a comment, and so is a # after a target. The file is read at start. A file that does not read stops the runtime, and the error names the line.

    Each rule has a queue of its own, in order. A target that is stopped or does not answer holds its messages, without holding up the broker or the other rules. The rule tries again after a pause that grows to five seconds. It holds up to 100000 messages; past that, the oldest are dropped and counted. What a rule holds goes into the snapshot, with messages in flight in their place, so a restart sends them again. A target gets each message at least once. stats names each rule with what it delivered, what its target refused, what was dropped, what it holds and its last error.

From the other runtimes. socketley mqtt-pub and a script's socketley.mqtt.publish publish as the broker itself. A storage's mqtt://runtime/topic notification target publishes the storage's events (see --notify-targets). The mqtt:// rules of another broker publish that broker's messages:

local ok, err = socketley.mqtt.publish("broker", "game/" .. id .. "/move", move, { qos = 1 })
socketley.mqtt.publish("broker", "chat/lobby", text, { retain = false }, function(ok, err) end)

The call answers true once the broker has the message, or nil and the reason. Inside a callback that can wait, it waits. Anywhere else, the last argument is a function that is called with the answer.

WebSocket. --ws port serves MQTT inside WebSocket on a second port, for browsers. Any path works, and /mqtt is the convention. The subprotocol mqtt or mqttv3.1 is chosen when offered. A packet may be carried in any number of frames, and a frame may hold any number of packets. A frame may be no longer than four times --max-packet. With --tls, it is wss.

On several cores. With --shards N the broker is N worker processes sharing its ports (SO_REUSEPORT), and its clients see one broker. Each shard tells the others what its clients subscribe to, and hands them the messages their subscribers want. Every shard keeps each retained message. A shared subscription's message goes to one member of the group, across all the shards. A client that connects to a different shard than before takes its session with it. The newest connection of a client id wins. A message still on its way to the shard a session left is handed on to the shard it went to, once, for ten seconds after the move; these are counted in session_forwards. A SUBACK for a filter the other shards do not know yet waits until every shard that answers has taken it, so a message published anywhere after the SUBACK reaches the subscriber. It waits a second at most, and then goes anyway. The SUBACKs that waited are counted in subacks_held, and those that went after the second in subacks_unheard. A connection whose old session does not come within three seconds is let in without it, as a new session. When the session comes later, it is folded into the new one: its subscriptions are added, and its queued and unanswered messages are sent first, with new packet identifiers. If the new session began with a clean start, the old one ends instead. A shard that is asked more than fifteen seconds late hands the session over once it hears of the new connection. These are counted in sessions_late, sessions_yielded and sessions_late_ended. A session handed over this way that is larger than 1 MiB goes in pieces of 1 MiB, so none is ended for its size; these are counted in sessions_pieced. A session moves as one answer to the claim when the way back carries it. When shards relay through the daemon (see SOCKETLEY_NO_SHARD_MESH), that answer holds 8 MiB, less what the shard still has queued to the daemon past 68 MiB. A larger session goes in pieces of 1 MiB the same way, and the connection waits for them as long as they keep coming, so a client is let in on whichever shard it lands on with its session whatever its size; these too are counted in sessions_pieced. When two connections of one client claim its session at once, the newer one keeps it: a session the older one was given meanwhile is passed on to the newer one's shard, with what was still on its way to it, counted in sessions_yielded. Relaying through the daemon also holds a packet to 8 MiB less 256 KiB, however large --max-packet is; the broker says so in its CONNACK, and a larger packet is refused as one past --max-packet is. A shard that starts is given the retained messages by shard 0 in as many answers as they take, each no longer than the way carries; one longer than the daemon carries is not given to it, and is counted in shard_dropped.

A shard may not take what another shard hands it as fast as it comes. It then holds back that other shard's publishers, rather than lose their messages: they are not read until it can take more. At QoS 1 and 2 this holds back all of them, and at QoS 0 those whose last message went to it. A shard that has answered nothing for a second holds back only QoS 1 and 2 publishers, whose answer waits. A message for that shard is then dropped at QoS 0, or once 8 MiB wait for it. At any QoS, a message is dropped once what the shard was handed has failed for three seconds. So is a message whose shared groups make it too large for the daemon to carry to a shard. Drops are counted in shard_dropped. Each shard keeps a snapshot of its own, file.shard, and publishes its figures under $SYS/broker/shard/n/.

Lua. A broker's --lua script may decide who connects and what passes. Each hook that decides answers true to allow, false to refuse, or nothing to keep what the broker decided. A hook that fails refuses. A client is a table of id, username, peer and version.

function on_auth(c)          -- c.id c.username c.password c.peer
    if c.username == "robot" then return c.password == "beep" end
end                          -- c.certificate c.authenticated c.account c.version
function on_publish(client, msg)              -- msg.topic msg.payload msg.qos msg.retain
    if msg.topic == "shout" then return { payload = string.upper(msg.payload) } end
end
function on_subscribe(client, filter, qos) return filter ~= "secret/#" end
function on_connect(client) self.publish("presence/" .. client.id, "online", { retain = true }) end
function on_disconnect(client, why) self.publish("presence/" .. client.id, "offline", { retain = true }) end

on_auth is told whether the credentials checked out (authenticated) and as whom (account). If it lets in a client whose credentials were refused, the user name the client gave becomes its user. on_publish may also answer a table: the message as it is to go on, with any of topic, payload, qos and retain. A refused publish is answered 0x87. self.publish(topic, payload [, {qos=, retain=}]) publishes as the broker. self.retained(topic) reads a retained payload. self.sessions() lists this shard's sessions. self.kick(client_id [, end]) disconnects one. While a hook decides, that connection's next packets wait.

--users file#

The accounts that sign in with a password, one user:hash per line, as socketley mqtt passwd writes them. The file is read again within two seconds of a change.

--idp runtime#

The idp runtime whose access tokens, given as the password, sign clients in. It takes only tokens given to a client that --idp-audience names.

--idp-audience clients#

The ids of the idp's clients whose access tokens the runtime takes, comma-separated. A token the provider gave any other application is refused, since it belongs to that application and is no key to this runtime. Without the flag no access token is taken, while the users file and client certificates sign in as before.

--acl file#

Who may publish and subscribe to what (see What each may do above).

--anonymous#

Lets in clients without credentials, as far as the rules allow.

--routes file#

Where messages go besides their subscribers (see Topic rules above).

--ws port#

A second port, which serves MQTT over WebSocket.

--persistent file|on#

The snapshot file that sessions and retained messages are kept in. on means state/mqtt/name.snapshot under the state directory.

--persistent-interval duration#

How often changes are written to the snapshot. Default: 1s.

--max-packet size#

The largest packet a client may send, from 64 bytes to 256M. Default: 256K. A larger packet is answered 0x95, and the connection is closed. The limit is told to 5.0 clients. No message larger than a client says it takes is sent to that client.

--session-expiry duration#

The longest a session outlives its connection, whatever the client asks. Default: 1d. A 3.1.1 session kept by clean session 0 lasts this long.

--session-queue n#

The most messages kept for one session while its client is away or slow. Default: 1000. Past it, the oldest are dropped and counted.

--retained-max size#

The most bytes that retained messages may take. Default: 64M. A new retained message past it is not kept, and is counted.

--max-sessions n#

The most sessions, connected or not. Default: 100000. A new client past the limit makes the broker look at the owner that holds the most sessions. An owner is a user or, for clients without one, an address (IPv6 by its /64). If that owner holds two or more, the broker ends its session that has been away longest, and counts it as sessions_evicted. So one owner filling the table locks nobody else out. Otherwise the new client is refused with 0x97.

--keepalive-max seconds#

The longest keep alive the broker grants. Default: 1200. A 5.0 client that asks for more, or for none, is told this value.

A client that leaves more than twice --write-buffer (default 8M) of what it was sent unread is not read until it has read half of it. So its pings and acks cannot grow what it is owed.

stats reports:

  • the sessions, and how many are connected;

  • the subscriptions, the retained messages and their bytes;

  • what is queued and in flight;

  • the messages received and sent at each QoS, and what was dropped and why;

  • the connects and the refusals;

  • the snapshots, and whether a change is in none yet;

  • each topic rule;

  • over shards, what was handed between them.
