sections.title: Runtime Methods (in Lua)
sections.html:
-- Every type
self.name      -- Runtime name (read-only)
self.port      -- Port number (read-only)
self.state     -- Current state (read-only)
self.type      -- Runtime type (read-only)
self.connections()         -- Current connection count (all four types).
                              With --shards, the whole runtime's count summed
                              across its worker processes, not the shard's own

self.protocol  -- server/client: "tcp" or "udp"; proxy: "tcp" or "http"
               -- (not set on a cache)
self.send(msg [, id])      -- Send message (client).  Without an id, on the
                           -- connection whose callback is running; with
                           -- --connections, refused outside every callback
self.send(client_id, msg)  -- Send to specific client (server)
self.broadcast(msg)        -- Broadcast to all clients (server).  Answers two
                           -- numbers: how many took it, and how many were
                           -- dropped because their queue was full.  See below.
self.pending(client_id)    -- Queued for that client and not yet on the wire,
                           -- in bytes (server); nil if the id is not one of
                           -- this runtime's connections.  See below.
self.respond_stream(id, status, headers)
                           -- Begin a response this script will write itself,
                           -- chunk by chunk (server).  See below.
self.send_chunk(id, data)  -- One chunk of it; false means it was not taken
self.end_response(id)      -- The last chunk has gone; finish the response
self.watermark()           -- The byte count on_writable fires on the way down
                           -- through (server and client).  Pace against this,
                           -- not a literal.  A call and not a field, because
                           -- --write-buffer is editable.  See on_writable.
on_http_body(id, chunk, n) -- A request body streamed, rather than gathered
                           -- whole (server).  Defining it is the opt-in.
self.pending([id])         -- The client's own form.  Bytes queued for its
                           -- server and not yet on the wire: for that id (nil
                           -- if it has none), or without one the connection
                           -- whose callback is running, or all of them
                           -- outside every callback.

-- ─── Sending faster than the socket ───
-- A write is queued, not performed, and the queue has a bound.  Reach it and
-- the runtime closes the connection -- which used to be the only way a script
-- found out: the message that filled the queue was dropped and answered true,
-- and the one after it was refused with "there is no open connection", the
-- sentence a peer hanging up gets.
--
-- self.send() now answers false for a message that was not taken, and names
-- the backlog when that is the reason, so a producer can tell "slow down" from
-- "it is gone".  self.pending() is the number to watch BEFORE sending, which
-- is the difference between pacing and a post-mortem:
--
--     if (self.pending(id) or 0) >= self.watermark() then return end
--
-- and on_writable(id) is how a producer that stopped there is started again,
-- which is what makes a body past the bound sendable rather than merely
-- survivable.  See on_writable in CALLBACKS.
--
-- self.broadcast() has the same bound at its own door, and used to report
-- nothing at all: a broadcast to 3000 clients that dropped a third of them was
-- indistinguishable from one that reached every single one.  It answers two
-- numbers now --
--
--     local taken, behind = self.broadcast(msg)
--
-- counting THIS shard's connections, which is the scope a script can act on; a
-- held message counts as taken, because an unclassified connection's hold is a
-- deferred take and not a drop.  And a client dropped by the broadcast gets
-- the backlog sentence from a later self.send() rather than the peer's, which
-- it did not before -- one flag, both entrances.
--
-- Measured with a client that connects and never reads, against 400 chunks of
-- 64 KB: 129 taken, 271 refused, and the queue standing at its bound.

-- ─── A response written rather than returned ───
-- on_http_request has to RETURN its body, so a generated answer had to fit in
-- memory.  A FILE of any size was already served by the splice path and a Range
-- of it by the 206 path; a generated one of any size was not expressible at all
-- -- transcoding, an export assembled from a cache, a CSV of ten million rows.
--
--     self.respond_stream(id, 200, {["Content-Type"] = "text/csv"})
--     for row in rows() do
--         if (self.pending(id) or 0) >= self.watermark() then return end   -- wait
--         self.send_chunk(id, row)
--     end
--     self.end_response(id)
--
-- Paced through self.pending()/on_writable like any other producer, which is
-- what makes it a stream rather than a slower way to run out of memory.
-- Measured: 200 MB of generated rows through an 8 MiB queue, delivered in
-- 51,200 chunks with on_writable resuming it 67 times, for 6 MB of resident
-- memory.
--
-- The handler returns nothing after starting one: the response is already on
-- its way, and the static-file and 404 fallbacks are skipped for this request.
-- A handler that only tried to send a chunk has NOT answered, so its ordinary
-- return still applies.
--
-- Content-Length, Transfer-Encoding and Connection are dropped from the header
-- table if given: a Content-Length beside a chunked body is a message carrying
-- two answers to its own length, which this server refuses with a 400 on the
-- way in.  Measured with it passed through: the client read 119 bytes where 5
-- were sent, having believed the wrong header.
--
-- send_chunk on a HEAD request answers false and names it, rather than dropping
-- the bytes: a HEAD asked for the headers and nothing else, and a script that
-- thinks it is sending a body to one has a bug this refusal is the only report
-- of.  An empty chunk is accepted and not sent, because a zero-length chunk is
-- how the terminator is spelled on the wire -- passing one through as payload
-- would end the response while the script was still writing it.

-- A question whose answer is somewhere else (server with --cache)
self.cache(command)        -- Run one command against the LINKED cache and
                           -- answer with what it said.  The handler STOPS here
                           -- and goes on when the reply arrives; the daemon
                           -- keeps serving meanwhile.  nil plus a reason when
                           -- the answer is not coming.

-- ─── A handler that waits ───
-- In a handler that can wait, a call that reaches outside the runtime
-- (self.cache, socketley.http) suspends the handler until the answer comes,
-- and the runtime keeps serving other clients meanwhile.
--
--     function on_client_message(id, msg)
--         local v, err = self.cache("get " .. msg)
--         self.send(id, v or ("miss: " .. err))
--     end
--
-- The handler runs on a coroutine.  At the call it suspends, the request goes
-- to the cache, and the event loop carries on with every other connection and
-- every other runtime; when the reply lands the handler picks up at the same
-- line with the answer as that call's return value.  Nothing else in the script
-- changes, and a handler that never calls it is not affected: a callback that
-- runs straight through costs the same as it did, measured at 0.158 us against
-- 0.161 for the plain call it replaced, because the coroutines are pooled.
--
-- Where it may be called from: on_message and on_client_message.  Anywhere
-- else -- a timer, on_http_request, a filter -- answers nil and says so,
-- because those call sites still expect an answer on the spot.
--
-- Three things are guaranteed, and each exists because the shape without it
-- was reachable:
--
--   * It always returns.  A cache that accepts the request and never answers
--     leaves the handler stopped for ever otherwise -- measured against a
--     SIGSTOPped cache worker, whose request is parked against a ticket nothing
--     completes.  After ten seconds the call answers nil, "timeout".
--
--   * The connection is still there.  While the handler waits, the connection
--     it is answering is held open exactly as a client's own `cache get` is:
--     a promised reply, which the close path defers on.  Without it every
--     `echo | nc` fails, because the peer half-closes the moment it has sent
--     its line and the answer does not exist yet.
--
--   * It cannot pile up.  4096 stopped callbacks per runtime, and a server that
--     is already owed as many answers as one connection may have refuses the
--     call with a reason rather than stopping the handler.
--
-- The command is the cache's own text protocol, so the answer is that
-- protocol's: `get` on a key that is not there answers the string "nil" rather
-- than a Lua nil, which is the same answer a client reading the port gets.
-- Upstream actions (server with -u)
self.upstream_send(conn_id, msg) -- Send to a specific upstream; false means
                                 -- the bytes are not going.  See below.
self.upstream_broadcast(msg)     -- Send to all connected upstreams.  Answers how
                                 -- many took it and how many were dropped
self.upstream_pending(conn_id)   -- Bytes queued for that upstream and not yet on
                                 -- the wire; nil if the id is not one of this
                                 -- runtime's upstreams
self.upstreams()                 -- Table of connected upstream conn_ids

-- ─── The same bound, pointed outwards ───
-- An upstream's write queue fills exactly as a client's does, and these used to
-- report none of it.  upstream_send() tested only whether the upstream was
-- connected; a queue that reached the bound sets `closing` and leaves
-- `connected` alone, so every later send answered TRUE for ever while nothing
-- left the process.  Measured, 400 sends of 64 KB at an upstream that accepted
-- the connection and then read nothing:
--
--     before   sent=400  failed=0    with 8,396,928 bytes standing in the queue
--     after    sent=129  failed=271  the same 129/271 the client-facing side
--                                    reports, because it is the same bound
--
-- The refusal names the backlog apart from a missing upstream, because "is not
-- connected" is false of a connected upstream whose queue this runtime filled --
-- and the two want opposite reactions.  Pace with self.upstream_pending() and
-- not self.pending(): that one resolves a CLIENT id, and an upstream is in
-- another map entirely.
--
-- on_upstream_writable(conn_id) is the other half, and without it the number
-- above is only a post-mortem: a producer could ask how deep the queue was and
-- never be told when there was room.  The same 400 sends of 64 KB, at an
-- upstream that reads:
--
--     unpaced   sent=129  failed=271   and the upstream closed
--     paced     sent=400  refused=0    resumed 6 times
--
-- Same messages, same bound, same upstream.  129 of 400 is what a producer that
-- does not look gets, and it is not a limit on how much can be sent.

-- Cache: mode
-- A call and not a field, because --mode is editable and a field written when
-- this table was built would go stale.  "readonly", "readwrite" or "admin" --
-- the same three names --mode, `show` and the wire protocol use.
self.cache_mode()   -- Which mode this cache is in

-- Cache: which keys are this process's
-- Under --shards the script runs in all N workers and the calls below act only
-- on the slice this one owns, answering a foreign key the way they answer a
-- refusal.  True for every key when the cache is one process.
self.owns(key)      -- Does this shard own the key?

-- Cache: strings
self.get(key)       -- Get string value
self.set(key, val)  -- Set string value; false in readonly mode
self.del(key)       -- Delete key (any type); false in readonly mode
self.exists(key)    -- Is the key there?  See below.

-- Cache: lists
self.lpush(key, val)        -- Push to front; false in readonly mode
self.rpush(key, val)        -- Push to back; false in readonly mode
self.lpop(key)              -- Pop from front; "" in readonly mode
self.rpop(key)              -- Pop from back; "" in readonly mode
self.llen(key)              -- List length

-- Cache: sets
self.sadd(key, member)      -- 1 added, 0 already a member,
                            -- nil refused (readonly mode)
self.srem(key, member)      -- Remove member; false in readonly mode
self.sismember(key, member) -- Check membership
self.scard(key)             -- Set cardinality

-- Cache: hashes
self.hset(key, field, val)  -- Set hash field; false in readonly mode
self.hget(key, field)       -- Get hash field
self.hdel(key, field)       -- Delete hash field; false in readonly mode
self.hexists(key, field)    -- Is the field there?  See below.
self.hlen(key)              -- Hash field count

-- Cache: TTL
self.expire(key, seconds)   -- Set expiry; false in readonly mode
self.ttl(key)               -- Get remaining TTL
self.persist(key)           -- Remove expiry; false in readonly mode

-- Cache: pub/sub
-- Under --shards the message reaches every shard's subscribers, but the count
-- is this shard's own: the siblings answer on a later turn and this call
-- answers on the turn it was made.
self.publish(channel, msg)  -- Publish to channel; returns this shard's count

-- Server: connection control
-- Every mutator below answers `true`, or `false, "reason"`.  They returned
-- nothing at all before, so an id that named no connection was a silent no-op.
self.disconnect(client_id)         -- Terminate a connection from Lua
self.peer_ip(client_id)            -- Get client IP (IPv4 or IPv6 string)
                                   -- also on a proxy, same meaning
self.ws_headers(client_id)         -- Get WS upgrade headers table (nil for TCP)

-- Server: client enumeration and multicast
self.clients()                     -- Return table of all connected client_ids
                                   -- also on a proxy, same meaning
self.multicast(ids, msg)           -- Send msg to a subset of clients (ids = array of
                                   -- client_ids).  Returns how many were reached.
                                   -- An entry that is not a whole number refuses the
                                   -- whole call rather than being dropped from it.

-- Server: named groups
self.join_group(id, group)         -- Add client to a named group
self.leave_group(id, group)        -- Remove client from a group
self.group_send(group, msg)        -- Send msg to all clients in a group.  Returns how
                                   -- many were reached; 0 is a group with nobody in it.

-- Server: zero-copy pipe pairing (bypasses Lua callbacks)
self.pipe(id_a, id_b)             -- Pair two clients: data forwarded directly between them
self.unpipe(id)                    -- Remove pipe pairing for a client
socketley.pipe(src, fd_a, src, fd_b)   -- Pair two connections of one server
socketley.pipe(src, fd, dst)           -- Route a connection to another server.
                                   -- Despite the name it hands no descriptor over:
                                   -- src keeps the socket and relays the bytes

-- Server: per-connection metadata
self.set_data(id, key, val)        -- Set string metadata on a connection (nil val deletes key)
self.get_data(id, key)             -- Get metadata string or nil

-- Server: client routing
self.route(client_id, target)      -- Forward client to sub-server, in this or
                                   -- any other process. This server keeps the
                                   -- socket and relays; the target answers.
self.unroute(client_id)            -- Stop forwarding
self.get_route(client_id)          -- Get current route (string or nil)

-- Server: owner-targeted sending (sub-server only)
self.owner_send(client_id, msg)    -- Send to a connection routed here, through
                                   -- the runtime that owns it. Returns false if
                                   -- that connection has gone.
self.owner_broadcast(msg)          -- Broadcast to all owner's clients

-- Proxy
self.clients()                     -- Table of connected client_ids
self.peer_ip(client_id)            -- Client IP (IPv4 or IPv6 string)
self.close_client(client_id)       -- Close one client connection
self.backends()                    -- Array of backend addresses, in the
                                   -- order on_route indexes them (1-based
                                   -- in Lua; on_route returns 0-based)
self.backend_health()              -- Circuit-breaker state per backend,
                                   -- same 1-based order:
                                   -- "closed" | "open" | "half_open"
self.stats()                       -- {connections, bytes_in, bytes_out,
                                   --  total_connections, total_messages,
                                   --  backend_count}

Why exists and hexists are there. self.get returns the value, and returns the empty string both for an absent key and for a key that holds an empty string. A script cannot tell the two apart from self.get alone, and this page's own example relies on that: examples/cache/cache-integration-handler.lua reads self.get("config:timeout") == "" as "not set yet".

Making get return nil for an absent key would answer the question, but it would break every script that reads the result that way. An empty string is also a value a cache may legitimately hold. So exists and hexists ask the question separately, under the names the wire protocol already uses.

The proxy table is smaller than the server's on purpose. A proxy relays between a client and a backend and speaks for neither. It has no message of its own to put on the wire, so it has no broadcast(), no send() and no per-connection metadata. To change what crosses a proxy, use on_proxy_request and on_proxy_response. To refuse a request, use the filter chain.
self.backends() is indexed from 1, like every Lua array, but on_route returns an index from 0. So when on_route returns n, the selected address is self.backends()[n + 1].
self.owner_send() accepts only a client_id that this runtime was actually given: one that arrived through self.route() and was reported by on_connect(). It returns false for any other id, including a client_id whose connection has since closed. A script that holds an id after its connection has ended therefore cannot write to whichever client later received that descriptor.

sections.title: Global Functions
sections.html:
socketley.log(msg)#

Writes one line to the daemon's log at INFO level, prefixed with the name of the runtime that wrote it: [12:04:31] [INFO] [lua my-server] .... The line goes through the daemon's logger, so log_level in the configuration file can suppress it like any other message. At the default level, every line is shown. Every Lua diagnostic carries the same [lua <runtime>] prefix. The prefix is what separates two scripts that share one stderr. Two runtimes often share one script file, so the file name in an error does not identify the runtime.

socketley.set_timeout(ms, fn) -> timer_id#

Calls fn once after ms milliseconds, using an io_uring timeout SQE. Returns an integer timer ID that can be passed to socketley.clear_timeout(). The timer shares the event loop with the runtime and uses no extra threads.

socketley.set_interval(ms, fn) -> timer_id#

Calls fn every ms milliseconds. Returns an integer timer ID that can be passed to socketley.clear_interval().

Details

Both kinds of timer are cancelled when the runtime stops, and are not restored if it is started again. A stopped runtime executes no script, so its timers do not survive the stop. This includes a timer armed inside on_stop, which is cancelled with the rest. The script registers its timers at its top level, which runs once, when the runtime's worker is forked. A start after a stop forks a new worker, which runs the top level again and so arms the timers again. Nothing the previous worker held is carried over: the timer is not restored, but re-armed by a script that runs from the beginning.

Both functions return 0 and arm nothing when ms is not greater than zero, when the runtime has no event loop, or when the runtime has been stopped. The last case covers a script that calls socketley.stop on its own runtime and carries on. Since stop returns to the script, everything after that line runs on a runtime that is already down. A start lifts the stopped state before on_start, so a restarted runtime arms its timers exactly as it did the first time. socketley.subscribe returns 0 in the same situation, for the same reason. Real ids start at 1, so 0 is unambiguous. The reason is written to the daemon's log, because a timer that will never fire would otherwise fail silently.

socketley.clear_timeout(timer_id)#

Cancels a pending timeout, so the timer does not fire. Calling it with an already-expired or invalid ID is safe and does nothing.

socketley.clear_interval(timer_id)#

Cancels a repeating interval, so the timer does not fire again. Calling it with an already-expired or invalid ID is safe and does nothing.

Details

Both functions remove the timer completely rather than just silencing it. The io_uring timeout is removed, the timer's storage is released, and the reference to the callback is dropped. The closure and everything it captured can then be garbage collected at once, not when the timer would have expired.

Both are safe to call from inside the timer's own callback. That is how to write a repeating timer that fires only once.

socketley.json_encode(value) -> string | false, why#

Encodes a Lua value (table, string, number, boolean, nil) as a JSON string. Tables with consecutive integer keys starting at 1 are encoded as JSON arrays; all other tables as objects.

Details

Object keys are written in sorted order, so encoding equal data twice gives the same string. A Lua table has no order of its own: a table filled with alpha, beta, gamma, delta may iterate as beta, gamma, delta, alpha. Without sorting, two tables holding the same data could encode differently. Anything that compares encoded documents depends on this: an ETag, a cache key, a signature, a deduplication hash, or a diff of two logged payloads.

Returns false and a reason when the value cannot be written as a document: a table that contains itself (directly or through any chain of fields), or a table nested deeper than 128 levels. A table reachable twice by different paths is not a cycle and encodes normally.

A string is truthy and false is not. So code such as local s = socketley.json_encode(t) needs no change, and if not s then tests for the refusal.

socketley.json_decode(str) -> value | false, why#

Decodes a JSON string into a Lua value. Objects become tables with string keys, arrays become tables with integer keys (1-based). Null becomes nil.

Details

Returns false and a reason for a document nested deeper than 128 levels, for bytes that are not a complete JSON document, and for trailing data after the document ends.

Refusing malformed input is what makes the return value trustworthy. Without it, a handler could not tell a truncated body from a complete one. For example, [1,2 (a request body cut short by a dropped connection) would decode to an ordinary two-element table, and {"a":} to an empty table. nul, garbage and an empty string would all decode to nil, the same result as a document that really is null.

The depth limit is not a formatting preference. This call is meant for data from the network, such as a request body or a message payload, so whoever sent the data chooses its nesting depth, and the decoder recurses to follow it. Without the limit, a few hundred kilobytes of [[[[ took the whole daemon down. No callback deadline covers this case: deadlines measure Lua execution, and this recursion is native code.

socketley.subscribe(cache_name, channel, fn) -> subscription_id#

Registers fn(channel, message) to be called whenever the named cache runtime publishes to channel. The function is called on the subscribing runtime's event loop turn, not from the cache itself. When several subscriptions exist for the same channel, all of them fire, in registration order.

Details

Returns an integer id for socketley.unsubscribe(). Ids start at 1 and are never reused, so 0 means the call was refused. The runtime has been stopped, and this registration would have outlived the stop that ended the others. See socketley.set_interval for the details: both calls refuse in the same cases, and a start lifts the refusal for both.

Messages are delivered only to a running runtime. Every registration a runtime holds is ended when it stops. A runtime that has never been started receives nothing either. Its top level has run, so the registration exists, but a runtime that is not running executes no script. The same rule cancels the timers. Both come back when the runtime is started again in a worker: a start forks a new worker, which runs the top level and on_start again (see socketley.set_interval). A server, client, proxy, cache, storage or dns runtime made by socketley.create runs in the daemon instead. There a start runs on_start but not the top level, so a subscription made in on_start comes back and a timer armed at the top level does not.

socketley.unsubscribe(subscription_id) -> bool#

Ends one subscription. Returns true when it removed a live one, and false when the id names none (never issued, or already unsubscribed).

Details

The id names one registration, not a channel, so two handlers on the same channel can be ended independently. It is safe to call from inside a subscriber's own callback; that is how to write a subscriber that runs only once. The removal takes effect from the next message, not in the middle of delivering the current one.

Unsubscribing explicitly matters while the runtime is up. stop ends all subscriptions, and remove and reload-lua destroy the context they live in. But none of those happens to a runtime that is simply serving. A script that subscribes from a callback that runs more than once, such as on_tick, registers the same handler again on every call unless it unsubscribes. Each publish is then delivered to every copy.

socketley.mqtt.publish(runtime, topic, payload [, {qos=, retain=}] [, fn]) -> true | nil, why#

Publishes a message on an mqtt runtime of this daemon, as if the broker itself had published it. Returns true once the broker has the message. See From the other runtimes under MQTT FLAGS.

socketley.mail.send(runtime, {to=, cc=, bcc=, from=, reply_to=, subject=, text=, html=, headers=, attachments=, raw=} [, fn]) -> id | nil, why#

Has a mail runtime of this daemon write a message and queue it. Returns the message's queue id once it is in the spool. to, cc and bcc each take one address or a list of addresses. Each attachment is a table {name=,type=,data=}. See MAIL FLAGS.

socketley.http(opts) -> table#

Makes an HTTP or HTTPS request and returns the response. In a callback that can wait, the callback suspends at the call, and the runtime serves everything else until the answer arrives. The callbacks that can wait are the ones socketley.db may be called from without a function, and an mcp tool's handler. Anywhere else (on_start, on_stop, a timer, on_http_request, a filter, an mcp resource or prompt), the call blocks the event loop thread until the exchange ends. In those places, use it only in on_start/on_stop or in low-frequency on_tick callbacks.

opts table keys:

url         string   Request URL (http:// or https://)
method      string   HTTP method (default "GET")
body        string   Request body (optional)
headers     table    Extra headers e.g. {["Content-Type"]="application/json"}
timeout_ms  number   Timeout in milliseconds, 1..3600000 (default 5000)

A key that is present but has the wrong type or is out of range makes the call return ok = false with the reason in error. The key is not replaced by its default, so `timeout_ms = "soon"` does not silently become 5000. A key that is absent keeps its default; that is not an error and is not reported.

Returns a table:

ok      bool    true if HTTP status 2xx
status  number  HTTP status code (e.g. 200, 404)
body    string  Response body
error   string  Error message on failure

timeout_ms is one deadline for the whole exchange, not a separate timeout per operation. Connecting, the TLS handshake, the request and the response are all measured against it. A call that blocks resolves the host name before the deadline is armed, on a thread of its own, with the resolution bounded by the same timeout. A call that waits counts the resolution against the deadline. A response larger than 8 MB is refused rather than buffered without limit.

A response that declares a Content-Length and then ends before reaching it is also refused, with the shortfall named in error. Nothing else in the answer would show the problem. The close that cut the response short looks the same as the close that ends a response with no length at all. Over HTTPS, the close_notify alert would tell the two apart, but many servers omit it, and this client accepts its absence. Only a response with a declared length can fall short. A chunked response, or one with no length, is read until the close and returned as usual.

HTTPS uses OpenSSL and validates the peer. The certificate chain is verified against the system CA store, and the certificate must have been issued to the host in the URL. A host name is matched against the certificate's DNS names, with partial wildcards refused; an address literal is matched against its IP SAN. TLS 1.2 is the minimum accepted protocol version. If either check fails, the request is aborted with the reason in error. There is no option to disable the checks. A service that presents a self-signed or private-CA certificate must have that CA in the trust store OpenSSL reads (overridable with SSL_CERT_FILE or SSL_CERT_DIR). If no CA store is available at all the call fails immediately with no system CA store available.

sections.title: Runtime Management API
sections.html:
Create, start, stop, and remove runtimes from Lua scripts:

socketley.create(type, name, config)  -- Create runtime
socketley.start(name)                 -- Start runtime
socketley.stop(name)                  -- Stop runtime
socketley.remove(name)                -- Stop + remove runtime
socketley.send(name, msg)             -- Send/broadcast to runtime
socketley.list()                      -- List all runtime names (table)
socketley.get(name)                   -- Get info table or nil
socketley.pipe(src, fd_a, src, fd_b)  -- Pair two connections of one server
socketley.pipe(src, fd, dst)          -- Route a connection to another server

Every call above answers true when it happened, or false , "reason" when it did not.

The reason is a sentence that names the runtime and what was wrong with the request. A script can use it to tell these four situations apart:

local ok, why = socketley.start("web")
--  false  there is no runtime called "web"
--  false  "web" is already running
--  false  "web" is failed, and a failed runtime cannot be started again ...
--  false  "web" could not be started; it is failed now, and the reason is
--         in the daemon's log        <- a held port, a TLS pair that is not one

This is the convention Lua itself uses, in io.open, os.remove and pcall. So assert(socketley.start(n)) prints the reason with no other change. Success returns ONE value, not true, nil.

What a second return value changes. Lua truncates a multiple-return call to one value everywhere except in three places. These are unaffected: assignment, if not f() then, and/or, concatenation, tostring, comparison, and any argument position that is not the last. These are affected:

  • print(f()) prints two values;

  • { f() } builds a two-element table;

  • g(f()) passes g two arguments instead of one.

socketley.pipe is two calls, and the number of arguments selects which one. With four arguments it pairs two connections of ONE server; both descriptors are named and both are used. With three arguments it hands the connection to another runtime, which decides what answers it. That form has no destination descriptor, so a fourth argument across two runtimes is refused rather than accepted and ignored.

Config table keys: port, config (or lua, a script path), target, mode (server only), http and http_cache (server only), group, on_parent_stop ("remove" or "stop"), and start (bool). The table is validated, and a refusal leaves nothing behind. Each of these returns false and a reason, which also goes to the log, and creates no runtime:

  • a port outside 0..65535;

  • a mode or policy that is not one of the listed values;

  • a key that is not on this list;

  • a script that will not load;

  • a start that cannot bind.

Runtimes created from Lua have parent-child ownership. port=0 creates an internal-only server that receives only forwarded messages.

Every call above works in a worker, which is where every runtime runs.

These calls act on the runtime map, which lives in the daemon. A script that uses them therefore runs in a process that does not hold the map. All of the calls still work there, in two different ways:

socketley.send, .list, .get and the four socketley.cluster calls are answered from a replica. The daemon pushes the worker a copy of the map and a snapshot of the cluster view, and refreshes both when they change.

socketley.create, .start, .stop and .remove change the map, and changing a copy would be wrong. The worker sends these calls to the daemon instead, over a socket it holds for exactly this purpose, and waits for the answer. So if socketley.create(...) then tests what actually happened. The wait is what makes the result accurate, and it is bounded. A call that does not fork anything took 9.95, 10.20 and 10.52 microseconds over three runs of 20000. A call that forks waits at most five seconds. These calls are made in on_start or on a rare control message, never per request, which is why a wait is affordable. Compare socketley.http() in the same table, which blocks the same loop for a network round trip.

The answers are the daemon's own, word for word what the same call says in the daemon: there is no runtime called "x" , "x" is already running , a runtime called "x" already exists. By design, a script cannot tell from them which process it runs in.

Calls that cross runtimes work there too. socketley.pipe across two runtimes and self.route() both work in a worker and cross the process boundary, with no change to how either is called.

One refusal remains; read it carefully if you meet it. socketley.create, .start, .stop and .remove raise an error in a worker that was forked without the socket these calls travel on. This happens with an older daemon, or with a daemon that could not create the socket. The error message says so and tells you to restart the daemon. It is not a permanent refusal.

Across two runtimes, socketley.pipe does not hand a file descriptor over at all, so no SCM_RIGHTS passing through shared/net/conn_transfer.h is involved. Both calls use route_client(), which writes into the target's connection maps, runs the target's on_connect, and then keeps the socket where it is and relays the bytes through it. This needs a way to name another runtime's connection and reach it, not a way to move one. That is shared/ipc/route_relay.h.

Nothing changes for a script: the same call, the same return value, the same target name. The origin stays in the data path either way, because that is what routing is. A message from a routed client reaches the target's on_client_message, and the target's reply reaches the client through the origin.

The four-argument form, socketley.pipe(src, fd_a, src, fd_b), pairs two connections of one server and crosses no process boundary. It must be called from that server's own script, because only that process holds its connections.

When a runtime that holds routed connections goes away (stopped, removed, crashed or killed), every runtime on the other end of those routes is told to release them, and the target's on_disconnect runs. The daemon does this, not the departing runtime, because a killed worker runs no teardown at all.

unroute(), get_route() and owner_send() read the runtime's own tables, in a worker as anywhere else.

Plan for where that error is raised, when one of those four calls raises it. At a script's top level it fails the load, and a worker whose script did not load does not serve: the create is refused with a reason and the runtime is left failed. Inside a callback, the error is caught and logged like any other callback error, and the runtime carries on. In on_start, that means the runtime is up and serving, but nothing on_start was meant to do has happened. ls shows it green and it accepts connections. So the command that started it exits 1 and names the callback and the reason. The runtime is left running either way; the exit code and the message tell the two cases apart.

Everything that does not use the runtime map works in a worker exactly as it does in the daemon: socketley.log, .http, .json_encode/.json_decode, the timers, .subscribe, the whole self table, and every connection and request callback. See Out-of-process runtimes under LIMITATIONS for the full account.

sections.title: Cluster Introspection API
sections.html:
When the daemon runs in cluster mode (--cluster), the socketley.cluster table provides read-only introspection into the full cluster topology. All functions return empty tables when not in cluster mode, so scripts work in both standalone and cluster setups without modification.

In a worker process the four functions are answered from a snapshot of the cluster view, which the daemon pushes before the frame that loads its script.

One exception remains, and it is in a worker only. A daemon that is in no cluster has no view to push. An empty table is also what a successful call returns for a daemon that is alone in a cluster. So when no view is installed, the four functions raise an error that names the function, instead of returning. If a daemon joins a cluster after a worker's script has loaded, that script keeps getting the error until it is reloaded.

socketley.cluster.daemons() -> table#

Returns an array of daemon info tables. Each entry has:

Details
name      string   Daemon name (from --name)
host      string   Advertised address, from gethostname(2), falling
                   back to the daemon name if that call fails
runtimes  number   Count of runtimes on this daemon

The local daemon is always the first entry. Remote daemons follow in discovery order.

socketley.cluster.runtimes() -> table#

Returns a flat array of all runtimes across every daemon in the cluster:

Details
daemon       string   Name of the daemon hosting this runtime
name         string   Runtime name
type         string   "server", "client", "proxy", or "cache"
port         number   Listen port (0 = internal-only)
group        string   Group tag (empty string if unset)
state        string   "created", "running", "stopped", or "failed"
connections  number   Current connection count

The type is the name of any runtime type the daemon knows, built in or registered, not only these four.

socketley.cluster.group(name) -> table#

Returns running members of the named group that have a valid port. Each entry has:

Details
daemon       string   Daemon name
host         string   Advertised address
port         number   Listen port
connections  number   Current connection count

Useful for building custom routing, health checks, or failover logic from Lua.

socketley.cluster.stats() -> table#

Returns aggregate cluster statistics:

Details
daemons   number   Total daemon count (local + remote)
runtimes  number   Total runtime count across all daemons
running   number   Count of runtimes in "running" state
groups    table    Maps group name (string) -> member count (number)

sections.title: Cluster Event Callbacks
sections.html:
These optional callbacks fire when the cluster topology changes. Events are detected during the 2-second scan/publish cycle, so callbacks may fire up to 2 seconds after the actual change. They fire only on a running runtime. A runtime that has been stopped or has never been started executes no script, and that includes cluster callbacks. If one event in a batch stops the runtime, the remaining events in that batch are not delivered to it. A daemon is considered stale and triggers on_cluster_leave after 10 seconds without a heartbeat update.

on_cluster_join(daemon)#

Fired when a new remote daemon is discovered in the cluster directory. daemon is a table with name (string) and host (string) fields.

on_cluster_leave(daemon)#

Fired when a remote daemon's heartbeat file becomes stale (>10s old) or is removed from the cluster directory. daemon is a table with a name (string) field.

on_group_change(group, members)#

Fired when the total member count of a group changes (a runtime joins or leaves the group, or a daemon with group members appears/disappears). It fires only on actual count changes, not on every scan cycle. group is the group name (string). members is an array of tables, each with daemon, host, and port fields representing the current group membership.

Example — log topology changes and maintain a local routing table:

local backends = {}

function on_cluster_join(daemon)
    socketley.log("daemon joined: " .. daemon.name .. " at " .. daemon.host)
end

function on_cluster_leave(daemon)
    socketley.log("daemon left: " .. daemon.name)
end

function on_group_change(group, members)
    if group == "api" then
        backends = members   -- update routing table
        socketley.log("api group now has " .. #members .. " members")
    end
end

function on_start()
    -- Initial snapshot
    local stats = socketley.cluster.stats()
    socketley.log("cluster: " .. stats.daemons .. " daemons, "
                  .. stats.running .. " running runtimes")
end

Fired when the total member count of a group changes (a runtime joins or leaves the group, or a daemon with group members appears/disappears). It fires only on actual count changes, not on every scan cycle. group is the group name (string). members is an array of tables, each with daemon, host, and port fields representing the current group membership.

sections.title: DASHBOARD
sections.html:
When daemon.metrics_port is set in the daemon configuration file, the metrics endpoint serves the following routes:

GET /#

Serves the web dashboard, which has the storage interface's look and takes its stylesheet and helpers from the same binary. The overview shows the daemon's runtimes, connections, messages, bytes in and out, CPU and resident memory, each with a line graph of its last three minutes. The runtime list shows each runtime with its state and the same figures, and can be filtered by type and name. Each runtime also has a page with its configuration and its stats.

Details

A signed-in user can start, stop, restart and remove a runtime, and reload its Lua. The user can also edit a runtime, either in a form for its type, filled in with what show prints, or as the JSON that import takes. To create a runtime, the user picks the type and then fills in a form of every flag that create takes for that type, grouped by section. The page shows the command it will send while the form is filled in.

If daemon.dashboard_idp names an idp runtime, the page offers sign-in through it. An account of the group admins that is signed in at that idp is signed in to the dashboard too. Signing out of the dashboard also signs out at the provider.

Otherwise, signing in takes the access key and secret of an admin in the credentials file that daemon.dashboard_credentials names. The file has a storage runtime's format, and the dashboard checks the key and secret the same way a proxy's --auth basic: does. An address that fails five times in fifteen minutes is refused with 429, even with the right secret. Behind a proxy on this machine, the address counted is the one in X-Forwarded-For.

The session is a cookie sealed with a key that the daemon generates at start. The cookie is HttpOnly and SameSite=Strict, and also Secure behind HTTPS. It is valid for twelve hours. The daemon ends a session when the user signs out, when the user's key is removed from the file, or when that key is given another secret. Each command also carries the page's own header, which a request from another site cannot carry. The command goes over the daemon's control socket, as a CLI command does, and is logged with who sent it. The page sends only create, edit, import, start, stop, remove, reload, reload-lua, show, stats, ls and ps, and never a word that contains a space.

When credentials are configured, every route except the page and the sign-in needs a session. /metrics needs a session too, except for a scraper on this machine that connects without a proxy in between. Without credentials, the page shows the figures but changes nothing. The log and a zone's text always need a session, whatever is configured.

The dashboard's history and alerts come from a metrics runtime (see METRICS FLAGS). The daemon creates one named metrics the first time it starts with the dashboard on and a way to sign in to it (daemon.dashboard_credentials or daemon.dashboard_idp), or with any of daemon.alert_webhook, daemon.alert_mail and daemon.events set. The metrics runtime listens on 127.0.0.1:9090, or on the next free port above it. The daemon creates it only once, so a metrics runtime that was removed stays removed. With no metrics runtime running, the page shows the current figures and no history. With several, the page reads the one named metrics, or else any running one that collects this daemon's series.

The graphs cover a chosen range: the last fifteen minutes, hour, six hours, day, week, month or year. The value and time under the pointer are shown. For each runtime and for the daemon, connections and memory are drawn as they are, and messages, bytes and CPU as rates per second. The figures are read from the metrics runtime's store, which keeps them as long as its --keep and --downsample allow. GET /api/history?runtime=name&range=seconds&points=n returns the history of one runtime, or of all runtimes together when no name is given, as n points. A point with no data is null. The answer is an object with from (in seconds since 1970), step (the seconds per point) and the arrays conn, msg, in, out, cpu (percent of one CPU) and rss. The range is held between a minute and a year, and the number of points between 10 and 1440.

The Alerts view shows the metrics runtime's rules. These are the built-in rules below, unless its --rules file changes them. A runtime failed, or was started again three times within the hour. A sync runtime cannot carry what it owes. A certificate that a runtime serves expires within two weeks; the alert is critical within three days, or once the certificate has expired. The disk under a storage runtime or under the state directory, or the host's memory, is at 90% (critical at 95%). A storage runtime is at 90% of its --max-bytes, or a cache that refuses writes is at 90% of its --maxmemory. A git repository's last pull failed. A mail runtime has a hundred messages waiting (critical at a thousand), or its own address is listed by a blocklist that its --dnsbl names. A scraped target does not answer for two minutes. A tunnel edge is missing an agent that joined it, or drops more than 1% of its datagrams. An idp runtime barred more than twenty sign-ins in ten minutes.

A critical alert silences the warning on the same thing. Each alert is logged, listed on the page with the recent notifications, and shown on the overview. When daemon.alert_webhook is set to an http or https URL, each alert is also posted to it as JSON. The content and text fields carry the message; these are the fields Discord, Slack and Telegram's sendMessage read. The state (firing, resolved) and alert fields carry the rest. If the hook does not accept a message with a 2xx status, the daemon posts it again after a pause that doubles each time, up to eight seconds. A message the hook has not accepted is kept in .notify in the state directory and posted after a restart.

When daemon.alert_mail is set to mail://runtime/address[,address...] that mail runtime mails each alert, as well as or instead of the webhook. The subject is the alert's first line. Mail is held the same way until the mail runtime runs. The metrics runtime keeps its alerts' state in its directory, so a metrics runtime that is started again does not report the same alerts a second time. GET /api/alerts lists the alerts, and POST /api/alerts/test sent with the page's header posts a test through the hook.

When daemon.events names an mqtt runtime, the daemon publishes the state of each runtime on it, at QoS 1 and retained. It publishes on socketley/runtimes/name/state as JSON with the runtime's name, type, state and port. It publishes at every change, and clears the topic when the runtime is removed. The daemon also publishes each alert while it holds, on socketley/alerts/id as the JSON that the alert field above carries, and clears it when the alert clears. A subscriber to socketley/# receives the current state as soon as it subscribes, and every change after that. The broker may be created after the daemon starts. Until it runs, the messages owed to it wait in .notify in the state directory, as the webhook's do.

The Logs view follows the daemon's recent log live, and filters it by runtime, by level and by text. Each runtime's page shows that runtime's own log. A failed runtime shows the last warning or error it wrote, both in the list and on its page, next to how often it was started again. Each worker writes its stderr into its own pipe, which the daemon reads. The daemon passes every line on unchanged to its own stderr, so the journal gets every line. It also keeps the last 10,000 lines in memory, its own and the workers', each tagged with the runtime's name: GET /api/logs?since=seq&max=n&runtime=name&level=warn.

The Domains view shows three things. The first is every certificate that a runtime serves: its names, its issuer, how long it has left, whether it is self-issued, whether a wildcard is waiting for its zone's delegation, and the last line of a failed issuance. The second is each entrance's routes, each mapping a name to the runtime it goes to. The third is the zones of the dns runtimes, whose records the page can edit. Before an edited zone is written, its text is checked the way the dns runtime reads a zone file. If the serial was left as it was, the dashboard raises it, so secondaries take the change. The view uses GET /api/edge, and GET and PUT /api/zone for a file a dns runtime serves and no other.

The endpoint listens on 127.0.0.1 only. To reach it on a server, open an SSH tunnel with ssh -L 9100:127.0.0.1:9100 host, and then open http://localhost:9100/. On an installed system the port is set in /etc/socketley/config.lua, as daemon = { metrics_port = 9100 }, and is read when the service starts.

GET /metrics#

Serves the daemon's metrics in Prometheus exposition format. It is suitable for scraping by Prometheus, Grafana Agent, or similar monitoring stacks.

GET /api/overview#

Returns a JSON object with high-level daemon statistics:

Details
{
    "version": "1.1.0",
    "uptime_seconds": 86400,
    "runtimes_total": 5,
    "runtimes_running": 4,
    "connections_total": 18230,
    "connections_active": 142,
    "messages_total": 9120044,
    "bytes_in": 12345678,
    "bytes_out": 9876543,
    "cpu_seconds": 812.40,
    "rss_bytes": 163577856,
    "memory_bytes": 94371840,
    "processes": 5,
    "cpus": 4
}

cpu_seconds is the user and system CPU time of the daemon and of every process its runtimes run in, read from /proc. The change between two readings, over the time between them, is the CPU used. rss_bytes is the sum of their resident memory, which counts a page shared between shards once per shard. memory_bytes is what they cost the machine: each shared page is counted by the share of it that each process holds (the kernel's Pss). So the runtimes' figures add up to the memory they hold between them. processes is how many processes there are, and cpus is the number of CPUs online.

GET /api/runtimes#

Returns a JSON array of all runtimes with name, type, port, state, connections and message/byte counters. Each entry also has cpu_seconds, rss_bytes, memory_bytes and processes for the runtime's own processes: one per shard, and none while it is stopped.

GET /api/runtime/name#

Returns a JSON object for the single runtime named name. Returns 404 if the runtime does not exist.

The dashboard CLI command prints the dashboard URL:

$ socketley dashboard
Dashboard: http://localhost:9100/

sections.title: SERVICE MESH
sections.html: The proxy runtime includes service-mesh primitives that can be combined to build sidecar proxies, API gateways, or resilient service-to-service communication layers.

sections.title: Health Checks
sections.html: Active health checks probe backends at a regular interval (--health-interval) using either a TCP connect or an HTTP GET (--health-check). A backend is marked unhealthy after --health-threshold consecutive failures and is excluded from the load balancer pool. A single successful check restores the backend.

sections.title: Circuit Breaker
sections.html:
The circuit breaker prevents cascading failures by tracking consecutive errors per backend. It has three states:

closed#

The normal state: requests are forwarded to the backend and errors are counted.

open#

The state the circuit enters when errors reach --circuit-threshold. All requests fail immediately, without attempting a connection. After --circuit-timeout seconds, the circuit moves to half-open.

half-open#

The circuit lets a single probe request through to the backend. It is one request in total, not one per selection: while that probe is outstanding, the backend is unavailable to every other request. If the probe succeeds, the circuit returns to closed. If it fails, the circuit re-opens.

entries.summary: The normal state: requests are forwarded to the backend and errors are counted.
The state the circuit enters when errors reach --circuit-threshold. All requests fail immediately, without attempting a connection. After --circuit-timeout seconds, the circuit moves to half-open.

The circuit lets a single probe request through to the backend. It is one request in total, not one per selection: while that probe is outstanding, the backend is unavailable to every other request. If the probe succeeds, the circuit returns to closed. If it fails, the circuit re-opens.

sections.title: Response Deadline
sections.html:
A backend that accepts connections and then stops answering fails no check. A TCP health probe connects to it successfully, and a request that never completes counts as neither an error nor a success, so the circuit breaker has nothing to open on. --backend-timeout (default 2 seconds) limits the wait for the first byte of a response. When it expires, the proxy records a backend error, which puts such a backend through the breaker like any other failure. The request is retried elsewhere if --retry allows it, and answered 504 Gateway Timeout otherwise.

The deadline covers the handshake as well as the answer. If a backend never completes its connect within the deadline, the client is also answered 504 Gateway Timeout, instead of being closed without a response. A request routed through an @group backend is charged to the member it actually reached. So a group member that stalls is taken out of rotation by the same breaker as a listed backend.

The deadline is on by default and covers only the wait for the first byte, so a large or streaming response body is not affected. An endpoint that legitimately needs more than 2 seconds to start answering must be given a longer --backend-timeout or --backend-timeout 0; otherwise the proxy treats it as hung. The deadline applies to HTTP mode only, because in TCP mode there is no request boundary to measure from.

sections.title: Request Framing
sections.html:
In HTTP mode the proxy is strict about how a request's header block is framed. It refuses anything that it and a backend could read differently. These are the same rules, from the same implementation, that a socketley server applies to a request it receives directly; see Request Framing under SERVER FLAGS. The proxy forwards bytes to a backend that parses them independently. If the two disagree about where a request ends, the next request on the same connection starts in the wrong place: this is request smuggling. Normalising the request instead would mean guessing how the backend will read it, so the proxy refuses rather than guesses.

A request is answered 400 Bad Request and its connection is closed, without contacting any backend, when the header block contains any of:

  • a bare LF or a bare CR — every line must end with CRLF

  • whitespace between a field name and its colon (Content-Length : 6)

  • a continuation (obs-fold) line, i.e. one starting with a space or tab

  • a field line with no colon

  • both Content-Length and Transfer-Encoding, or more than one Content-Length field

  • a Content-Length that is not a whole decimal number (Content-Length: 6x)

  • a Transfer-Encoding whose final coding is not chunked (Transfer-Encoding: gzip, Transfer-Encoding: chunked, gzip, or chunked listed twice); such a request has no determinable body length at all

Every request on a connection is framed and checked on its own, including one pipelined behind another. Only the body that a request declares travels with it. Bytes past its Content-Length are not body: the proxy holds them back and parses them as the next request instead of forwarding them. Pipelining still works, and a second request sent before the first is answered is still served. But it is answered in turn, after the same checks. A smuggling attempt hidden behind a clean request is refused exactly as if it had been sent first.

A request held this way has the same 10 second deadline as a half-arrived one. The exchange in front of it may never reach an end this proxy can detect, for example when a backend frames its response in a way the proxy cannot read. Then the held request is answered 408 Request Timeout rather than left waiting. A chunked request is the one body this proxy cannot measure, because it never de-chunks. Its body is forwarded as an opaque stream, so a request pipelined behind a chunked one is framed by the backend alone.

Compliant clients send none of these. A request whose header block is still arriving is held until the terminating blank line. It is subject to the 16 KiB header limit (431 Request Header Fields Too Large) and a 10 second header deadline (408 Request Timeout).

Behind the header limit there is a second, larger limit. It counts everything buffered for an exchange, not just one header block. At most 1 MiB is held for a connection whose request has already been forwarded. That covers the body the client sends past its declared Content-Length, and the requests pipelined behind it. Nothing drains this buffer until the response in front of it is finished. So a client that writes faster than the backend answers can reach the limit on a well-formed connection. The client is then answered 413 Request Entity Too Large and the connection is closed. The one exception is the same as for the gateway statuses. If part of the backend's response is already on that client's wire, no status line is written behind it, because it would land at an offset that is not a message boundary. Instead, the connection is closed with the response left visibly truncated.

The header deadline starts at the first byte of a request and ends when its header block is complete. It is fixed and not configurable. It is deliberately independent of --idle-timeout, which defaults to 0 (never) and so cannot be relied on to end a half-sent request. A client that sends a request line and then stops sends no more bytes for the 16 KiB limit to count. Without the deadline, that client could hold its connection, its descriptor and its 64 KB buffer for as long as it liked. The deadline does not measure an idle keep-alive connection between requests, or a slow request body. It measures only the gap between a request's first byte and its terminating blank line.

The proxy applies the same strictness to backend responses, but only to decide whether the backend connection may be reused. Sometimes the length of a response cannot be established with certainty: its header block was split across reads, or was not strictly CRLF-framed, or more bytes arrived than the length it declared. Such a response is forwarded to the client unchanged, and its connection is closed instead of returned to the pool. A backend that answers Connection: close is not pooled either, because it has said the socket is going away.

A Connection: close sent by the client does not do this. It is a hop-by-hop field about the client's own connection to the proxy. So the proxy does not forward it upstream, and it does not end the backend connection. The proxy answers the request, returns the backend socket to the pool, and closes the client connection as asked. The field is a comma-separated list. As on the server, it is parsed token by token and case-insensitively. So Connection: keep-alive, close counts as close, while a value that merely begins with those letters, such as Connection: clientinfo, does not. A client that opens a connection per request (curl, a health checker, any HTTP library used without a session) therefore costs one accept and no backend connect, the same as a keep-alive client.

Before a connection from the pool is handed to the next request, the proxy checks it. A connection with unread data on it is closed rather than reused. Nothing was asked of an idle pooled socket, so anything waiting on it was sent unbidden by the backend. It is the tail of an answer whose length was mis-declared, or a second answer volunteered behind the first. Reusing the socket would make those bytes the head of the next client's response, so the connection is dropped and a fresh one opened. The proxy logs this once per instance.

Reuse covers an @group backend as well as a listed one. A pooled connection is filed under the endpoint it was opened to, never under the group. So it is only ever handed back to a request routed to that same member. When a member leaves the group, its pooled connections are closed at once rather than left to the idle sweep.

Reuse covers a TLS backend too. The session is pooled together with the descriptor, so a reused connection continues on the record layer it already had, at the sequence number it had reached. A TLS connection carries more than an address: a negotiated session, a peer identity verified against a name, a client certificate that may have been presented, and a record layer part way through a stream. The endpoint the socket is filed under accounts for three of those. That is because the name was pinned to that endpoint before the handshake, and the certificate was checked against it. The client certificate and the trust store belong to the runtime and are rebuilt on every start, and the pool is emptied on every stop. So a pooled session can never outlive the configuration that verified it.

A pooled TLS socket must not inherit an answer nobody asked for. A cleartext socket with bytes waiting on it is destroyed rather than reused, because a socket in the pool has been asked nothing since its last answer completed. That test cannot be carried across a record layer unchanged. A TLS peer that has said nothing still sends records: a session ticket, a key update, a close_notify. So the proxy drains the socket into the session, and puts the question to the record layer instead of to the kernel. Records that produce no application data are the peer's own housekeeping, and the connection is kept. Application data is a response that belongs to a previous exchange, and the connection is dropped. The second case is logged once per runtime.

sections.title: Retries
sections.html: When --retry is set, failed requests are automatically retried on the next backend in the load balancer pool. By default only idempotent methods are retried; use --retry-all to include POST and PATCH.

sections.title: mTLS
sections.html:
Both legs can be encrypted. --tls --cert --key terminates TLS on the proxy's own port, and --client-ca makes the proxy demand a certificate from its callers. An https:// backend address, or any of --ca, --client-cert and --client-key, switches the backend leg to TLS. On that leg the proxy verifies the chain and the endpoint's name, and presents a client certificate when one is configured. A full sidecar pair looks like this:

socketley create proxy edge -p 8443 \
    --tls --cert edge.pem --key edge-key.pem \
    --client-ca mesh-ca.pem \
    --backend https://10.0.0.7:8443 \
    --ca mesh-ca.pem \
    --client-cert edge.pem --client-key edge-key.pem \
    --sidecar -s

A TLS backend connection is returned to the connection pool and reused, so a busy sidecar pays for one handshake per idle period rather than per request. The pooled socket keeps its session and goes back only to the endpoint it was opened to. It is dropped rather than reused if the backend has left application data on it. --health-check http works against a TLS backend and probes it over TLS, verified to the same standard as the data path. See LIMITATIONS for what the probe does and does not establish. See mTLS Flags under PROXY FLAGS for what is verified and what cannot be switched off.

sections.title: Sidecar Deployment
sections.html:
The --sidecar flag enables a production-ready set of defaults: TCP health checks, a circuit breaker (threshold 5, timeout 30s), 2 retries, and graceful drain. Deploy it alongside your application:

socketley create proxy myapp --sidecar \
    --backend 127.0.0.1:3000 -p 8080 -s

The proxy listens on port 8080 and forwards to the local application on port 3000. Unhealthy backends are removed automatically, and the circuit breaker prevents thundering-herd retries during outages.

--sidecar does not change --backend-timeout. That deadline is 2 seconds by default, and its expiry is charged to the circuit breaker that --sidecar enables. If the application can take longer than that to send its first response byte, set a longer timeout explicitly:

socketley create proxy myapp --sidecar --backend-timeout 30 \
    --backend 127.0.0.1:3000 -p 8080 -s

sections.title: RUNTIME STATES
sections.html:
created#

The initial state after a runtime is created.

running#

The runtime is active and processing I/O.

stopped#

The runtime is stopped and can be started again.

failed#

The runtime could not start, or its worker died more than five times in ten seconds. ls shows the reason. It stays failed until it is started again: fix the cause, then run socketley start.
