sections.title: EXAMPLES
sections.html:
Create a simple server (on an installed system, systemd manages the daemon):

socketley create server myserver -p 9000 -s

Create a client that connects to the server:

socketley create client myclient -t 127.0.0.1:9000 -s

Create an HTTP proxy with load balancing:

socketley create proxy gateway -p 8080 \
    --backend 127.0.0.1:9001,127.0.0.1:9002 \
    --strategy round-robin -s

Create a server with bash output (messages go to stdout):

socketley create server echo -p 9000 -b -s
# With timestamp and prefix:
socketley create server echo -p 9000 -bpt -s

Send a message to a runtime:

socketley send myserver "Hello from CLI"
socketley send myclient "Message to server"

Create a persistent cache with a memory limit:

socketley create cache store -p 9000 \
    --persistent /data/cache.bin \
    --maxmemory 256M --eviction allkeys-lru -s

Create a cache in RESP mode (Redis-compatible):

socketley create cache redis-compat -p 6379 --resp -s
redis-cli -p 6379 SET mykey myval
redis-cli -p 6379 GET mykey

Create a server with a connection limit and rate limiting:

socketley create server api -p 9000 \
    --max-connections 100 --rate-limit 1000 -s

View runtime statistics:

socketley stats myserver
# Output: name, type, port, connections, total_messages, bytes_in/out, ...

Restart a running runtime:

socketley reload myserver
# Stops and restarts the runtime
socketley reload *
# Restarts all running runtimes

Hot-reload a Lua script:

socketley reload-lua myserver
# Re-loads the Lua script without stopping the runtime
socketley reload-lua *
# Hot-reloads Lua on all runtimes with scripts

Start, stop or remove all runtimes:

socketley start *
# Starts all non-running runtimes
socketley stop *
# Stops all running runtimes
socketley remove *
# Stops all and removes everything

Multiple names and glob patterns:

socketley stop myserver myclient
# Stops both runtimes
socketley stop my*
# Stops all runtimes starting with "my"
socketley stats cache?
# Shows stats for cache1, cache2, etc.
socketley start myserver cache*
# Starts myserver and all cache-prefixed runtimes
socketley remove api-* test-*
# Removes all api- and test- prefixed runtimes

Interactive mode (live terminal session):

# Start server and enter interactive session
socketley create server echo -p 9000
socketley start echo -i
# Type messages to broadcast, see received messages
# Press Ctrl+C to detach (server keeps running)

# Attach to already-running cache
socketley start mycache -i
# Type cache commands: set foo bar, get foo, etc.

Edit interactively (opens the JSON configuration in $EDITOR):

socketley edit myserver           # Opens config in editor
socketley edit myserver -r        # Opens editor, auto-reloads Lua after save
socketley edit myserver -p 9001   # Flag-based edit (direct)

Cache replication (leader-follower):

socketley create cache leader -p 9000 -s
socketley create cache follower -p 9001 --replicate 127.0.0.1:9000 -s

Encrypted server. The listener terminates TLS itself. Everything above it (line protocol, HTTP, WebSocket, RESP) runs on the decrypted stream, so this one runtime serves https:// and wss:// on the same port:

socketley create server secure -p 9443 \
    --tls --cert server.pem --key server-key.pem -s
curl --cacert server.pem https://localhost:9443/

Mutual TLS, where a client must present a certificate signed by the given CA:

socketley create server mtls -p 9443 \
    --tls --cert server.pem --key server-key.pem \
    --ca trusted-clients.pem -s

Renewing a certificate: the files are read at start, so reload picks up a new one.

socketley reload secure

An incomplete configuration is refused rather than served in the clear:

socketley create server oops -p 9443 --tls --cert server.pem
# --tls: a TLS listener needs --key <file> to go with --cert
# exit status 1

Encrypted client. The client mirrors the listener above: one flag turns TLS on. The client verifies the peer in two ways: the chain against the trust store, and the certificate against the host in -t.

# verify against the system trust store
socketley create client feed -t events.example.com:9443 --tls -s

# verify against a private CA instead
socketley create client feed -t 10.0.0.7:9443 \
    --tls --ca internal-ca.pem -s

# and present a certificate of our own, for a peer that demands one
socketley create client feed -t 10.0.0.7:9443 \
    --tls --ca internal-ca.pem \
    --cert client.pem --key client-key.pem -s

If the peer's certificate does not verify, the client closes the socket. It re-dials on its backoff and never falls back to cleartext. There is no skip-verify flag. Encryption without verification protects against somebody recording the wire, but not at all against somebody sitting on it, and from the outside the two look identical.

The same rules apply as on the listener. Half a certificate pair is refused, and a trust store without --tls is refused. reload installs a renewed client certificate:

socketley create client bad -t host:9443 --tls --cert client.pem
# --cert: needs --key <file> as well -- a certificate with no key
# presents nothing
# exit status 1

Graceful shutdown (drain pending writes):

socketley create server api -p 9000 --drain -s
socketley stop api   # Flushes write queues before closing

UDP server (fire-and-forget messaging):

socketley create server stats -p 9000 --udp -b -s
echo "cpu.load 0.42" | socat - UDP:localhost:9000

UDP client:

socketley create client udpcli -t 127.0.0.1:9000 --udp -s

Create a read-only cache (for shared lookups):

socketley create cache lookup -p 9000 --mode readonly -s

Master mode server (one controller, many viewers):

socketley create server broadcast -p 9000 \
    --mode master --master-pw secret -s
# Client A: sends "master secret" -> "master: ok"
# Client A: sends "hello" -> broadcast to all others
# Client B: sends "hello" -> silently dropped

Master mode with forwarding:

socketley create server ctrl -p 9000 \
    --mode master --master-pw admin123 --send-to master -s
# Non-master messages forwarded to master as "[<fd>] msg"

WebSocket server (auto-detected, no flags needed):

socketley create server ws -p 9000 -s
# Browser: new WebSocket("ws://localhost:9000")
# Raw TCP clients also work on the same port

Cache access through a server:

socketley create cache db -p 9001 -s
socketley create server api -p 9000 --cache db -s
# Client sends: "cache set user:1 alice" -> "ok"
# Client sends: "cache get user:1" -> "alice"
# Client sends: "hello" -> broadcast as usual

Dynamic proxy with group-based backend discovery:

socketley create server api1 -p 9001 -g api -s
socketley create server api2 -p 9002 -g api -s
socketley create proxy gw -p 8080 --backend @api -s
# Proxy routes to all running members of group "api"

# Add a new member dynamically (no proxy restart needed)
socketley create server api3 -p 9003 -g api -s

# Mix group and direct backends
socketley create proxy gw2 -p 8081 \
    --backend @api,10.0.0.5:9000 -s

Lua HTTP worker (auto-detected, no flags needed):

socketley create server api -p 9000 --lua handler.lua -s
# handler.lua:
# function on_http_request(req)
#     return {status=200, headers={["Content-Type"]="application/json"},
#             body='{"hello":"world"}'}
# end
# curl http://localhost:9000/api

Sidecar proxy with health checks and circuit breaker:

socketley create proxy sidecar -p 8080 --sidecar \
    --backend 127.0.0.1:3000 -s

Proxy with HTTP health checks and retries:

socketley create proxy gateway -p 8080 \
    --backend 10.0.0.1:9000,10.0.0.2:9000 \
    --health-check http --health-path /ready \
    --health-interval 10 --health-threshold 5 \
    --retry 3 --circuit-threshold 10 -s

Proxy with mTLS on both legs. The listener terminates TLS and demands a certificate from its callers. The backend leg dials TLS, verifies the chain and the endpoint's name, and presents a certificate of its own:

socketley create proxy secure -p 8443 \
    --tls --cert proxy.pem --key proxy-key.pem \
    --client-ca trusted-clients.pem \
    --client-cert backend-client.pem --client-key backend-client-key.pem \
    --ca mesh-ca.pem \
    --backend https://10.0.0.1:9000 -s
# Backend connections are pooled with their sessions: a handshake per
# idle period, not per request.
# --health-check http probes over TLS and verifies the backend too.

TLS to the backend only. The proxy listens in cleartext on loopback and encrypts the hop that leaves the machine:

socketley create proxy egress -p 8080 \
    --backend https://api.example.com -s
# Verified against the system CA store, name checked against the certificate.
# A private CA goes in --ca; there is no way to skip verification.

Open the live dashboard:

socketley dashboard
# Dashboard: http://localhost:9100/
# Open in browser for live runtime view

Query the dashboard API:

curl http://localhost:9100/api/overview
curl http://localhost:9100/api/runtimes
curl http://localhost:9100/api/runtime/myserver

Load a complex configuration from a Lua file:

socketley --lua /etc/socketley/setup.lua

sections.title: CLUSTER MODE
sections.html:
The cluster directory is as privileged as the daemons that read it. A proxy with an @group backend picks its targets from the files in that directory, so whoever can write there decides where that traffic goes. Treat write access to it exactly as you would treat access to the control socket: it belongs to the daemons and to nobody else. The intended arrangement is a shared volume between containers you control, not a directory that any other workload can write to.

Multi-daemon cluster discovery lets proxies route to runtimes on remote daemons. Each daemon publishes its state to a shared directory (typically a Docker volume) every 2 seconds. Entries whose heartbeat is older than 10s are stale, and are excluded automatically.

How it works:

  • Each daemon writes its state to dir/name.json

  • Every 2 seconds, each daemon scans the directory for peer files

  • Proxy @group resolution includes both local and remote group members

  • On graceful shutdown, the daemon deletes its file

Restarting a node, and name conflicts:

A name belongs to one node. If two daemons published the same file, every peer would get an endpoint set that belongs to neither of them. Traffic for api1 would also be split between two machines that each believe they are api1. So a daemon that finds its name held by a live entry is refused --cluster, and is told so.

A node that was killed and restarted is a different case. Every restart policy this project documents (a container restart, a redeploy, systemd's Restart=on-failure, a crash loop) brings the node back within a second or two. That is well inside the 10s threshold, so the node finds its own entry still fresh, and it reclaims it.

The entry records who wrote it: the advertised host, the daemon's control socket path, the kernel boot id, and the pid. A daemon may take over a fresh entry only when the first three are its own. That is a proof rather than a guess. A unix socket path admits one process at a time, and everything else that reaches a daemon connects to that path instead of binding it. So on one machine, under one hostname, whoever holds the path is the daemon, and an entry carrying our own three values was written by a process that is gone. A different machine has a different boot id, and a fresh entry cannot predate a reboot. The pid is published for the operator and never used to decide, because a restarted container has a new pid namespace.

What this cannot tell apart is two containers on one host that are given the same hostname and both use the default socket path. Their entries are identical, and so is the address every peer would dial for either of them.

A daemon that could not join keeps serving: it is a working server that is not in a cluster. It reports the failure in three places:

  • the exit status of the command;

  • an ERROR line in its log that names the holder;

  • every socketley cluster subcommand, which reports cluster mode is off with the reason, instead of the "not in cluster mode" that a daemon never given --cluster reports.

Clustering is never accepted and silently not applied.

Docker Compose example:

A complete, working example is examples/cluster/docker-compose.yml, and test/docker/ holds the same setup with assertions on it. Three things about it are not optional:

  • seccomp. Docker's default profile does not permit io_uring_setup(2), io_uring_enter(2) or io_uring_register(2). socketley's whole I/O layer is a ring, so under that profile every node dies at startup with failed to init event loop. Run the containers with a profile that allows those three syscalls; during development, use security_opt: [seccomp:unconfined].

  • entrypoint. The image's ENTRYPOINT is socketley, so a compose command: is passed to it as arguments. A node that needs a shell must set entrypoint: ["/bin/sh", "-c"], and give its script as a one-element list. Compose splits a bare string into an argv, and everything past the first & is lost.

  • Readiness. daemon --name and daemon --cluster are configuration commands sent to a daemon that is already running. When the socket does not answer, they start a detached daemon automatically. Sleeping for a second before running them is a race. If the race is lost, a second daemon is forked and the container goes down without a message. Wait for the daemon's own daemon started line instead.

Alternatively, use a Lua config file. socketley --lua does not start a daemon; when none answers yet, it fails and applies nothing. The one-second sleep below is the same race, so a real entrypoint should wait for the daemon started line here too:

-- /etc/socketley/setup.lua
daemon = { name = "api1", cluster = "/cluster" }
runtimes = {
    { type = "server", name = "web", port = 9001, group = "api", start = true }
}
socketley daemon &
sleep 1 && socketley --lua /etc/socketley/setup.lua

Inspecting the cluster:

socketley cluster ls
socketley cluster ps
socketley cluster group api
socketley cluster stats
socketley cluster watch

Stale detection:

ScenarioBehaviorRecovery
Graceful shutdownFile deletedImmediate
Container killedStale heartbeat~10 seconds
Container restartFile overwrittenImmediate

sections.title: Raft mode (experimental, opt-in)
sections.html:
Experimental. A daemon started with --raft-listen runs one Raft node on its own loop. Nothing else changes: the cluster directory above, and every runtime, proxy and cache that is not declared as a cluster runtime, behave exactly as they do without it. The Raft cluster elects a leader, replicates a log to disk and keeps the membership. The state machine behind the log holds the cluster's runtimes (see Cluster runtimes below). A cluster runtime is declared once, and the leader places it on distinct nodes. When a node dies, its runtimes are started on a survivor. A cache is replicated. When the node that holds its primary dies, the leader promotes the follower that holds the most (see Cluster caches below).

Flags (given on the command line that starts the daemon, like --cpus; refused together with --name and --cluster):

--raft-listen ip:port#

Enables Raft mode and accepts peer connections on this address. The address must be numeric, because a peer's address travels through the replicated log and is dialled without a DNS lookup.

--raft-advertise ip:port#

The address that peers dial, when it differs from the listening address. Required when --raft-listen is a wildcard.

--raft-name name#

This node's name in the membership, which its certificate must also carry. The certificate carries it as a DNS subjectAltName or common name. Default: the advertised address. A name belongs to one node. The leader refuses a node that joins under the name of a member. It also refuses a name that reads the same as a member's once {node} has made it safe for a command line (see Cluster runtimes). The refused node stops, with the reason in its log and in cluster raft-status. Two nodes with the same name would give every cluster runtime the same socket path or file.

--raft-init#

Founds a new cluster with a single voter, on first start only.

--raft-join ip:port#

Joins the cluster that the member at this address belongs to, on first start only. The node is added as a learner and receives the log without voting. Once its log has caught up to the leader's commit index, a single-server change promotes it to voter. The leader logs the promotion when it proposes it, and the node logs it once the change is committed. A member that is not the leader passes the request on.

--raft-cert file --raft-key file --raft-ca file#

Mutual TLS between members, which is required. Every member's certificate is signed by the CA. A connection is closed if its certificate does not name the member it introduces itself as. That name is the one the membership records for its id or, for a newcomer, the name it claims. The join target's id is not known yet, so its certificate is held to the address that was dialled.

--raft-insecure#

Runs Raft in cleartext. It is refused together with the certificate flags. Without this flag and without the certificate flags, the daemon refuses to start.

--raft-down-after duration#

How long the leader waits for a node's lease request before it declares the node down and moves its replicas. Takes seconds, or a value with an s or ms suffix (4, 4s, 3500ms). Default: four times the shortest election timeout, which is 4 s at the default tick. Values below three times the shortest election timeout (3 s at the default tick) are refused, because a leader change would then look like a node loss. Every member of one cluster should use the same value; see Cluster runtimes for what depends on it.

A daemon whose state directory already holds Raft state ignores --raft-init and --raft-join, and comes back as the member it was. A daemon with no state and neither flag refuses to start. A daemon that cannot bind the port or read its state exits 2, rather than serve without the cluster it was asked for.

On disk: state-dir/raft/ holds node-id (a random 64-bit id, generated once), wal-seq.log (CRC32C-checked records: hard state, entries, truncations) and snap-index-term files, all with mode 0600. Every write is followed by an fsync linked behind it in io_uring. Nothing a node says to a peer leaves before that fsync reports. Recovery cuts off a torn tail at the first bad record. The log is compacted every 1000 applied entries.

Timing: Raft ticks every 100 ms, measured from elapsed monotonic time. The election timeout is 1–2 s, a heartbeat is sent every tick, and pre-vote and check-quorum are used. A leader stopped by SIGTERM hands leadership to its most up-to-date voter (TimeoutNow) before it exits, so the cluster does not wait out an election timeout.

socketley cluster raft-status prints this node's id and name, role, term, leader, commit and applied indexes, the log's range, the voters and the learners. It also prints whether a quorum of voters was heard from within an election timeout, and the transport and WAL counters. It exits 0 when there is a leader and a reachable quorum, and 2 when there is not, saying so on its last line. It exits 1 on a daemon that is not in Raft mode.

Cluster runtimes. A cluster runtime is declared once, for the whole cluster, and every node applies the same log:

socketley cluster create server api -p 8080 --replicas 2
socketley cluster create server api --listen unix:/run/api-{node}.sock
socketley cluster scale api 3
socketley cluster remove api
socketley cluster placement

cluster create takes type, name and the flags that create takes, plus --replicas (default 1). The type is a server, a proxy, a client or a cache (see Cluster caches). The flags are stored as a list of arguments, so a value with a space in it stays one argument. They are run as they are on every node that holds a replica, so a file they name must exist on each node. A relative path is made absolute against the caller's directory, as for create. Any {node} in the flags is replaced by the name of the node running the replica (--raft-name, with every character other than letters, digits, -, _ and . replaced by _). That is what lets several nodes of a test share one host. Two replicas that both ask for -p 8080 would collide, and --listen unix:/run/api-{node}.sock does not. On separate hosts, each node binds its own -p and needs no placeholder. The node that takes the command also runs the flags through create --test. So a typo is refused there, with exit 1, instead of being found on every node at once. --test itself is refused in a spec.

A command may be given to any node; a follower hands it to the leader. Success is silent. When the command returns, it has taken effect on the node that took it. If it has not within five seconds, the CLI says so and exits 2. Exit 1 is a refusal: a duplicate, an unknown name, a replica count outside 1 to 64, a runtime of that name already on this node, or bad flags. Exit 2 means the cluster has no leader that can take the command. On a daemon that is not in Raft mode, every verb says so and exits 1.

cluster scale changes the replica count. When the count shrinks, it takes a replica from the most loaded node. A cluster runtime has no edit: remove it and declare it again.

Placement. The leader alone decides placement, and writes each assignment to the log, so every node agrees on it. The replicas of one runtime go to distinct nodes. Each replica goes to the node that holds the fewest replicas, and to the lowest node id on a tie. When a node is declared down, its replicas are moved to live nodes. A node that comes back, or a new node that joins, is not given work back. Nothing is rebalanced, so a running replica is never moved for tidiness. If more replicas are asked for than there are live nodes, the cluster runs what fits, and cluster placement says how many replicas are unplaced. cluster placement prints:

  • the runtimes with their replicas, where each is placed and how many are unplaced;

  • each cache's primary and the copies it has (see Cluster caches);

  • the nodes with the number of replicas each holds and, on the leader, whether the leader counts each one up and when it last heard from it;

  • this node's replicas with what each is doing: running, waiting for a lease, failed with the reason, or blocked by a local runtime of the same name.

On each node, a reconciliation runs at the end of every Raft tick. It compares what the log says the node owns with what the node runs. It creates a replica with create -s and stops, starts and removes it with stop, start and remove. This is the same code the CLI uses, and nothing else spawns a replica. The reconciliation never waits for a worker to come up, and runs at most four commands per tick. So a replica whose startup hangs, or fifty replicas arriving at once, cannot stall the Raft loop; a failure shows as the replica's state on a later tick. A replica that fails to start is tried again every three seconds. Its reason is logged once and shown by cluster placement. A local runtime with the same name is never touched. A replica is marked [cluster] after its state in ls and ps, "cluster":true in --json, and cluster:replica in stats. A replica has no state file, so a node that restarts does not bring back replicas that have moved away. stop, start, remove and edit refuse a replica by name, since the next tick would undo them.

Liveness and the lease. Every quarter election timeout, a follower asks the leader to count it alive. The leader answers when it holds a quorum. The leader declares a node down when it has not heard a request from it for --raft-down-after (the failure timeout). A new leader starts every node's clock at its own election. A node may run its replicas only while it holds a lease. The lease lasts three quarters of the failure timeout, counted from when the request was sent, so a late answer shortens it and a stalled loop cannot extend it. The leader's own lease is its last look at a quorum. The margin between the lease and the failure timeout is a quarter of the failure timeout (1 s by default). That margin is the time a node has to stop its replicas before the leader gives them to another node. A lease that had lapsed is used again only once the node has applied the leader's log up to where it ended when the lease was granted. So a node that comes back does not run a replica that moved while it was away.

Partitions and duplicates. A node that cannot reach a quorum stops serving its replicas within its lease. At the defaults this was measured at 2.9–3.8 s after the last answer. The node keeps the replicas defined, so they start again the moment it is granted a lease. The majority moves them after the failure timeout, at least a quarter of that timeout later. So a minority never serves what it cannot confirm it owns, even a minority that holds the old leader, and a healed node runs only what the log still gives it. The same holds for a leader that loses its quorum. It means that a cluster that loses its quorum stops serving every cluster replica, on every node, until it has a quorum again: the cluster chooses one copy or none over two.

A leader change can take longer than the lease, as with a split vote (about one in ten kills of a leader in simulation). It then stops a survivor's replicas until the new leader has granted a lease, a few hundred milliseconds after it is elected. The lease is enforced by the daemon's loop. So a daemon that is hung and not dead (SIGSTOP, a blocked disk) cannot stop the workers of a server, a proxy or a client, which are separate processes. A cache's worker fences itself (see Cluster caches). Whatever a replica does on its way down, such as a --drain that flushes its connections, spends part of the margin.

Failover time, from kill -9 of a node to its replica running on a survivor, was measured at the defaults. It was measured on one host with a real daemon, and in 60 seeds of a simulation of the same logic. It is about 3.9–4.3 s when the node was a follower (the failure timeout and a commit). It is about 5.1–6.0 s when the node was the leader (an election first). In the simulation it reached 8.7 s when a split vote stretched the election.

Cluster caches. A cache is a cluster runtime that holds data, so keeping it running is not enough:

socketley cluster create cache db -p 6379 --replicas 3
socketley cluster create proxy gw -p 7000 --backend @db --replicas 3

The leader places the replicas as for any runtime, and the log names one of them the primary of an epoch. An epoch is a number that only grows, so two leaders that race to promote agree on which was first. The other replicas are its followers. They follow it with the cache's own replication (--replicate: a full dump, then every write), dialling the primary's -p on the host that its node advertises to Raft. That is why a cluster cache needs -p. It is refused with --listen, --shards, --tls, --replicate (the cluster sets it) and without a port. On one host each replica needs its own port, which is what {node} is for: with nodes named 1, 2 and 3, -p 630{node} gives ports 6301, 6302 and 6303. On separate hosts a follower is a peer on another machine, and a cache serves such a peer only with --public. Put it in the spec (the tests here ran on one host and did not try it). A cache with one replica has a primary and nothing to promote. The first primary is the replica on the lowest node id. It is chosen once every replica has said it exists, or after an election timeout. A replica is a process the log can name (its incarnation). A restarted replica is another incarnation, holding nothing the old one did.

Who may write. A replica takes a client's command only under its worker's last order from its daemon. The daemon sends an order every 100 ms, and each order stands for the lease the daemon held when it sent it. A replica is in one of three roles:

  • a fenced replica answers every command, reads included, with an error, and refuses replicate;

  • a follower answers reads and refuses writes;

  • the primary takes writes.

A replica starts fenced. It leads only if this node holds a lease AND the log names the very process it runs as the primary. Otherwise it follows whoever the log names, or waits when nobody is named. A fence keeps the data: the process stays up. So a node that lost its quorum for a minute and got it back is the primary again, with everything it had. A follower keeps its link and its copy through a period without a lease. When the orders stop for any reason (the node lost its quorum, or the daemon hung or died), the worker fences itself when the last order runs out, without the daemon's help. Measured in nine runs with real daemons, a worker whose daemon was stopped with SIGSTOP refused writes after 2.7–3.1 s. A primary that lost its quorum stopped taking writes after 2.8–3.2 s. The lease is three quarters of the failure timeout, 3 s at the defaults.

Promotion. The leader replaces a primary in three cases:

  • nobody leads;

  • the primary's node has been declared down (in the same round that takes its replica away);

  • the primary's node is alive, but for the failure timeout it has not named, in a lease request, the process the log calls the primary.

The third case covers a primary whose daemon restarted: it comes back empty and does not lead, and a replica that has the data is promoted after that timeout. For each cache replica a node runs, every lease request carries the replica's incarnation, the epoch of the primary whose stream its copy came from, its offset in that stream, and whether it leads. The offset is a count of records. The primary counts every record it produces, whether or not a follower is connected. The end-of-dump marker carries the count at which the dump was taken. A follower's offset is that number plus the records it has applied since. A copy is empty from the first line of a dump to its last.

The leader promotes the replica whose copy is the most up to date. It compares epochs first (offsets of two primaries are not on one scale), then offsets, then the lowest node id. It writes the chosen replica to the log with the next epoch. The offsets the leader has are up to about half a second old (a stats push and a request interval). But by the time the leader looks, the primary has been gone for the failure timeout, so the followers' last reports are their final positions. A primary that comes back, or a node that is given a replica again, is a new process. It follows the primary of the epoch it finds, and takes a full dump that replaces whatever it held. So nothing it wrote that the cluster did not have survives, and it does not lead a cache whose log names another primary. A cache that is scaled down never loses its primary.

How long, from kill -9 of the node that holds the primary to a survivor taking a write, was measured on one host with real daemons at the default timing. It was 3.9–4.1 s when the node was not the Raft leader (the failure timeout and a commit; eleven kills). It was 5.2–5.7 s when the node was the leader (an election first; four kills). In a simulation of the same logic over 60 kills it was 4.1–4.2 s and 5.6–7.2 s; the longer ones were split votes. A follower dials the new primary within about a fifth of a second of being told. A proxy follows through the endpoint group that the primary is published as. The first write through a proxy on a survivor succeeded 20–95 ms after the first write made directly to the new primary (five runs).

What a failover can lose. Replication is asynchronous: the primary answers a write and streams it afterwards. So when the primary's node dies, the promoted follower lacks the acknowledged writes it had not received. What survives is always a prefix of the primary's history. Replication is ordered, and the tests read every acknowledged key back to check that no write is lost that a later one outlived. How long the lost tail is depends on how far behind the best follower was. It was measured with a client writing continuously and kill -9 of the primary's node, three kills each:

  • one connection writing one key at a time, about a thousand a second (4,500 to 4,900 acknowledged): none missing;

  • 200 writes pipelined at a time, as fast as one connection goes (630,000 to 720,000 acknowledged, some 230,000 a second): none missing;

  • the same, with both followers' workers stopped (SIGSTOP) for the four seconds before the kill, so that neither was receiving: about 1.6 million acknowledged and 876,000 to 922,000 of them missing. That is every write the primary took while no follower had it.

So the window is how far behind the best follower was when the primary died. It is a few writes when the followers keep up (the first two conditions lost none), and everything since a follower stopped reading when they do not. Only what a follower had already received survives. In a separate check, a stopped follower held about 20,000 of 925,000 acknowledged keys after its leader was killed. A primary drops a follower that is 8 MiB behind. After that, the primary keeps acknowledging writes that no follower is receiving, until that follower dials again. A machine that loses power, or a network that is cut, could not be tried without root. There is no synchronous mode: a write that must survive its primary is written to two caches.

Finding the primary. cluster placement prints, under CACHE PRIMARIES, each cache's primary and epoch. For each replica it also prints the epoch and offset of its copy, and how old that news is. The leader hears every node's news; the other nodes hear only their own. A proxy with --backend @name follows the primary. On every node that holds a lease, the cache's name is published as a group of one, the primary's host and port, and it is republished when the primary moves. The stats of a replica carry cluster_role, cluster_epoch, cluster_offset and cluster_incarnation.

Limits. A cache whose replicas all die at once starts again empty, because the data lived in memory. A --persistent file is loaded by a restarted process, but it does not take part in choosing the primary. It is replaced when the replica syncs from the primary that was chosen. A cache with one replica loses its data with its node. A worker that answers its daemon but takes no orders is not replaced.

Not yet:

  • removing a member;

  • snapshots sent in chunks (a snapshot goes in one frame of at most 16 MiB);

  • a cluster id that keeps two clusters from mixing;

  • editing a cluster runtime in place;

  • moving a replica off a node before the node is stopped for maintenance (a node stopped with SIGTERM keeps its assignments until the failure timeout);

  • a worker of a server, a proxy or a client that fences itself when its daemon is hung (a cache's worker does);

  • synchronous replication of a cache;

  • a replica that fails to start on one node being tried on another.

sections.title: Release Package
sections.html:
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/HiImSmiley/Socketley/main/install.sh | sudo sh

The script installs the newest release .deb. It asks before it installs each dependency that is missing. If the package was built for a newer distribution than this one, the script stops without changing anything. The script can also install a package you already have, answer every question with its default, and remove socketley; its --help describes these options.

sections.title: From Source
sections.html:
git clone https://github.com/HiImSmiley/Socketley
cd Socketley
bash scripts/install-from-source.sh

The script performs these steps:

  • checks the kernel, architecture and compiler;

  • installs the build dependencies;

  • builds liburing and the static archives the tree links against;

  • builds the Release configuration;

  • installs the binary, this manual page and the systemd service;

  • starts the daemon.

Its --help explains how to list every command without running any, and how to remove what the script installed.

sections.title: Quick Install
sections.html:
To install from a tree that is already built:

sudo bash packaging/install.sh
sudo systemctl start socketley

sections.title: Debian Package
sections.html:

sections.title: STATE PERSISTENCE
sections.html:
The daemon persists runtime configurations as JSON files. When a runtime is created, its configuration is saved. When the daemon starts, it restores all persisted runtimes. Runtimes that were running when the daemon stopped are started again automatically.

Runtimes therefore survive daemon restarts and system reboots, like Docker containers with the restart-always policy.

State is saved after the create, start, stop, remove and edit commands. The was_running field records whether a runtime should be started automatically when the daemon starts.

sections.title: A State File Is A Secret
sections.html:
A runtime's state file is not a note about the runtime: it is the runtime. The file holds these fields in plaintext:

master_pw#

The password given to --master-pw, stored verbatim.

key_path, mesh_client_key#

The paths of the TLS and mTLS private keys that this runtime uses.

lua_script#

The path of the handler script that the daemon loads. The handler runs with the daemon's privileges; see Handler Privileges under LUA CONFIGURATION.

The daemon restores every runtime from these files when it starts. Whoever can write one of these files therefore chooses what the daemon runs at its next start. That is the same power as being able to send the daemon commands.

For this reason the daemon creates the files with mode 0600, set explicitly at creation rather than inherited from its umask. The packaged state directory has mode 0750 and is owned by socketley:socketley. Neither mode is configurable, and there is no supported reason to widen them. An operator reaches this data through the CLI, over a socket with the same group boundary, not by reading the directory.

Earlier versions wrote these files 0666 & ~umask. That gave 0644 under systemd's default umask, and 0666 for a daemon started from a shell with umask 0. Any local user could read a master password, and in the 0666 case could also rewrite the record. On its first start after an upgrade, the daemon narrows every file it finds in its state directory to 0600 and logs how many it changed:

state: tightened 3 file(s) in /var/lib/socketley/runtimes to 0600 ...

The repair only ever narrows modes, and it is idempotent. It does not touch the directory itself, which belongs to the installer. If this line appears on every start, something outside socketley is putting the old modes back.

A password that was exposed should be treated as exposed. The repair closes the hole, but it cannot un-read what was already readable. Rotate any --master-pw that lived on a multi-user machine under an affected version, either with socketley edit or by recreating the runtime.

sections.title: ENVIRONMENT
sections.html:
All of these variables are optional. Each is read by the process that needs it, which for most is a runtime's worker process rather than the daemon. SOCKETLEY_SOCKET and SOCKETLEY_CONFIG select which daemon this is and which file it reads. EDITOR, VISUAL and TMPDIR are read by the command line, and the SOCKETLEY_GIT_* variables by the command that uses them. SOCKETLEY_FAST_LO is set by the daemon for its workers. The entries that begin "A test hook" are for the test suite. The rest are tuning knobs. Their defaults suit a general-purpose deployment and only need changing for an unusual workload.

You can also set each knob in the settings table of the daemon's configuration file, using its name in lower case and without SOCKETLEY_ (see Daemon Configuration). socketley settings lists every knob with its value and where that value came from. If a variable in the environment holds a number outside the knob's range, or not a whole number, the process that reads it logs this once and uses the default. The same value in the settings table stops the daemon instead (see Daemon Configuration).

SOCKETLEY_SOCKET#

Selects which daemon this is, or which daemon the CLI talks to. It overrides the default socket lookup (/run/socketley/socketley.sock when installed and privileged, otherwise /tmp/socketley.sock).

Details

No workload calls for setting it. A deployed node, whether a container or a host, has a filesystem namespace to itself. One daemon on the default path is then the whole arrangement, and that is what the systemd unit ships. Clustering does not use this variable either. Cluster members publish themselves into a shared directory and reach each other over network addresses, never over socket paths. See CLUSTER MODE.

The variable exists to run several daemons inside one namespace, which happens only in development and testing. Without it, two checkouts on one workstation, or two test runs at once, end up as the same daemon. Whichever process binds the default path first owns it, and every later one silently talks to that process instead of starting its own. Anything that starts a daemon on the default path claims the identity that the real daemon runs under. The test suite therefore gives every test a socket of its own.

The variable selects the state directory as well as the socket, and it must. Several daemons in one namespace that read one state directory do not behave as separate daemons. Each one restores everything in the directory at startup, including the others' runtimes, onto ports the others are already serving. And each remove deletes a state file that another, still running daemon depends on. See WHERE STATE LIVES.

SOCKETLEY_CPUS=max|0-3|0,1,2,3#

Sets the CPUs that the daemon's I/O thread may run on. Default: max, which applies no pinning at all, rather than a mask of the CPUs that happen to be online now.

Details

If the set names a CPU this machine does not have, or comes out empty, the daemon refuses it, logs a warning and runs unpinned. It never rounds the set up to max.

socketley daemon --cpus set sets the same thing on the command line, and wins when both are given. On the command line, an impossible set is refused outright and the daemon does not start. The reason is that a flag typed for this one run is a requirement, not an inherited default.

SOCKETLEY_CACHE_BUF_SIZE#

Sets the size in bytes of each buffer in a cache runtime's io_uring provided-buffer ring. Default: 65536. Larger buffers let one read completion carry more commands. The cost of the ring is its footprint (count times size) competing for the core's cache; see the section on the receive ring for what was measured.

SOCKETLEY_CACHE_BUF_COUNT#

Sets the number of buffers in that ring. Default: 64. Together with the buffer size, it bounds how much concurrent traffic the runtime can absorb before the pool runs dry. When the pool is dry, reads fall back to a slower per-read path. The pool costs count times size of memory per cache runtime.

SOCKETLEY_STORAGE_KILL_AFTER_RENAME#

A test hook that kills a sharded storage worker in the middle of a commit. When a commit's key begins with this string, the worker is killed with SIGKILL after it renames the body into place and before it writes the journal record. A test can thus put a crash at the one step that leaves a file the journal does not name. Unset by default.

SOCKETLEY_STORAGE_KILL_AFTER_EVENT#

A test hook that kills a storage worker after it records an event and before it makes the change. It applies to a change of a key that begins with this string, in a bucket that sends events for that change. The worker is killed with SIGKILL once the change's event record is durable and before the change itself is made. A test can then show that the restarted worker sends no event for the change. Unset by default.

Details

Inherited by worker processes, which have no command line of their own.

SOCKETLEY_STORAGE_HOLD_CONFIRM#

A test hook that makes a storage worker answer a change but never confirm it. For a key that begins with this string, the worker makes the change and answers it. It never writes the record that says the change was made, and never sends the change's events. This is the state a crash right after the answer would leave. A test can then kill the worker and show that the restarted worker sends the events. Unset by default.

Details

Inherited by worker processes, which have no command line of their own.

SOCKETLEY_STORAGE_PART_LIST_MAX#

A test hook that limits how many bytes a multipart object's part lists may take in its header. The limit applies separately to the part sizes, to the part numbers of an encrypted object, and to the parts' checksums. A list that would take more is stored after the object's body instead. Default: 4096, which takes some five hundred parts of unequal sizes to exceed. A small value lets a test reach a list stored after the body with only a few parts.

Details

Inherited by worker processes, which have no command line of their own.

SOCKETLEY_STORAGE_DOC_FAULT#

A test hook that makes a sharded storage runtime drop one phase of a bucket document change. The value is a directory. While a file named shard.phase (prepare, commit or abort) exists in it, that shard answers the message for that phase as an unreachable sibling would, without acting on it. A test can thus lose a message at each step of the change. Unset by default.

Details

Inherited by worker processes, which have no command line of their own.

SOCKETLEY_PROXY_HTTP3#

Set to 0 to stop a --tls entrance from opening a UDP socket for HTTP/3. The entrance then offers HTTP/3 to no client and names none in Alt-Svc. HTTP/2 over TCP is unaffected.

Details

Inherited by worker processes, which have no command line of their own.

SOCKETLEY_PROXY_HTTP2#

Set to 0 to turn HTTP/2 off at an entrance. The entrance then speaks HTTP/1.1 to every client over --tls. See the entrance under the dns runtime's --proxy.

Details

Inherited by worker processes, which have no command line of their own.

SOCKETLEY_STORAGE_HTTP2#

Set to 0 to turn HTTP/2 off for storage runtimes. A storage runtime then speaks HTTP/1.1 to every client. See HTTP/2 under the storage runtime.

SOCKETLEY_STORAGE_HTTP3#

Set to 0 to stop a --tls storage runtime from opening a UDP socket for HTTP/3. The runtime then offers HTTP/3 to no client. See HTTP/3 under the storage runtime.

SOCKETLEY_STORAGE_HTTP3_ADVERTISE#

Sets the port that the Alt-Svc header names for HTTP/3. Use it when a proxy in front forwards UDP from a port other than the runtime's own. 0 advertises no port. Default: the runtime's port.

SOCKETLEY_STORAGE_HTTP3_CC#

Selects the congestion controller that HTTP/3 sends with: bbr, cubic or reno. Default: bbr.

SOCKETLEY_STORAGE_HTTP3_RETRY_AFTER#

Sets how many QUIC handshakes may be under way before a new client is sent a Retry. A client that is sent a Retry must prove its address first. 0 sends a Retry to every client. Default: 64.

SOCKETLEY_STORAGE_SPLICE_MIN#

Sets the body size in bytes from which a storage GET is sent by splice from the file to the socket. Smaller bodies are read into memory and written instead. Default: 65536; 0 splices every body. Below the default, a read and a write cost less than the pipe a splice needs. This setting changes what zero_copy_bytes counts and how much CPU a GET takes, never what a GET returns.

Details

Inherited by worker processes, which have no command line of their own.

SOCKETLEY_STORAGE_HOT_BYTES#

Sets how many bytes of small objects a storage shard keeps in memory to answer repeated GETs. An object counts as small up to 60000 bytes. A GET for a kept object is answered without opening its file. A shard keeps objects of any key, whichever shard owns it. Default: 33554432 (32 MiB); 0 keeps nothing. This changes CPU use, GET throughput and the memory a worker holds, never what a GET returns.

Details

Inherited by worker processes, which have no command line of their own.

SOCKETLEY_STORAGE_COMPACT_FLOOR#

A test aid that sets the fewest records a bucket's journal must hold before a storage shard compacts it. Compaction rewrites the journal without its superseded records. Default: 4096. A test lowers it to see compactions without thousands of writes. This changes how often a journal is rewritten, never what it holds.

Details

Inherited by worker processes, which have no command line of their own.

SOCKETLEY_STORAGE_HASH_THREADS#

Sets how many helper threads a storage worker uses to compute the digests of large uploads. The digests are the ETag's MD5, any x-amz-checksum- the request asked for or the default CRC64NVME, and the SHA-256 that verifies a signed body (a hex payload hash or aws-chunked signatures). The threads keep the worker's loop from being the one core that all upload hashing has to fit in. Default: 3, or the machine's cores divided by the runtime's shards when that is fewer, but at least one. This way the shards' threads together do not outnumber the cores. 0 hashes on the loop.

Details

The first upload of 256 KiB or more (or of unknown length) starts the threads, and they end with the runtime. Smaller bodies are hashed in line, because the hand-off costs more than their digest. For the same reason, a body that arrives a few segments at a time is handed over 64 KiB at a time. This changes CPU use and the throughput of large puts, never what is stored.

Inherited by worker processes, which have no command line of their own.

SOCKETLEY_STORAGE_LIFECYCLE_DAY_SECS#

A test aid that sets how many seconds a bucket lifecycle rule counts as one day. The range is 1 to 86400. Only the lifecycle sweep reads it, and the sweep then also runs as often as every second. Unset, a day is a day. Because it changes when objects expire, never set it for a runtime holding data anyone wants (see Bucket lifecycle).

Details

Inherited by worker processes, which have no command line of their own.

SOCKETLEY_SHARE_NOTIFY_ALLOW#

Lists the URL prefixes, comma-separated, that a share link's webhook may begin with. Unset, the allowed prefixes are the webhooks of Discord, Slack and ntfy.sh (see Drive, links, media and the web interface).

Details

Inherited by worker processes, which have no command line of their own.

SOCKETLEY_SHARE_BURN_GRACE_SECS#

A test aid that sets how many seconds a burning share link's files outlive its last allowed download. Default: 600 (see Drive, links, media and the web interface).

Details

Inherited by worker processes, which have no command line of their own.

SOCKETLEY_RESOLV_CONF#

A test aid that names the file from which the resolver on a runtime's loop reads its nameservers, search list and options. The file uses the resolv.conf(5) format, so a test can point the resolver at a nameserver of its own. Default: /etc/resolv.conf (see What can stop the event loop). A mail runtime's SPF, DKIM and DMARC lookups also ask these nameservers.

Details

Inherited by worker processes, which have no command line of their own.

SOCKETLEY_MAIL_MX_PORT#

A test aid that sets the port on which a mail runtime hands mail to a domain's exchangers. Default: 25. A test's own server can then act as an exchanger.

Details

Inherited by worker processes, which have no command line of their own.

SOCKETLEY_MAIL_TLS_CA#

A test aid that names the CA file a mail runtime checks an exchanger's certificate against. It applies where DANE or MTA-STS asks for that check. Default: the system's roots. A test's own exchanger can then be trusted.

Details

Inherited by worker processes, which have no command line of their own.

SOCKETLEY_MAIL_STS_CA#

A test aid that names the CA file a mail runtime checks an MTA-STS policy server against. Default: the system's roots.

Details

Inherited by worker processes, which have no command line of their own.

SOCKETLEY_MAIL_STS_CONNECT#

A test aid that sets the host:port from which every MTA-STS policy is fetched. The name in the policy's URL is still the one checked. A test can thus serve the policies of domains it does not own. Default: each policy's own host.

Details

Inherited by worker processes, which have no command line of their own.

SOCKETLEY_MAIL_DELAY_NOTICE_MS#

A test aid that sets how many milliseconds a mail runtime tries a message before it tells the sender the message is late. This applies only to senders who asked for the notice (NOTIFY=DELAY). Default: four hours.

Details

Inherited by worker processes, which have no command line of their own.

SOCKETLEY_MAIL_SPOOL_MOVE_MS#

A test aid that sets how many milliseconds a sealed spool segment waits before it is used again. Before the segment is reused, the few messages still in it are moved. Default: one minute.

Details

Inherited by worker processes, which have no command line of their own.

SOCKETLEY_MAIL_DEAD_DOMAIN_MS#

A test aid that sets how many milliseconds a mail runtime holds on to a domain that cannot take mail. This covers a domain it found not to exist or to take no mail. After this time, the runtime looks the domain up again. Default: ten minutes.

Details

Inherited by worker processes, which have no command line of their own.

SOCKETLEY_MAIL_PUSH_CONNECT#

A test aid that sets the host:port to which every JMAP push is posted. The certificate is still checked for the name in the push URL. A test can thus receive the pushes of a URL it does not own. Default: the URL's own host.

Details

Inherited by worker processes, which have no command line of their own.

SOCKETLEY_MAIL_PUSH_CA#

A test aid that names a file of CA certificates for checking a JMAP push URL's certificate. Default: the system's CA certificates.

Details

Inherited by worker processes, which have no command line of their own.

SOCKETLEY_MAIL_IDLE_MS#

A test aid that sets how many milliseconds a connection to a mail runtime may stay quiet before it is closed. The same limit applies to how long a TLS handshake may take. The runtime tells the client before it closes the connection. Defaults: five minutes for SMTP, POP3 and ManageSieve, thirty minutes for IMAP, and thirty seconds for a handshake.

Details

Inherited by worker processes, which have no command line of their own.

SOCKETLEY_MAIL_BAYES_FOLD_MS#

A test aid that sets how many milliseconds new spam filter learning stays in a mail runtime's journal. After this time, the first shard folds it into the filter's file. Default: ten minutes.

Details

Inherited by worker processes, which have no command line of their own.

SOCKETLEY_MAIL_LET_GO_MS#

A test aid that sets how many milliseconds a shard of a mail runtime, other than the first, keeps a user's index in memory after nothing on that shard asked for it. The index is read again from its files when it is next asked for. Default: ten minutes.

Details

Inherited by worker processes, which have no command line of their own.

SOCKETLEY_IDP_CLIENT_CA#

A test aid that names a file of CA certificates for checking the client metadata documents an idp fetches. The certificate served with each such document is checked against this file. Default: the system's CA certificates.

Details

Inherited by worker processes, which have no command line of their own.

SOCKETLEY_IDP_CLIENT_CONNECT#

A test aid that sets the host:port from which every client metadata document is fetched. The name in the document's address is still the one sent and checked. Default: the host in that address.

Details

Inherited by worker processes, which have no command line of their own.

SOCKETLEY_IDP_COMPACT_AFTER#

A test aid that sets how many account changes an idp runtime journals before it folds them into its snapshot. A test can thus see the snapshot written while changes go on. Default: 1000.

Details

Inherited by worker processes, which have no command line of their own.

SOCKETLEY_MAIL_SPOOL_FROZEN_US#

A test aid that names every message of a mail runtime after this fixed microsecond instead of the clock. Writers in two shards then produce the same name, as they would if they wrote in the same microsecond. Default: the clock.

Details

Inherited by worker processes, which have no command line of their own.

SOCKETLEY_MAIL_QUEUE_SCALE#

A test aid that runs a mail runtime's retries and --queue-lifetime this many times faster. A test can then see a message tried again and given up within seconds. Default: 1.

Details

Inherited by worker processes, which have no command line of their own.

SOCKETLEY_MAIL_BUSY_HOLD_MS#

A test aid that sets how many milliseconds a mail runtime pauses a domain after one of its exchangers answered 421. During the pause, the runtime opens no new connection to that domain. Each further 421 doubles the pause, up to fifteen minutes, until a message is taken. Default: thirty seconds.

Details

Inherited by worker processes, which have no command line of their own.

SOCKETLEY_MAIL_SPOOL_KEEP_BYTES#

A test aid that sets how many bytes of message bodies a mail spool keeps in memory beside its segments. Default: 64 MiB. A small value lets a test have bodies read back from disk.

Details

Inherited by worker processes, which have no command line of their own.

SOCKETLEY_STORAGE_NOTIFY_HOSTS#

A test aid that names a hosts file for a storage runtime's notification webhooks. The file holds one name address pair per line. The webhooks' resolver reads it before the system resolver, on every resolve, so a test can point a webhook's host name at another address. Unset, a name is asked of the resolver on the loop and then of the system's resolver (see Event notifications).

Details

Inherited by worker processes, which have no command line of their own.

SOCKETLEY_STORAGE_NOTIFY_QUEUE#

Sets the most undelivered events a storage shard holds. Beyond that, a new event is dropped and counted in notify_dropped. Default: 10000. A test lowers it to reach the bound.

Details

Inherited by worker processes, which have no command line of their own.

SOCKETLEY_STORAGE_CLUSTER_QUEUE#

Sets the most changes a storage shard queues for another node of its cluster. Beyond that, the shard lets the queued changes go. Once that node answers, the shard sends it everything instead (see Cluster). Default: 100000. A test lowers it to reach the bound with a few writes.

Details

Inherited by worker processes, which have no command line of their own.

SOCKETLEY_STORAGE_REPLICATION_HOSTS#

A test aid that names a hosts file for a storage runtime's replication targets. The file holds one name address pair per line. The targets' resolver reads it before the system resolver, on every resolve, so a test can name a target by a host name. Unset, a name is asked of the resolver on the loop and then of the system's resolver (see Replication).

Details

Inherited by worker processes, which have no command line of their own.

SOCKETLEY_STORAGE_STOP_HOLD_MS#

A test aid that makes a storage shard's stop wait before it lets go of its directory. The value is in milliseconds, 0 to 3000. The wait starts after the shard's in-flight work has finished, and it is multiplied by the shard's number plus one. A test can thus start a runtime beside shards that are still stopping. Unset, a stop waits only for its own work. It slows every stop and restart, so never use it on a runtime in use.

Details

Inherited by worker processes, which have no command line of their own.

SOCKETLEY_STORAGE_START_SPIN_MS#

A test aid that makes a storage shard's start keep the CPU busy before it opens its store. The value is in milliseconds, 0 to 30000. The shard uses CPU the way reading a large store's files does.

Details

Inherited by worker processes, which have no command line of their own.

SOCKETLEY_STORAGE_START_SLEEP_MS#

A test aid that makes a storage shard's start wait idle before it opens its store. The value is in milliseconds, 0 to 60000. This imitates a wedged start.

Details

Inherited by worker processes, which have no command line of their own.

SOCKETLEY_STORAGE_LOG_FLUSH_MS#

A test aid that sets how long a storage shard holds server access log lines before it delivers them. The value is in milliseconds, 100 to 3600000. Default: one minute.

Details

Inherited by worker processes, which have no command line of their own.

SOCKETLEY_STORAGE_RECOVERY_THREADS#

Sets how many threads a storage worker uses to read its object headers when it starts after an unclean stop. The range is 1 to 64. Default: the number of CPUs the worker may run on, at most 16. The threads end before the listener opens. This changes how long such a start takes, never what it finds.

Details

Inherited by worker processes, which have no command line of their own.

SOCKETLEY_STORAGE_RECOVERY_DEPTH#

Sets how many opens and header reads each recovery thread keeps in flight on an io_uring of its own. The range is 0 to 256. Both this value and the thread count are lowered to fit within half of what RLIMIT_NOFILE leaves. Default: 32; 0 reads one file at a time without a ring. This changes how long a start from a cold cache takes, never what it finds.

Details

Inherited by worker processes, which have no command line of their own.

SOCKETLEY_STORAGE_RECV_BUFS#

Sets how many 16 KiB buffers a storage worker's receive ring holds; the value must be a power of two. Default: 64; 0 removes the ring, and every connection reads into a buffer of its own. A connection borrows a buffer only for the length of one completion, so an idle keep-alive connection holds none. When a receive finds the ring empty, it uses a buffer of its own for that one read. Such reads are counted as recv_fallbacks in stats. This changes the memory a worker holds, never what it returns.

Details

Inherited by worker processes, which have no command line of their own.

SOCKETLEY_TLS_FAILURE_REPORT_SECS#

Sets how often a runtime serving TLS logs one line counting the inbound handshakes that failed since its last report. Default: every 60 seconds; the range is 1 to 3600. A failed handshake comes from a port scanner far more often than from a client, so each one is counted rather than logged.

SOCKETLEY_TLS_TICKET_SECS#

A test aid that sets how many seconds one session ticket key seals new tickets. The key still opens its tickets for as long again, and is then wiped. The range is 1 to 86400. Default: an hour.

Details

Inherited by worker processes, which have no command line of their own.

SOCKETLEY_WRITE_STALL_SECS#

A test aid that sets how many seconds a server or proxy client with no --idle-timeout may take nothing of its answer before the connection is reset. The range is 1 to 86400. Default: 120 seconds.

Details

Inherited by worker processes, which have no command line of their own.

SOCKETLEY_ACME_DIRECTORY#

Sets the directory URL of the ACME CA that --acme and acme issue use. Default: Let's Encrypt, https://acme-v02.api.letsencrypt.org/directory. Its staging CA is https://acme-staging-v02.api.letsencrypt.org/directory. Each CA has an account of its own.

Details

Inherited by worker processes, which have no command line of their own.

SOCKETLEY_ACME_CHALLENGE#

Sets the challenge type that acme issue and --acme use to prove a name when no type is requested. The values are http-01 (the default), tls-alpn-01 and dns-01. A wildcard name is always proven over DNS-01, whatever this variable says.

Details

Inherited by worker processes, which have no command line of their own.

SOCKETLEY_ACME_DNS_WAIT#

Sets the seconds between publishing a DNS-01 answer and telling the CA to look for it. The answer is published where the dns runtimes serve it. The wait is the time a secondary of the zone has to take the new serial, and the delegation probe gives the secondary the same time. Default: 10, at most 3600. A secondary that is told by NOTIFY and transfers on it takes seconds. For a secondary that waits for its refresh, set this to the minutes the refresh takes.

Details

Inherited by worker processes, which have no command line of their own.

SOCKETLEY_ACME_DNS_PROBE#

Names the resolver that acme issue asks whether a zone is delegated to this daemon's dns runtimes. The value has the form host[:port]. acme issue asks about a zone of --dns-zones before it proves anything there over DNS-01. It then asks each name server of the zone, by its IPv4 addresses, the way a CA would. off asks nothing and treats every zone as delegated. Default: the first nameserver of /etc/resolv.conf.

Details

Inherited by worker processes, which have no command line of their own.

SOCKETLEY_ACME_CA#

Names a PEM file of root certificates for checking the ACME CA's own HTTPS. Use it for a CA whose certificate no system store holds, such as Pebble. Default: the system's roots.

Details

Inherited by worker processes, which have no command line of their own.

SOCKETLEY_GIT_ACCESS_KEY#

Holds the access key that git-sync uses to write into a library. A storage runtime that starts git-sync gives it temporary credentials of the user for whom the repository is kept.

SOCKETLEY_GIT_SECRET#

Holds the secret of that access key.

SOCKETLEY_GIT_SESSION_TOKEN#

Holds the session token of temporary credentials, sent as x-amz-security-token.

SOCKETLEY_GIT_TOKEN#

Holds a GitHub token that git-sync uses to read a private repository. git-sync gives it to git as an http.extraHeader in git's environment, never on a command line.

SOCKETLEY_FFMPEG#

Names the ffmpeg that a storage runtime uses to make thumbnails and streams under /~media/. The runtime reads what a film is with the ffprobe beside that ffmpeg, or the one on PATH. Default: the first ffmpeg on PATH. With neither, a media request is answered 501. The runtime reads this variable at its first media request.

Details

Inherited by worker processes, which have no command line of their own.

SOCKETLEY_MEDIA_HWACCEL#

Selects where a storage runtime encodes its renditions. off always uses x264 on the CPU. A render node such as /dev/dri/renderD129 uses that GPU. The default is /dev/dri/renderD128.

Details

At its first medium, a worker runs one second of test picture through the GPU's whole chain (upload, scale, H.264 encode). It tries the full encoder and then the low-power one. The worker uses the GPU for renditions only when one of them works; until it knows, renditions use x264. A rendition keeps the encoder that its first job chose. If a rendition's first GPU job fails before anything is made, that rendition continues with x264. HLG is tone-mapped on the CPU, HDR10 on the GPU. vaapi-unchecked:node skips the test run, for testing that fallback.

Inherited by worker processes, which have no command line of their own.

SOCKETLEY_MEDIA_CACHE_MB#

Sets the size in MiB beyond which a storage runtime removes the media it made from dir/.media/. It removes the least recently requested media first. Default: 10240. The medium made last is kept even when it alone is larger, and no medium is removed while it is being made.

Details

Inherited by worker processes, which have no command line of their own.

SOCKETLEY_CACHE_TTL_SWEEP_MS#

Sets the interval in milliseconds between periodic sweeps for expired cache keys. Default: 500. This never affects correctness: an expired key is not served no matter when the sweep runs, because every read path checks the expiry itself. The interval controls only how quickly keys that are never accessed again release their memory.

SOCKETLEY_CACHE_SNAPSHOT_MB#

Sets how many MiB a cache shard's journal (--persistent-interval) may hold before the shard snapshots, unless its last dump is larger, in which case that size is the bound. Default: 64. The snapshot is written by a forked child, so the shard goes on serving; the journal is then cut to what came after the snapshot began.

SOCKETLEY_LUA_TIMEOUT_MS#

Sets how long, in milliseconds, one Lua callback invocation may hold the event-loop thread. Default: 10000. 0 switches the bound off entirely: nothing is armed or written for a callback. LuaJIT's trace compiler is on either way. The budget is measured from the start of the callback's loop turn and checked every 100 milliseconds, and a compiled callback that cannot be interrupted is ended by replacing its worker. See Callback Deadline.

Details

This is the default for every script that does not declare its own callback_timeout_ms global; a script that declares one overrides it. A value that is not a whole number of milliseconds in 0–3600000 is refused with a warning, and the default is used.

Inherited by worker processes, which have no command line of their own.

SOCKETLEY_HTTP_REVALIDATE#

Set to 0 to switch off the response cache of plain --http. Each request then costs an open, a read and a close again. Any other value, or leaving the variable unset, keeps the cache on. The variable is read when the runtime starts, so a restart picks up a change. The server serves the same content either way, because the cache is revalidated on every request. The switch exists for measurement, and for ruling the cache out when diagnosing something else.

Details

Inherited by worker processes, which have no command line of their own.

SOCKETLEY_KERNEL_TLS#

Set to 0 to keep every TLS record in this process. Otherwise, some TLS 1.3 connections hand their sending to the kernel's TLS layer. This happens in six cases. A server, storage or proxy connection sends a file or object over 256 KiB. A TCP proxy's backend streams that much to the client. An HTTP/1.1 proxy sends a client an answer body of that known length. A cache connection is owed 2 MiB or more at once. An mqtt client is sent a packet of 256 KiB or more. A mail client is sent a reply of 4 MiB or more, without COMPRESS.

Details

The connection then changes its send key and hands the new key to the kernel's TLS layer. The kernel encrypts what is sent, by sendfile from the page cache or spliced from the backend, at about half the CPU of encrypting a copy in this process. A cache's answer is in memory and has no sendfile to gain, so the kernel only spares it the copies OpenSSL makes: measured over loopback, 2 MiB answers cost 0.83 and 8 MiB 0.53 of the CPU, while 1 MiB and smaller cost the same or more, which is why a cache waits for 2 MiB. A connection that never sends that much stays as it was, because for small answers encrypting a copy here costs less. An mqtt payload under kernel TLS is not copied at all, so the broker gains from 256 KiB: measured over loopback, a 1 MiB publish to 20 TLS subscribers costs 0.56 of the CPU, a 256 KiB one 0.68. A mail FETCH of 8 MiB costs 0.61, of 4 MiB 0.79, while at 1 and 2 MiB the move gains nothing it can hold to, so mail waits for 4 MiB. The move is for the rest of the connection: a 1 KiB answer on a moved cache connection costs what it did, a 256 KiB one about a tenth more. HTTP/2 connections are never moved.

This needs the kernel's tls module (modprobe tls). Without the module, the connection continues in user space under its new key, and the runtime says so once in its log. The variable is read when the runtime starts.

Inherited by worker processes, which have no command line of their own.

SOCKETLEY_PROXY_SPLICE#

Makes a --protocol tcp proxy splice a pair from its first byte to its last, not only while a side streams. Unset by default; any value other than 0 turns it on. It is read once per process and inherited by worker processes.

Details

Without the variable, each side of a pair decides for itself. A side copies through a buffer until four reads in a row have filled it, which marks a stream. It then moves its bytes with splice(2) through a pipe. The splice is called on the event loop, with both sockets non-blocking for the call. It never goes through io_uring, whose splice is an io-wq hand-off per transfer. Four splices in a row that would not have filled the buffer mark messages. The side then goes back to copying and gives its pipe back. Each switch waits until nothing of the other path is in flight or queued, so no byte overtakes another. Measured on one core, over loopback, through the proxy:

                        copy             adaptive         from the first byte
4 GB stream             3.4-4.2 GB/s     9.3-9.9 GB/s     10.1 GB/s
  CPU per GB            0.24-0.30 s      0.08-0.11 s      0.08-0.10 s
64 B messages, 32 conns 6.95 us           6.86 us          10.36 us
4 KB messages           7.41 us           7.37 us          9.28 us

So the variable is for measuring, not for speed. A TLS listener or TLS backend never splices. Neither does a pair with a 127.0.0.1 leg while the daemon runs with --fast-lo. A proxy with an on_proxy_request or on_proxy_response hook never splices either, because the kernel would move those bytes without the script ever seeing them. Nor does a proxy with a --rate-limit or --global-rate-limit, which is charged per read.

SOCKETLEY_FAST_LO#

Set by a daemon started with --fast-lo once the shortcut is attached; it is not a setting. The value is own, all or trust. It tells the daemon's workers to keep a proxied pair with a 127.0.0.1 leg off splice. The daemon clears any inherited value at startup.

SOCKETLEY_NAPI_BUSY_POLL_US#

Enables io_uring NAPI busy polling with this timeout in microseconds. Unset by default. It trades CPU for lower receive latency on busy links.

SOCKETLEY_HUGEPAGE#

Set to 0 to stop cache workers from asking glibc for transparent huge pages. On by default, and only a cache asks for them. A cache's hot path walks a keyed structure larger than the TLB covers, which is what a huge page is for. A server showed no measured gain for the extra resident memory. glibc reads the tunable at process startup, and a running process cannot ask for itself. The daemon therefore puts it in the worker's environment at exec.

SOCKETLEY_RECV_MULTISHOT#

Set to 0 to arm one read at a time instead of a multishot receive. On wherever the kernel supports it. A multishot arm is one submission for a stream of messages instead of one per message. The switch exists so that the two can be measured against each other on one binary. A dns runtime's TCP connections read one at a time either way: a client's pipelined queries arrive several to a read, and there a multishot receive cost more CPU per query than the submissions it saved.

SOCKETLEY_RECV_BUNDLE#

Set to 0 to stop packing several provided buffers into one receive (IORING_RECVSEND_BUNDLE). On where the kernel supports it. Support is probed once rather than assumed, and the receive falls back to the plain multishot arm wherever the flag is refused.

Details

Both of these variables read only the exact string 0. SOCKETLEY_RECV_MULTISHOT=off leaves multishot on, which is the opposite of what it looks like. The SOCKETLEY_NO_* switches below follow the other rule: any value except 0 turns the feature off.

SOCKETLEY_NO_SHARD_MESH#

Any value but 0 stops shards from linking to each other directly. The shards then relay through the daemon, and the daemon logs at startup that the mesh is off. This is the measurement control for the mesh: the two paths differ only in the route, not in the build. A request or answer longer than the 8 MiB one frame holds goes in pieces, through the daemon as over a link, up to 256 MiB. Requests and answers for a shard that has not read them yet wait on each side of the daemon up to 64 MiB, and beside that one of up to 256 MiB; past that, an asker is answered at once, as the runtime is overloaded: its request backlog is full, not as no such runtime. Everything else the daemon and a shard tell each other (configuration, publishes, deliveries) waits up to 4 MiB of its own beside them.

SOCKETLEY_CACHE_HANDOFF#

0 stops a sharded cache from handing a client connection to the shard that owns its keys; it then relays each of that connection's commands there instead. On by default for every cache with two or more shards. A connection is handed once 28 of its last 32 single-key commands named one other shard, over the link between the two shards, and only between commands: never inside MULTI or WATCH, while subscribed, blocked or replicating, with a reply or crossing outstanding, or over TLS, a unix socket or a per-shard port. A connection handed on waits a second at its new shard before it may move again, twice as long after each further move. stats shows handoff_out, handoff_in, handoff_aborted and handoff_busy per shard while it is on.

SOCKETLEY_NO_PEER_LINKS#

Any value but 0 stops runtimes from opening direct links to their peers. It exists for the same reason as SOCKETLEY_NO_SHARD_MESH and is read the same way.

SOCKETLEY_NO_COMPANION#

Any value but 0 stops a unix-socket listener from being placed beside a port.

RES_OPTIONS#

Passes options to glibc's resolver; socketley itself does not read it. If you have not set it, socketley sets it for worker processes to timeout:1 attempts:2.

Details

It is set because getaddrinfo(3) blocks the thread that calls it. In a worker, that thread is the event loop, with the daemon's control socket armed on the same ring. While a lookup waits, stop and stats go unanswered. glibc's own default is five seconds, twice. Against a nameserver that drops packets, that measured 10.0 s for one lookup. And a client re-resolves on every reconnect once its cached address stops accepting. One second twice has the same ceiling as two seconds once, and still retries a lost packet.

If you set it yourself, your value is used unchanged, for the daemon and every worker. Raise it if a slow but working nameserver is being given up on. The cost of giving up is one more reconnect round, not a failed runtime.

EDITOR , VISUAL#

Name the editor that socketley edit opens when given no flags. VISUAL is tried first.

TMPDIR#

Sets where that editor's temporary file is written. While the editor is open, the file holds the runtime's entire configuration; for a cache, that includes master_pw. If /tmp is shared, point this at a directory of your own. The file is created 0600 and removed when the editor exits.

SOCKETLEY_DNS_CACHE_MS#

Sets how long, in milliseconds, socketley.http() reuses a resolved address before it asks the resolver again. Default: 60000. 0 disables reuse and makes every call resolve.

Details

This is a ceiling, not a promise. If a connect to the cached address is refused or times out, the entry is dropped at once. An endpoint that moved is then followed on the next call. So this value only decides how long the cache stays wrong about an endpoint that moved without refusing, which is when something else answers on the old address.

The cache exists because getaddrinfo(3) blocks the thread that calls it, glibc caches nothing of its own, and in a worker that thread is the event loop. Every other resolver in this daemon is bounded by something. A client and a server re-resolve at most once per second of reconnect backoff, a proxy once per thirty-second sweep, and the rest once at start. Without the cache, socketley.http() would resolve on every call. It resolves on a thread of its own and gives up at the call's deadline. A resolver that does not answer therefore costs a call its timeout, rather than costing the loop every retry the resolver makes.

SOCKETLEY_RAFT_TICK_MS#

Sets the Raft tick, in milliseconds, of a daemon started with --raft-listen. Default: 100. The election timeout is ten to twenty ticks, and a heartbeat is sent every tick. Every member of one cluster should therefore use the same value.

SOCKETLEY_RAFT_COMPACT_EVERY#

Sets how many applied Raft entries go by between snapshots. Default: 1000. A small value makes a joining node catch up through a snapshot; the test suite sets it for that purpose.

SOCKETLEY_CONFIG#

Sets the path to the daemon configuration file.
