Sets the size in bytes of each buffer in a cache runtime's io_uring provided-buffer ring. Default: 65536. Larger buffers let one read completion carry more commands. The cost of the ring is its footprint (count times size) competing for the core's cache; see the section on the receive ring for what was measured.

Sets the number of buffers in that ring. Default: 64. Together with the buffer size, it bounds how much concurrent traffic the runtime can absorb before the pool runs dry. When the pool is dry, reads fall back to a slower per-read path. The pool costs count times size of memory per cache runtime.

A test aid that sets the fewest records a bucket's journal must hold before a storage shard compacts it. Compaction rewrites the journal without its superseded records. Default: 4096. A test aid that sets how many seconds a bucket lifecycle rule counts as one day. The range is 1 to 86400. Only the lifecycle sweep reads it, and the sweep then also runs as often as every second. Unset, a day is a day. Because it changes when objects expire, never set it for a runtime holding data anyone wants (see Bucket lifecycle).

Lists the URL prefixes, comma-separated, that a share link's webhook may begin with. Unset, the allowed prefixes are the webhooks of Discord, Slack and ntfy.sh (see Drive, links, media and the web interface).
A test aid that sets how many seconds a burning share link's files outlive its last allowed download. Default: 600 (see Drive, links, media and the web interface).

A test aid that names the file from which the resolver on a runtime's loop reads its nameservers, search list and options. A test aid that names the CA file a mail runtime checks an MTA-STS policy server against. Default: the system's roots.

Set by a daemon started with --fast-lo once the shortcut is attached; it is not a setting. The value is own, all or trust. It tells the daemon's workers to keep a proxied pair with a 127.0.0.1 leg off splice. The daemon clears any inherited value at startup.
Enables io_uring NAPI busy polling with this timeout in microseconds. Unset by default. It trades CPU for lower receive latency on busy links.

Set to 0 to stop cache workers from asking glibc for transparent huge pages. On by default, and only a cache asks for them. A cache's hot path walks a keyed structure larger than the TLB covers, which is what a huge page is for. A server showed no measured gain for the extra resident memory. glibc reads the tunable at process startup, and a running process cannot ask for itself. The daemon therefo

Set to 0 to arm one read at a time instead of a multishot receive. On wherever the kernel supports it. A multishot arm is one submission for a stream of messages instead of one per message. The switch exists so that the two can be measured against each other on one binary. A dns runtime's TCP connections read one at a time either way: a client's pipelined queries arrive several to a read, and ther

Set to 0 to stop packing several provided buffers into one receive (IORING_RECVSEND_BUNDLE). On where the kernel supports it. Support is probed once rather than assumed, and the receive falls back to the plain multishot arm wherever the flag is refused.

Any value but 0 stops shards from linking to each other directly. The shards then relay through the daemon, and the daemon logs at startup that the mesh is off. This is the measurement control for the mesh: the two paths differ only in the route, not in the build. A request or answer longer than the 8 MiB one frame holds goes in pieces, through the daemon as over a link, up to 256 MiB. Requests an

0 stops a sharded cache from handing a client connection to the shard that owns its keys; it then relays each of that connection's commands there instead. On by default for every cache with two or more shards. A connection is handed once 28 of its last 32 single-key commands named one other shard, over the link between the two shards, and only between commands: never inside MULTI or WATCH, while s
Any value but 0 stops runtimes from opening direct links to their peers. It exists for the same reason as SOCKETLEY_NO_SHARD_MESH and is read the same way.
Any value but 0 stops a unix-socket listener from being placed beside a port.
Passes options to glibc's resolver; socketley itself does not read it. If you have not set it, socketley sets it for worker processes to timeout:1 attempts:2.
Name the editor that socketley edit opens when given no flags. VISUAL is tried first.

Sets where that editor's temporary file is written. While the editor is open, the file holds the runtime's entire configuration; for a cache, that includes master_pw. If /tmp is shared, point this at a directory of your own. The file is created 0600 and removed when the editor exits.
Sets how long, in milliseconds, socketley.http() reuses a resolved address before it asks the resolver again. Default: 60000. 0 disables reuse and makes every call resolve.

Sets the Raft tick, in milliseconds, of a daemon started with --raft-listen. Default: 100. The election timeout is ten to twenty ticks, and a heartbeat is sent every tick. Every member of one cluster should therefore use the same value.
Sets how many applied Raft entries go by between snapshots. Default: 1000. A small value makes a joining node catch up through a snapshot; the test suite sets it for that purpose.
Sets the path to the daemon configuration file.

sections.title: THE IPC SOCKET
sections.html:
Every socketley command travels over the socket above, and through it a client can reach everything the daemon can do. That includes stopping a runtime, reading stats, rewriting a runtime's configuration with edit, and running arbitrary code as the user the daemon runs as. The last is possible because a --lua handler runs with the daemon's privileges; see Handler Privileges under LUA CONFIGURATION.

Opening the socket is therefore an administrative right, and the socket's mode reflects that:

/run/socketley/socketley.sock   0660  socketley:socketley
any other path                  0600  the user who started the daemon

The packaged daemon runs as socketley, and the operator does not. The packaged socket is therefore shared with one group, and membership of that group grants the right:

sudo usermod -aG socketley "$USER"     # then log in again

A daemon on any other path keeps its socket to itself. This covers a development daemon and a daemon started with SOCKETLEY_SOCKET. The mode is owner-only rather than owner-and-group because a shared primary group is not unusual. Several distributions put every user in users, and there the daemon's group is every human on the machine.

Earlier versions made this socket 0666 (world-writable) on both paths. Any local uid could drive any daemon on the machine, whoever it belonged to. After an upgrade, a user who has been running socketley against a system daemon without being in the socketley group gets this error:

not permitted to open the daemon socket at /run/socketley/socketley.sock

That user needs to be added to the group. A user who is not added is not locked out of the program. With the system socket unreachable, the CLI falls back to development mode and starts a daemon of the user's own, with that user's privileges and that user's runtimes.

On a machine where two people use development mode at once, the second person gets the same message about /tmp/socketley.sock. The path has one owner, and the socket is no longer shared. Sharing it was never a supported arrangement; it was a shared daemon that nobody had asked for. Give each person a socket of their own:

export SOCKETLEY_SOCKET="/tmp/socketley-$USER.sock"

This also gives each person a state directory of their own; see WHERE STATE LIVES.

sections.title: WHERE STATE LIVES
sections.html:
The two directories above are where a daemon's runtimes live when the daemon serves the default socket. That covers every deployed daemon, and every daemon that has never heard of SOCKETLEY_SOCKET. This has not changed and will not change.

A daemon on any other socket path gets a directory of its own. The directory is a sibling of the default one and is named after the socket path: the leading slash is dropped, and every character outside A-Za-z0-9._- becomes an underscore.

SOCKETLEY_SOCKET unset          ~/.local/share/socketley/runtimes
SOCKETLEY_SOCKET=/tmp/a.sock    ~/.local/share/socketley/runtimes.tmp_a.sock
SOCKETLEY_SOCKET=/tmp/socketley.sock
                                ~/.local/share/socketley/runtimes

Setting the variable to the path that would have been used anyway counts as the default, not as a second daemon. A script that spells out the default therefore keeps the default directory. The directory name is readable rather than hashed on purpose: the answer to "which of these is mine" should come out of an ls.

At startup the daemon logs the directory it is using (state directory: ...), and that line is the authoritative answer. Learn where to find it before you need it.

Upgrading. The first time a daemon uses one of these keyed directories, it copies everything from the shared directory it used to read into the new directory, once. An INFO line says how many runtimes were adopted and from where. The originals stay exactly where they are, so an older binary rolled back onto the machine still finds what it has always found. A .adopted file in the new directory records what happened, and makes the copy a one-time event. Without that file, an operator who later removed every runtime would find them all back after the next restart.

...but never out from under a running daemon. Adoption is skipped entirely while a daemon is serving the default socket path. Those runtimes belong to that daemon, and adopting them would mean binding ports it is already serving. The check is a probe of the default path; anything answering there, daemon or not, is enough to skip adoption.

This is not a rare corner. An operator debugging beside a running daemon gets into this situation with one command. The second bind succeeds under SO_REUSEPORT, so nothing but the port count would ever have reported the problem.

The daemon logs the skipped adoption at WARN, with both directory paths and what to do about it, because from the outside it looks exactly as if the runtimes had vanished. It writes no .adopted marker, because "somebody is using these right now" is a fact about this minute, not a decision. So once the daemon on the default path is stopped, restarting this one adopts the runtimes as normal.

The failure this trades against. A daemon started with a SOCKETLEY_SOCKET that it did not have last time finds no runtimes. On a development machine that is correct: it is a different daemon, and it owns nothing. It cannot happen to a deployed node. A deployed node runs on the default path with the variable unset, and the default path is exempt from the rule for exactly that reason. If it happens anyway, nothing has been destroyed. The other directory is still on disk with everything in it, and starting the daemon with the variable it had before brings it all back.

The alternative, one state directory for every daemon in the namespace, is not the safe direction. Two daemons then bind each other's ports on boot, and each reports the other's runtimes as its own. A remove sent to either one deletes a state file the other is still serving, and that cannot be undone.

sections.title: Daemon Configuration
sections.html:
The daemon configuration file is a Lua script that sets a daemon table:

daemon = {
    name = "node1",          -- this daemon's name in a cluster
    cluster = "/shared/dir", -- cluster directory; needs name
    log_level = "info",      -- debug, info, warn, error
    metrics_port = 9100,     -- Prometheus metrics HTTP endpoint
    dashboard_credentials = "/etc/socketley/admin.creds",
                             -- the dashboard's admins sign in from here
    dashboard_idp = "auth",  -- or as admins of this idp runtime
    alert_webhook = "https://discord.com/api/webhooks/...",
                             -- where alerts are posted
    alert_mail = "mail://m/ops@example.com",
                             -- and mailed, by this mail runtime
    events = "bus",          -- an mqtt runtime the runtimes' states and
                             -- the alerts are published on
    cpus = "0-3",            -- where this daemon's I/O runs
    settings = {             -- any SOCKETLEY_* knob, by its short name
        storage_hash_threads = 4,
        lua_timeout_ms = 2000,
        proxy_splice = true,
    }
}

config is the older name of the same table and still works. A file that sets both is refused rather than merged. name and cluster are the two keys that socketley --lua can also set on a daemon that is already running. Every other key is read only from this file, when the daemon starts. A --cpus typed on socketley daemon outranks the file.

settings sets any variable under ENVIRONMENT that an operator may change, by its name in lower case and without SOCKETLEY_. For example, storage_hash_threads is SOCKETLEY_STORAGE_HASH_THREADS. Write a number as a number, an on-or-off value as true or false, and anything else as a string. The daemon puts each setting in the environment it starts its workers with, so a runtime reads the file's value just as it would read the variable's.

The file takes precedence. A variable in the daemon's own environment counts only for a setting that the file does not name. The default applies only when neither sets a value. The daemon reports each of these on standard output and does not start:

  • a name that is not a setting;

  • a value outside the setting's range;

  • a variable that a command reads from its own environment: the SOCKETLEY_GIT_* variables, and SOCKETLEY_SOCKET and SOCKETLEY_CONFIG, which choose this file; also a variable the daemon sets for its workers, such as SOCKETLEY_FAST_LO.

socketley settings shows the values that were taken.

When metrics_port is set, the daemon starts an HTTP endpoint. It serves a live web dashboard at GET /, Prometheus exposition format metrics at GET /metrics, and JSON API endpoints at /api/overview, /api/runtimes, and /api/runtime/<name> (see DASHBOARD). The metrics include runtimes total/running, connections total/active, messages total, bytes in/out, and per-runtime breakdowns. Among the per-runtime metrics are socketley_runtime_cpu_seconds_total, socketley_runtime_resident_memory_bytes (resident memory, with a shared page counted once per shard) and socketley_runtime_memory_bytes (what the runtime costs the machine, with a shared page counted by the share it holds). The daemon's own metrics are socketley_daemon_cpu_seconds_total and socketley_daemon_memory_bytes.

Each running runtime also exports the figures of its own stats. Each figure becomes a metric in a family named after the runtime's type, with the label name. The families are:

  • socketley_server_*

  • socketley_client_*

  • socketley_proxy_*, among them _backends, _healthy_backends, _backend_responses_total and _backend_failures_total

  • socketley_cache_*, among them _keys, _get_hits_total and _get_misses_total

  • socketley_db_*

  • socketley_dns_*, with socketley_dns_queries_total by transport and socketley_dns_responses_total by rcode

  • socketley_idp_*, among them _sign_ins_barred_total (sign-ins refused for too many failures)

  • socketley_mqtt_* (messages by qos, drops by reason)

  • socketley_sync_*, among them _failing

  • the storage, mail and tunnel families under STORAGE FLAGS (Metrics). A tunnel edge also adds socketley_tunnel_agents_joined (the agents expected to be linked) and socketley_tunnel_agents_connected (the agents that are linked).

Counters end in _total. A figure that no family names is exported as socketley_type_stat with its name in the label stat.

Beside these are the facts that the daemon's alerts look at. Each is a series that an alert rule can read:

  • socketley_runtime_state (labels name, type, state): 1 for the state a runtime is in, 0 for the other three.

  • socketley_runtime_restarts_total: the times a worker went down and was started again.

  • socketley_cert_expiry_seconds (labels name, path): the seconds until the certificate a runtime serves with ends, below 0 once it has ended. It is read every five minutes.

  • socketley_disk_free_ratio, socketley_disk_free_bytes and socketley_disk_size_bytes (label path): the state directory's disk and each storage runtime's disk, each disk once.

  • socketley_host_memory_available_ratio, _available_bytes and _total_bytes.

  • socketley_runtime_quota_ratio: how much of its limit a storage with --max-bytes, or a cache with --maxmemory and no eviction, holds.

  • socketley_mail_blocklisted: 1 while a blocklist from a mail runtime's --dnsbl names the address the runtime sends from.

  • socketley_git_mirror_failed (labels name, repo, id): 1 when the last pull of a storage's git mirror failed, read every minute. The error label holds what the failed pull said.

  • socketley_runtime_failure (labels name, type, reason): 1 for a runtime that failed, with its last warning or error line as the reason.

  • socketley_runtime_bytes_received_total and _sent_total, per runtime.

The time work takes is a Prometheus histogram per runtime. The buckets start at 64 microseconds and double up to 16.8 seconds, plus +Inf. Each request is measured from the start of the loop turn that read it to the start of the turn that answered it. A request answered in the turn it came in therefore measures 0, and no clock is read for it. The histograms are:

  • socketley_proxy_request_duration_seconds (from an HTTP request's head to its answer's last byte)

  • socketley_proxy_backend_connect_duration_seconds and socketley_proxy_backend_first_byte_seconds

  • socketley_server_http_request_duration_seconds

  • socketley_cache_batch_duration_seconds (from a read's commands to their replies being handed on)

  • socketley_db_request_duration_seconds

  • socketley_idp_sign_in_duration_seconds

  • socketley_mail_delivery_duration_seconds

  • socketley_storage_request_duration_seconds

Each histogram has _bucket (le), _sum and _count, with the shards' values added together. For example, histogram_quantile(0.99, rate(socketley_proxy_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])) reads the 99th percentile of the proxy request histogram.

sections.title: C++ SDK
sections.html:
Socketley ships a modular C++ SDK in three tiers, in include/linux/socketley/. Tiers 1 and 3 are self-contained, header-only files. Copy them anywhere and compile with g++ -std=c++17; no library is needed. Tier 2 must be built from source.

TierHeaderUse CaseDependencies
1socketley/control.hControl a running daemonNone (POSIX)
2socketley/{server,cache,proxy,client}.hEmbed the full enginelibsocketley_sdk.a
3socketley/attach.hRegister with a daemonNone (Tier 1)

sections.title: Tier 1: Daemon Control (header-only)
sections.html:
socketley/control.h gives a program full control over a running daemon. It uses the same Unix socket IPC as the CLI and needs nothing beyond POSIX.

Result type:

struct socketley::result {
    int         exit_code;  // 0=success, 1=bad input, 2=fatal, -1=connect fail
    std::string data;       // response body
};

Runtime management functions (all in namespace socketley::ctl):

command(cmd)               // raw command (glob patterns work)
command(socket_path, cmd)  // custom socket path
create(type, name, flags)  // "server", "client", "proxy", "cache"
start(name)                stop(name)
remove(name)               send(name, message)
ls()   ps()   stats(name)  show(name)
reload(name)               reload_lua(name)
edit(name, flags)

Cache string operations (over direct IPC; no TCP connection is needed):

cache_get(cache, key)           cache_set(cache, key, value)
cache_del(cache, key)           cache_exists(cache, key)
cache_incr(cache, key)          cache_decr(cache, key)
cache_incrby(cache, key, n)     cache_decrby(cache, key, n)
cache_append(cache, key, val)

Cache list operations:

cache_lpush(cache, key, val)    cache_rpush(cache, key, val)
cache_lpop(cache, key)          cache_rpop(cache, key)
cache_llen(cache, key)          cache_lrange(cache, key, start, stop)
cache_lindex(cache, key, idx)

Cache set operations:

cache_sadd(cache, key, member)  cache_srem(cache, key, member)
cache_sismember(cache, key, m)  cache_scard(cache, key)
cache_smembers(cache, key)

Cache hash operations:

cache_hset(cache, key, f, v)    cache_hget(cache, key, field)
cache_hdel(cache, key, field)   cache_hlen(cache, key)
cache_hgetall(cache, key)

Cache TTL:

cache_expire(cache, key, sec)   cache_ttl(cache, key)
cache_persist(cache, key)

Cache pub/sub:

cache_publish(cache, ch, msg)

Cache admin:

cache_size(cache)               cache_memory(cache)
cache_keys(cache, pattern)
cache_flush(cache [, path])     cache_load(cache [, path])

To find the daemon's socket, the functions check the SOCKETLEY_SOCKET environment variable first, then /run/socketley/socketley.sock, then /tmp/socketley.sock. Set the variable only to reach a daemon other than the one for this namespace. In practice that means a second daemon on a development machine. A deployed node runs one daemon on the default path.

Example: lifecycle management

#include <socketley/control.h>
#include <cstdio>

int main() {
    auto r = socketley::ctl::create("server", "myapp", "-p 9000 -s");
    if (r.exit_code != 0) return 1;

    socketley::ctl::send("myapp", "Hello from C++!");
    auto stats = socketley::ctl::stats("myapp");
    printf("%s\n", stats.data.c_str());

    socketley::ctl::stop("myapp");
    socketley::ctl::remove("myapp");
}
// g++ -std=c++17 myapp.cpp -Iinclude/linux -o myapp

Example: fleet management with globs

for (int i = 0; i < 5; ++i) {
    std::string name  = "api_" + std::to_string(i);
    std::string flags = "-p " + std::to_string(9000+i) + " -s";
    socketley::ctl::create("server", name, flags);
}
socketley::ctl::command("start api_*");    // start all
socketley::ctl::command("stats api_*");    // query all
socketley::ctl::command("stop api_*");     // stop all
socketley::ctl::command("remove api_*");   // remove all

Example: cache operations

socketley::ctl::create("cache", "store", "-p 6379 --mode admin -s");
socketley::ctl::cache_set("store", "user:1", "alice");
auto r = socketley::ctl::cache_get("store", "user:1");
printf("user:1 = %s\n", r.data.c_str());  // "alice"
socketley::ctl::cache_del("store", "user:1");
socketley::ctl::cache_flush("store", "/tmp/store.bin");

sections.title: Tier 2: Embed Engine (build from source)
sections.html:
Tier 2 embeds the full io_uring event loop and all four runtime types in your own binary. It gives maximum performance, with no IPC overhead. It requires libsocketley_sdk.a and the link flags -luring -lssl -lcrypto [-lluajit].

Headers: socketley/core.h (event_loop, runtime_manager, enums), socketley/server.h , socketley/client.h , socketley/proxy.h , socketley/cache.h .

Define SOCKETLEY_NO_LUA to build without LuaJIT, and omit -lluajit from the link flags.

High-Level Wrapper Classes (recommended)

The socketley::server, socketley::client, socketley::proxy, and socketley::cache classes wrap the raw engine API in a fluent, chainable interface. They handle all the boilerplate (event loop, runtime manager, signal handling) internally.

socketley::server

server(uint16_t port)

// Config (all return server& for chaining)
tls(cert, key)         // terminates TLS on this listener
client_ca(ca)          // mutual TLS on it: clients must present a certificate
                       // (tls_ca(ca) is the older spelling; it also sets tls)
max_connections(n)     rate_limit(r)
global_rate_limit(r)   idle_timeout(s)       lua(path)
mode(m)                udp()                 http_dir(path)
http_cache()           upstream(addr)        master_pw(pw)
drain()                group(g)              tick_interval(ms)

// Callbacks (return server& for chaining)
on_start(void())                             on_stop(void())
on_connect(void(int fd))                     on_disconnect(void(int fd))
on_message(void(int fd, string_view msg))    on_tick(void(double dt_ms))

// Actions
send(fd, msg)       broadcast(msg)      disconnect(fd)
peer_ip(fd)         clients()           multicast(fds, msg)
set_data(fd,k,v)    get_data(fd,k)

// Lifecycle
start()   stop()

// Escape hatches (raw engine access)
instance() -> server_instance*
manager()  -> runtime_manager&
loop()     -> event_loop&

socketley::client

client(string_view host, uint16_t port)

// Config
tls()              // dial over TLS; the host from the constructor is pinned
                   // and the chain verified against the system trust store
tls_ca(ca)         // verify against that CA instead of the system store
client_cert(c, k)  // the certificate this client presents when the peer asks
                   // for one - the client half of mutual TLS; needs tls()
reconnect(max)     mode(m)            udp()
lua(path)          tick_interval(ms)

// Callbacks
on_start    on_stop    on_connect    on_disconnect
on_message(void(string_view msg))   on_tick

// Actions
send(msg)

// Lifecycle: start()  stop()
// Escape hatches: instance()  manager()  loop()

socketley::proxy

proxy(uint16_t port)

// Config
backend(addr)      strategy(s)        protocol(p)
tls(cert, key)     // terminates TLS on this proxy's listener
client_ca(ca)      // mutual TLS on it: clients must present a certificate
backend_ca(ca)     // trust store for the backend leg; turns that leg to TLS
client_cert(c, k)  // the certificate presented to a backend that asks
max_connections(n) idle_timeout(s)
lua(path)          group(g)

// Callbacks: on_start  on_stop
// Lifecycle: start()  stop()
// Escape hatches: instance()  manager()  loop()

socketley::cache

cache(uint16_t port)

// Config
persistent(path)   max_memory(bytes)   eviction(policy)
resp()             mode(m)
tls(cert, key)
max_connections(n) idle_timeout(s)     replicate(target)
lua(path)          group(g)

// Callbacks: on_start  on_stop
// Lifecycle: start()  stop()
// Escape hatches: instance()  manager()  loop()

Limitations: Only one start() may run per process, because the signal handler points to one event_loop. start() blocks until SIGINT or SIGTERM. For several runtimes in one process, or for asynchronous patterns, use the raw API, either through the escape hatches or directly.

TLS: on a server, a proxy, a client and a cache. server().tls() and proxy().tls() terminate TLS on that runtime's listener. proxy().backend_ca(), proxy().client_ca() and proxy().client_cert() configure the proxy's two legs, exactly as the CLI flags do. This works because start() goes through runtime_manager::start and reaches the same gate as the CLI. client().tls() dials over TLS, and cache().tls() terminates it on the cache's listener, through the same gate. See TLS under LIMITATIONS.

Example: echo server (3 lines)

#include <socketley/server.h>
#include <cstdio>

int main() {
    socketley::server srv(9000);

    srv.on_connect([](int fd) {
        printf("client %d connected\n", fd);
    });
    srv.on_message([&](int fd, std::string_view msg) {
        srv.send(fd, "echo: " + std::string(msg));
    });
    srv.on_disconnect([](int fd) {
        printf("client %d disconnected\n", fd);
    });

    srv.start();
}
// g++ -std=c++23 echo.cpp $(sdk/socketley-config --cflags --libs)

Example: server with Lua scripting

int main(int argc, char* argv[]) {
    socketley::server srv(9000);
    srv.lua(argv[1]);
    srv.start();
}

Example: TCP proxy

socketley::proxy px(8080);
px.backend("127.0.0.1:9001")
  .backend("127.0.0.1:9002")
  .protocol(protocol_tcp)
  .strategy(strategy_round_robin);
px.start();

Example: Redis-compatible cache

socketley::cache c(6379);
c.persistent("/var/data/store.dat")
 .resp()
 .max_memory(256 * 1024 * 1024)
 .eviction(evict_allkeys_lru);
c.start();

Example: client with auto-reconnect

socketley::client cli("127.0.0.1", 9000);
cli.reconnect(0);  // 0 = infinite
cli.on_connect([&](int) { cli.send("hello"); });
cli.on_message([](std::string_view msg) {
    printf("%.*s\n", (int)msg.size(), msg.data());
});
cli.start();

Raw Engine API (advanced)

For processes with several runtimes, or for custom control of the event loop, use the raw types directly. The wrapper classes use this API internally.

Core pattern: create an event_loop, create a runtime_manager, create the runtimes, configure them, run them, and run the loop.

C++ callbacks (an alternative to Lua scripts; they can be set on any runtime):

set_on_start(function<void()>)
set_on_stop(function<void()>)
set_on_connect(function<void(int fd)>)
set_on_disconnect(function<void(int fd)>)
set_on_client_message(function<void(int fd, string_view)>)
set_on_message(function<void(string_view)>)
set_on_tick(function<void(double dt_ms)>)

Common runtime setters:

set_port(uint16_t)            set_event_loop(event_loop*)
set_runtime_manager(mgr*)     set_cache_name(string_view)
// set_tls / set_cert_path / set_key_path / set_ca_path are honoured
// on a server runtime and refused on every other type (see LIMITATIONS).
set_max_connections(uint32_t)
set_rate_limit(double)        set_idle_timeout(uint32_t)
set_log_file(string_view)     set_group(string_view)
set_drain(bool)               load_lua_script(string_view)

Server-specific:

set_mode(mode_inout|mode_in|mode_out|mode_master)
set_udp(bool)          set_http_dir(string_view)
broadcast(msg)         send_to(fd, msg)
disconnect(fd)         peer_ip(fd)
clients()              multicast(fds, msg)

Cache-specific:

set_mode(cache_mode_readonly|readwrite|admin)
set_persistent(path)   set_max_memory(bytes)
set_resp_forced(bool)  set_replicate_target(host:port)

Proxy-specific:

set_protocol(protocol_http|protocol_tcp)
set_strategy(strategy_round_robin|random|lua)
add_backend(addr)      clear_backends()

Example: multi-runtime with raw API (server + cache)

#include <socketley/server.h>
#include <socketley/cache.h>

// ... (event_loop + runtime_manager setup as above)

mgr.create(runtime_cache, "store");
auto* cache = static_cast<cache_instance*>(mgr.get("store"));
cache->set_port(6379);
cache->set_mode(cache_mode_admin);
cache->set_runtime_manager(&mgr);
cache->set_event_loop(&loop);

mgr.create(runtime_server, "api");
auto* srv = static_cast<server_instance*>(mgr.get("api"));
srv->set_port(9000);
srv->set_cache_name("store");  // clients can "cache set k v"
srv->set_runtime_manager(&mgr);
srv->set_event_loop(&loop);

mgr.start("store", loop);
mgr.start("api", loop);
loop.run();

sections.title: Cross-Platform SDK (Windows / macOS)
sections.html:
These header-only TCP clients connect to Socketley runtimes from non-Linux platforms. One copy lives in include/portable/socketley/, and a program reaches it as <socketley/ws_client.h> from any of include/linux, include/darwin or include/windows.

socketley/ws_client.h is a WebSocket (RFC 6455) and raw TCP client for server runtimes. It embeds its own SHA-1 and Base64, so it needs no OpenSSL. Its modes are ws_mode::websocket and ws_mode::raw_tcp.

socketley/cache_client.h is a text-protocol client for cache runtimes. It supports all cache commands (get, set, del, lpush, sadd, hset, expire, publish, subscribe, etc.). It returns a cache_result with the fields ok, value, values, integer.

Build with C++17; there are no external dependencies:

# MSVC
cl /std:c++17 /I include\windows app.cpp

# clang++ (macOS)
clang++ -std=c++17 -I include/darwin app.cpp -o app

# g++ (Linux)
g++ -std=c++17 -I include/linux app.cpp -o app

sections.title: Tier 3: Daemon Attach (header-only)
sections.html:
socketley/attach.h registers your own process as a runtime with a running daemon. After it attaches, your process shows up in socketley ls, socketley stats, and socketley ps. The header is self-contained (it builds on control.h). It deregisters automatically on exit().

API:

bool daemon_attach(name, type, port)  // register, auto-detach on exit
void daemon_detach(name)              // explicit deregister
void daemon_detach()                  // deregister attach'd name

Example:

#include <socketley/attach.h>
#include <cstdio>

int main() {
    // Start your own TCP server (any framework)
    // ...bind, listen on port 8080...

    if (socketley::daemon_attach("myservice", "server", 8080))
        printf("registered with daemon\n");
    else
        printf("daemon not running (standalone mode)\n");

    // Your accept loop here...
    // atexit() automatically calls daemon_detach()
}
// g++ -std=c++17 myapp.cpp -Iinclude/linux -o myapp

daemon_attach() returns false when the process is not allowed to open the daemon's IPC socket. Every socketley command needs the same permission; see THE IPC SOCKET under FILES. A program that runs as a different user from the daemon must be in the socketley group to register with it. A false result is not an error to abort on. The example above shows the intended pattern: the program runs standalone and is simply not listed in the daemon's inventory.

sections.title: Mixed: Engine + Daemon Attach (Tier 2 + 3)
sections.html:
Embed the full engine for maximum performance, and register with the daemon for fleet monitoring. This combines the strengths of both tiers.

#include <socketley/server.h>
#include <socketley/attach.h>

socketley::server srv(9000);
srv.on_message([&](int fd, std::string_view msg) {
    srv.send(fd, msg);
});

// Register with daemon so socketley ls/stats can see it
socketley::daemon_attach("app_srv", "server", 9000);

srv.start();  // daemon sees the runtime

When to use each tier:

Tier 1#

Use it for orchestration scripts, deployment tools, monitoring and CI/CD.

Tier 2#

Use it for custom daemons, game servers, IoT gateways and performance-critical services.

Tier 3#

Use it for legacy services, third-party processes, and fleet visibility for external apps.

Mixed#

Use it for an embedded engine with daemon monitoring: maximum performance with fleet management.

sections.title: WebSocket and other protocol upgrades
sections.html:
A proxy in http mode relays a connection that has switched protocols. This is what lets a ws:// client work through it. This section describes what that relay does, and what it deliberately does not do.

Only the two endpoints negotiate the upgrade; nothing between them takes part. The proxy forwards the request's Upgrade and Connection headers unchanged, instead of stripping them as hop-by-hop headers. It relays the 101 response verbatim and computes no part of it. It does no Sec-WebSocket-Accept calculation, does not check that the key matches, and has no opinion about the protocol named. The proxy reacts to the 101, not to the token, so it relays any upgrade that two endpoints agree on in the same way. The exception is h2c (and h2). The proxy strips that offer, together with its HTTP2-Settings field, and answers it as a plain request. HTTP/2 behind a 101 would carry every later request past the checks the proxy makes on each request head.

Frames are never parsed. After the 101, the connection carries opaque bytes. The proxy does not know where one frame ends and the next begins. So it does no fragmentation handling, answers no ping or pong on a backend's behalf, negotiates no permessage-deflate, and applies no per-message limit. --max-connections still counts connections; nothing counts frames. The on_proxy_request and on_proxy_response callbacks still see these bytes. However, they see whatever one read delivered, not whole frames. A callback that rewrites them corrupts the stream, because a frame carries its own length and a client-to-server frame is masked.

A tunnelled backend connection is never pooled. There is no message boundary at which to return it to the pool. So one WebSocket uses one backend TCP connection for its whole life, however long that is. A proxy in front of many long-lived WebSocket clients holds that many backend sockets.

The deadlines behave as follows. --backend-timeout limits the wait for the backend's first response byte, and the 101 is that byte. So it applies to the handshake and stops applying the moment the protocol switches. A tunnel is not measured against it, and the proxy never answers 504 because a tunnel is quiet. That is intended: on a tunnel, nothing may arrive for minutes. --idle-timeout still applies. On a tunnelled connection it counts bytes in either direction, not only what the client sends, so a stream the backend is feeding is not idle. A tunnel that is silent in both directions for longer than the timeout is closed, like any other connection.

The circuit breaker counts a tunnel as one successful response (the 101) and nothing more. A session that ends is a connection closing, and the proxy does not charge it to the backend. In stats, the bytes relayed after the 101 are counted in bytes_in and bytes_out. total_messages counts the reads that carried them, not frames or requests. So a proxy carrying WebSocket traffic reports figures that do not match messages in either protocol's sense.

A proxy in --protocol tcp mode is not affected by any of this. It was already a byte relay and never looked at a status line.

sections.title: What can stop the event loop
sections.html:
A process serves its runtimes on one thread: a worker serves its one runtime, and the daemon serves the runtimes that scripts make in it. A call that waits therefore stops every runtime of that process. Five places make such calls, and they are listed here.

The figures were measured where measuring was possible, on a Lua echo server and a static file server under load. Each cost is given as a share of a worker's CPU on a healthy machine. The figures do not say what the same call costs when the disk is busy or the resolver is down, which is the case where they matter.

  • socketley.http() outside a callback that can wait. The whole exchange blocks, once per call from a script: name resolution, the connect and the transfer. It is bounded by the call's timeout_ms and by the callback's remaining budget. In on_message, on_client_message, an mcp tool's handler and the other callbacks that can wait, the call instead waits on the loop and blocks nothing.

  • open(2) and fstat(2) in the static file path, once per request that --http-cache does not answer. Measured at about 4.8 per cent of the worker: 1.7 in the kernel's open path and 3.1 in statx, which is what glibc turns an fstat into.

  • getaddrinfo(3) on a client's first dial and in a proxy's setup. Both happen before the runtime serves anything, so a start against a resolver that is not answering takes as long as the resolver does. Other lookups ask the nameservers of /etc/resolv.conf from the loop itself, after checking /etc/hosts. These are a client's reconnect, a server's upstream, a cache's --replicate, a proxy's later lookups, and every webhook, replication target and tier named by a host. They use UDP on a socket that never waits, and take the answer the next time they look. No call there takes longer than a tenth of a millisecond, even when a nameserver does not answer; that nameserver is passed over for the next one at its timeout. A name these lookups cannot answer, such as one only an NSS module knows or an answer that was cut short, goes to the system's resolver on a thread.

  • The mutation journal's flush, once per --persistent-interval while anything is buffered. On a healthy disk this is only a write to the page cache. On a full or slow disk, the write keeps a whole interval's worth of clients waiting.

  • The cache's snapshot and its fsync, at teardown rather than periodically. That is why it is listed last among the disk costs rather than first. A stop takes as long as the dump takes.

A runtime's state file is not among them. The runtime writes and syncs it, together with its directory, on a thread of its own whenever its state changes, so no loop waits for that disk.

A storage runtime blocks twice, and never while it serves. On start, before its listener exists, it reads the directory and removes temporary files. After any stop that was not clean, it also reads every object's header to reconcile the journals. That start takes as long as the object count requires. The work runs on threads with many reads at once, and all of it has ended before the runtime serves. On stop, the runtime syncs a marker file that records a clean stop. Between the two, every file read and write is an io_uring operation. So a slow disk adds latency to the requests waiting for it; it does not stop the runtime from answering its other connections.

What is NOT on this list, though it was suspected and measured. A static file server spends 7.3 per cent of its worker in the kernel clearing pages. That looks like allocation churn, but it is not. The same server took fourteen minor page faults in total while answering half a million requests. So the pages are the kernel's own, for the 1.7 GB a second it puts on the wire. The malloc and free around each file buffer are served from the heap and never reach the kernel.

sections.title: Out-of-process runtimes
sections.html:
Every runtime made with create or restored at boot, of any type, runs in its own supervised worker process. There is no flag to keep one in the daemon. Only a server, client, proxy, cache, storage or dns runtime that a script makes with socketley.create runs in the daemon. This section states plainly what that costs.

The script runs in the worker and nowhere else. An out-of-process runtime exists twice. The worker owns the listening socket and serves every byte. A placeholder in the daemon carries the runtime's name, port, group and state, so that ls, stats and the endpoint table have something to answer with. The script belongs to the worker. The placeholder compiles the script and then discards it without executing a line. Because it compiles the script, create still refuses a file that does not parse on the spot, instead of reporting "the worker exited and the runtime is failed".

The script's routes declaration still reaches the daemon. The declaration is produced by running the script, and only the worker runs it. The worker encodes the declaration into a routes frame on the control socket it already holds. The supervisor decodes the frame onto the placeholder, and the daemon publishes the worker's copy in preference to a local one. Without it, publish_endpoints would publish nothing for the runtime. A gateway in front of it would then forward every method instead of refusing undeclared ones at the edge with a 405, and that enforcement would stop existing without notice. A reload-lua on such a runtime waits for the new declaration before republishing. So the gateway never enforces the old script's methods against the new script's handler. The declaration belongs to a handler rather than a proxy, which is why it matters now that every type has its own process by default.

create waits for the worker's verdict. Compiling the script in the placeholder catches a file that does not parse, and nothing else. The rest of the configuration is judged in the worker, where the script actually runs, the port is actually bound and the TLS pair is actually read. So create does not answer as soon as it has forked a process. It waits until that process says whether it can serve what it was given.

Three things end the wait. If the worker reports that it is serving, create exits 0. If the worker refuses, or starts but cannot bind, resolve its backend or load its certificates, create exits 1 and the daemon's log gives the reason. The runtime is then left failed, where ls shows it, rather than removed, so there is still something to ask about. If neither answer arrives within two seconds, create exits 2 and says so. The runtime stays under supervision, and ls reports whatever state it settles on.

The two-second bound is a backstop, not a budget. A worker that has to compile a script, build its ring and bind a listener reports back in about 20 ms. A refusal comes back sooner, because the child stops at the script. Only a worker that has wedged reaches two seconds. create never blocks indefinitely on a child.

A runtime in a worker can still ask another runtime by name. --cache works across the process boundary in both directions. When a process gets a request for a name it does not hold, it sends the request out on the control socket. The daemon holds the whole map and is the only process that can route. It looks the name up, posts the request to whatever answers for it (in the daemon or in another worker), and writes the answer back. Neither the asking runtime nor the client on the other end of the socket can tell which arrangement served it. A request for a name that nothing answers to is refused with the same error: no such runtime that an in-process runtime gives; it is not dropped silently.

The cross-runtime management API works inside a worker. socketley.create, .start, .stop, .remove, .send, .list, .get, .pipe and the socketley.cluster table are answered as they are in the daemon; see Process Isolation under PROXY FLAGS. A worker refuses them only when the daemon that forked it could give it no control socket, which means an older build.

self.route() crosses the boundary. It names another runtime, but it works from a worker. route_client() does not need a file descriptor to travel to the other process. It needs the target's connection tables, which it reaches by conn_ref through shared/ipc/route_relay.h. The origin keeps the socket and relays the bytes, exactly as it does when both runtimes are in one process.

unroute(), get_route() and owner_send() answer from this runtime's own tables.

Cross-runtime pub/sub reaches a worker. A cache's PUBLISH is delivered to a worker's subscribe callbacks over the worker's control socket. The daemon does not run those callbacks against the placeholder it keeps for the runtime. Delivery is one-way and best-effort, like every other frame on that socket. A publish is an event, not a state. So a frame dropped because the child is not reading is not re-sent. A frame that arrives before the worker has been configured is discarded, not replayed to a subscriber that did not exist when it happened.

Interactive mode (start -i) is not offered for a proxy, on either path. Interactive mode is a stream. What is typed reaches a server's clients, a client's server, or a cache's command parser. A proxy relays between a client and a backend and speaks for neither. So typed input has nothing to mean, and offering it would mean inventing a meaning rather than exposing one. The command refuses and exits 1 without starting anything.

A worker's figures are read when they are printed. For an out-of-process runtime, connections, total_connections, total_messages, bytes_in and bytes_out are summed from a small shared-memory region at the moment the command prints them. Each worker stores its own line in that region once per turn of its event loop, and the daemon adds the lines up. There is no round trip, and nothing waits on a child that may be wedged. There is also no interval between reading and printing in which a figure could go stale.

So every figure is identical on both paths, which is the property the split exists to have. The figures:pushed and figures_age_ms:n lines of earlier releases no longer exist, and nothing replaces them: there is no age left to report.

The part of stats that is not a summable counter is still computed inside the worker. Examples are a cache's key count, a proxy's healthy backends and the ring's granted polling mode. They are walks of tables that exist only in the worker. The worker sends this part over the control socket when it changes. For a runtime with no traffic, that is never: an idle worker sends nothing. It wakes only for a TLS listener's check of its certificate files, once every two seconds.

Until the first such report arrives, stats prints worker_report:none in place of those figures. Ordinarily that window is the first fraction of a second after a start. A runtime that shows it while serving traffic has a worker that is alive but not publishing: it is wedged, or its frames are being lost. That line is the difference between "no data" and "no traffic".

And which process it is. stats prints pid:n for a runtime that has its own process: an out-of-process proxy's worker, or a managed external runtime's child. Nothing else in the output says that the runtime runs elsewhere. So this line names the process to strace, to read /proc for, or to charge a machine's memory to. An in-process runtime prints no such line. Neither does a runtime whose worker has been stopped or reaped. A pid that has been returned to the system is worse than none, because somebody will go and look at that number.

A sharded runtime prints shards:n and shard_pids: instead, because there are n processes and naming one of them arbitrarily would be wrong. Its counters are still one set of figures: the shared region has one line per shard, and the sum over them is what the runtime is serving.

Every type is split, and no flag keeps one in the daemon. The management API, self.route() and the figures work in a worker as they do in the daemon.

sections.title: TLS
sections.html:
Every runtime type speaks TLS. This covers a server's and a cache's own listener, both legs of a proxy, and a client runtime's dial. A server created with --tls --cert file --key file accepts connections, handshakes and moves records itself. OpenSSL never touches the socket. Each connection gets a memory BIO pair. The same io_uring submissions that carry every other byte in the daemon carry the ciphertext in and out. The handshake advances one completion at a time, so nothing blocks the event loop. Protocol detection, WebSocket, HTTP and RESP all run on the decrypted stream, so wss:// and https:// work on a listener configured this way. --ca file adds mutual TLS: a client must present a certificate signed by that CA.

A peer that opens a connection and never finishes the handshake is dropped after 30 seconds. This limit is fixed, not configurable, and deliberately separate from --idle-timeout. A connection that completed its handshake and then went quiet is legitimate on a daemon built for long-living ones. A peer that has sent nothing the record layer accepted has not become a client at all. Without the limit, it could hold a slot against --max-connections for as long as it liked. The clock starts when the handshake does, and later bytes do not move it. So a peer that dribbles inside an unfinished record is dropped on the same schedule as one that sends nothing at all. A client runtime applies the same 30 seconds to a target that accepts its connection and then never handshakes. After that, --reconnect applies to it like any other lost connection.

A proxy runs the same record layer on both of its legs. The same three flags terminate TLS on its listening port, and --client-ca file makes it demand a certificate from its callers. The backend leg uses TLS when the backend address is https://, or when --ca, --client-cert or --client-key is given; those three apply to every backend. --client-cert and --client-key present a certificate to a backend that asks for one. The proxy always verifies a TLS backend connection: against --ca or the system store, with the endpoint's name checked, and with TLS 1.2 as the minimum version. There is no option to turn that off. These connections are pooled and reused together with their sessions, so a handshake is paid once per idle period rather than once per request. A pooled socket is only ever returned to the endpoint it was opened to, which is the name it was verified against.

--health-check http works against a TLS backend and probes it over TLS. The probe uses the same record layer as the data path: a memory BIO pair, records carried by ordinary io_uring submissions, and a handshake advanced one completion at a time. It is held to the same standard. The chain is checked against --ca or the system store, the certificate against the endpoint's own name, and TLS 1.2 is the minimum. A backend whose certificate does not verify is marked unhealthy rather than reported healthy. That is the only answer that agrees with what the data path would do with it. Everything above the record layer is unchanged: the probe fetches the same --health-path path, and only a 2xx counts.

A client runtime runs the dialling half of the same record layer on its outbound socket. When created with --tls, it puts a ClientHello on the wire as soon as it has a socket. It advances the handshake one completion at a time, exactly as the server and the proxy do. The line framing and the Lua callbacks above it see the same plaintext they always did. The client verifies the peer against --ca file or the system store. The certificate must be valid for the host in -t: its DNS SAN must match, or its IP SAN for an address literal. --cert file and --key file present a certificate to a peer that asks for one. By design, there is no skip-verify option. When a peer fails either check, the client drops the socket and re-dials on its usual backoff. It never retries in cleartext.

A cache terminates TLS on its own listener with the same three flags a server uses, and --ca file demands a client certificate there in the same way. RESP is auto-detected from the first byte of the decrypted stream. So an existing Redis client speaks the protocol it always did, one layer up, and the line protocol works on the same port.

A cache still cannot replicate over TLS. Replication is not a listener, and nothing encrypts it. A follower dials its leader itself, in cleartext. On a leader, a promoted follower is written to by a second writer that goes around the record layer by design. So the combination is refused rather than half-honoured. --tls together with --replicate is rejected at create, by edit and import, and again at every start. A state file that carries both leaves the runtime failed rather than letting it come up quietly wrong. A TLS cache that a REPLICATE command asks to become a leader answers with an error instead of promoting itself. A cache encrypted for its clients but cleartext for its replicas would be worse than an honestly cleartext one, because only the first looks safe.

Two further combinations are refused for the same reason: --udp on a client or a server, because DTLS is not implemented; and, on a server, --upstream, because the upstream connection would still be made in cleartext. A proxy in --protocol tcp mode terminates TLS on its listener like any other proxy and forwards the decrypted stream to its backend. On any connection with a TLS session, it bypasses the zero-copy splice path, because a splice would move bytes the record layer never saw.

There is one outbound exception, and it is not transport. socketley.http() in a Lua callback speaks HTTPS. It verifies the certificate chain and the host name, with TLS 1.2 as the minimum version (see Global Functions). It is a client call that a script makes. It encrypts nothing that socketley itself serves or forwards.

Anything that is not implemented fails closed, and so does every incomplete configuration:

  • create rejects --tls, --cert, --key and --ca on a dns, sync, idp, db, tunnel, metrics or mcp runtime, which has no handshake, and --client-ca, --client-cert and --client-key on anything but a proxy. It exits with status 1 and a message that names the flag.

  • On a server, client or proxy runtime the same flags are accepted, but only as a complete set. --tls without a certificate and key on a server or proxy is refused, and no runtime is created. So is a certificate or trust store without --tls on any of the three. Either would describe a listener that could only serve cleartext, or a dial that would be made in cleartext. On a client, --tls alone is complete, but half a --cert/--key pair is refused: it would present nothing while the flags said a certificate was configured. On a proxy, --client-ca without --tls is refused, and so is half a --client-cert/--client-key pair, for the same reason.

  • Flag-based edit applies the same rule. It restores the previous TLS settings if the edit would leave them incomplete. edit accepts a subset of the flags of create, so most flags it does not accept come back as unknown flag. These flags do not, because changing TLS on a live runtime is exactly what an operator would be attempting.

  • import applies the same rule to the JSON document's fields.

  • start, reload and the daemon's own boot-time restore refuse a runtime whose configuration cannot be honoured. This is how a runtime restored from a state file written by an older release is caught. Nothing is brought up, and the runtime goes to failed.

  • A certificate or key that cannot be read, or a key that does not match its certificate, fails the runtime at start. The port is never bound.

To clear the settings from a runtime whose configuration is refused, dump it, delete the TLS fields, and import it back (see import).

The embedded C++ SDK reaches the same gate, because its start() goes through runtime_manager::start. So server().tls(cert, key) and proxy().tls(cert, key) terminate TLS exactly as a daemon-managed runtime does. client().tls() dials over TLS, and cache().tls(cert, key) terminates it, through the same gate.

For encrypted transport on a server's upstream connections, terminate TLS in a front-end proxy (nginx, HAProxy, stunnel). Have it forward over loopback or another trusted network path. A socketley proxy can play that part.

sections.title: EXIT STATUS
sections.html:
0#

Success.

1#

An error, such as an invalid command, a runtime that was not found, or a rejected TLS flag.

2#

A fatal error, or no answer in time: the daemon could not be reached, or a runtime's workers stopped answering before it was serving (see create and start). The runtime may still come up; check with socketley ls.

flags.label: Path

flags.label: Server's root

flags.label: Index script

flags.label: Client CA

flags.label: Journal every

flags.label: Max memory

flags.label: Redis protocol only

flags.label: Follow

flags.label: Public

flags.label: Cluster map

flags.label: Cluster replica

flags.label: Directory

flags.label: Credentials

flags.label: Website names

flags.label: TLS proxies

flags.label: Quota

flags.label: Sync to disk
flags.help: When an answered write is on the disk.

flags.label: Sync every
flags.help: How often --fsync interval syncs to disk.

flags.label: Scrub every

flags.label: Compress after
flags.help: Compress a version once it has not been written for this long; off unless given.

flags.label: Abort uploads after
flags.help: Abort a multipart upload open this long; never unless given.

flags.label: Encryption key
flags.help: The 32-byte master key of server-side encryption.

flags.label: Sync runtimes
flags.help: Runtimes that pull users' git repositories: none, one for all, or one each.

flags.label: ACLs
flags.help: Accept ACLs on buckets that have no ownership controls; otherwise the bucket owner owns everything.

flags.label: Webhooks
flags.help: The webhooks event notifications may go to.

flags.label: Replication targets

flags.label: Tiers
flags.help: The S3 endpoints lifecycle may move versions to.

flags.label: Federation
flags.help: The OIDC provider and LDAP directory STS trusts.

flags.label: Cluster nodes
flags.help: Make it a node of a storage cluster.

flags.label: Zones
flags.help: Zone names (a file is written) or zone files. Required.

flags.label: Public addresses
flags.help: The addresses runtimes' names are answered with.

flags.label: Entrance
flags.help: The entrance proxy it creates; none for no entrance.

flags.label: Entrance port
flags.help: The entrance's port; 443 also makes the redirect on 80.

flags.label: Transfer to
flags.help: Addresses that may copy the zones (AXFR): secondaries.

flags.label: Notify
flags.help: Secondaries told of each change.

flags.label: Rate limit
flags.help: Response rate limit: answers a second to one network; 0 turns it off.

flags.label: DNSSEC
flags.help: Signs its zones; the parent takes the DS that socketley <name> dnssec prints.

flags.label: Directory
flags.help: The directory whose files are carried. Required.

flags.label: Storage
flags.help: Where they go: a runtime and a bucket, or a URL and one. Required.

flags.label: Direction
flags.help: Direction: out to the storage, in from it, or inout for both.

flags.label: Credentials
flags.help: A file holding access_key and secret_key. Required.

flags.label: Prefix
flags.help: The key everything is written under, below the bucket.

flags.label: Walk every
flags.help: How often the whole directory is rescanned; never to sync on changes only.

flags.label: Exclude
flags.help: Patterns of paths, relative to the directory, that are not synced.

flags.label: Clients
flags.help: The applications that sign users in through it, one per line: id, secret (or -) and redirect addresses.

flags.label: Issuer
flags.help: The https address it is reached at; https://<first name> when not given.

flags.label: Identity provider
flags.help: The idp runtime the web interface signs in with; its users are the users of the same name here.

flags.label: Cookie domain
flags.help: The domain whose names share one sign-in, for a proxy's --auth idp:.

flags.label: Mode
flags.help: An edge agents dial out to, or an agent dialling one.

flags.label: Edge
flags.help: The edge an agent dials, its https address.

flags.label: Invitation
flags.help: What `socketley tunnel <edge> invite` printed, used once to join.

flags.label: Offers
flags.help: What an agent carries the edge's streams to: service=host:port each.

flags.label: Forward
flags.help: Where an edge forwards a signed-in user's stream, as ssh's ProxyCommand needs.

flags.label: Identity provider
flags.help: The idp runtime whose signed-in people may use --forward.

flags.label: Audiences
flags.help: The clients whose access tokens --forward takes.

flags.label: Resource servers
flags.help: Resource servers an access token may be issued for, by their https address. With any set, an application may also sign in by the URL of its metadata document.

flags.label: SSH certificates
flags.help: Sign SSH certificates for signed-in users, valid for this many hours; off unless given.

flags.label: Schema
flags.help: The collections, a line each: name, access (private, owner, shared, public, catalog) and indexed fields.

flags.label: Keys
flags.help: Service keys a backend sends as Authorization: Bearer, one name and secret per line.

flags.label: Identity provider
flags.help: The idp runtime whose accounts own documents and sign in by its cookie or access tokens.

flags.label: Token clients
flags.help: The idp's clients whose access tokens it takes; a token of any other is refused.

flags.label: Web origins
flags.help: Web origins whose pages may call it with the user's sign-in; * lets any page call it, without the sign-in.

flags.label: Quota
flags.help: The most bytes the documents hold.

flags.label: Cache
flags.help: Memory for the documents read most recently; the rest are read from disk.

flags.label: Its key

flags.label: Backups

flags.label: Back up every

flags.label: Keep

flags.help: The file a storage writes for a user's own sync runtime, which pulls their git repositories.

flags.label: Anonymous
flags.help: Anyone may call it without a key; only for a port no other machine can reach.

flags.label: Origins
flags.help: The web origins a browser may call it from, or * for any.

flags.label: Daemon tools
flags.help: This daemon's runtimes as tools: listed and read by every key, started and stopped by an admin's.

flags.label: Instructions
flags.help: What a client is told the server is for.

flags.label: Identity provider
flags.help: The idp runtime whose people sign in, by an access token for https://<first name>/mcp.

flags.label: Token clients
flags.help: The idp's clients whose own access tokens it takes as well.

flags.label: Document root
flags.help: The directory whose files are the site. Required.

flags.label: Index page
flags.help: The file a directory's address is answered with, index.html unless given.

flags.label: Fallback page
flags.help: The page an address with no file is given, with 200, as a single-page app routes; 404.html, if there, otherwise.

flags.help: The targets it scrapes, a line each: name url, then every=, timeout= or labels.

flags.label: Keep

flags.label: Tiers
flags.help: Coarser tiers kept for longer, as step:keep pairs separated by commas, or none.

flags.help: The most series it keeps; a new one past it is refused and counted.

flags.help: Log every sample as it comes, so a crash loses none.

flags.help: This daemon's own series, taken without text; the default.

flags.label: Identity provider
flags.help: The idp runtime whose sign-ins and access tokens may read it.

flags.label: Token clients
flags.help: The idp's clients whose access tokens it takes.

flags.label: Rules

flags.label: Notify
flags.help: Where the daemon's own alerts go: webhook, mail and events, or none.

flags.help: Store what a Prometheus or agent sends to /api/v1/write.

flags.label: Users

flags.help: The idp runtime whose access tokens sign clients in, given as the password.

flags.label: Token clients
flags.help: The idp's clients whose access tokens it takes; a token of any other is refused.

flags.label: Access rules
flags.help: Who may publish and subscribe to what: user, topic and pattern lines, read again when it changes.

flags.label: Anonymous
flags.help: Let clients in without credentials, as the access rules allow.

flags.label: Topic rules
flags.help: Where messages go besides their subscribers: a cache, a db, a storage, a server or another broker.

flags.label: WebSocket port
flags.help: A port browsers reach the broker on over WebSocket.

flags.label: Persist to

flags.label: Write every
flags.help: How often what changed reaches that file.

flags.label: Max packet

flags.label: Session expiry

flags.label: Retained bytes

flags.label: Max sessions
flags.help: The most sessions it keeps, connected or not; 100000 unless given.

flags.label: Max keep alive
flags.help: The longest keep alive a client is granted, in seconds; 1200 unless given.

flags.label: Mail domains

flags.label: Token clients

flags.help: A port mail clients read the mailboxes on over TLS.

flags.label: LMTP port

flags.label: MTA-STS port

flags.label: Greylist delay
flags.help: Ask a sender, recipient and network seen for the first time to retry after this long.

flags.label: Rspamd

flags.label: Subaddress delimiter
flags.help: What divides a user from a tag, user+tag; none for no tags.

flags.label: Send reports
flags.help: Send the DMARC and TLS reports other domains ask for.

examples.title: Every flag a proxy has, from a configuration file

Setting them meant a `create` command line, which meant they lived somewhere other than the file describing the deployment. This file is what closing that gap buys.

examples.title: Register and Start a Managed External Binary
examples.summary: This example compiles a C++ echo service and registers it with the daemon using `socketley add`. The daemon fork+exec's the binary, manages its lifecycle, and auto-restarts it on crash.

examples.title: Daemon Auto-Restarts Crashed Managed Binaries
examples.summary: Demonstrates the key advantage of managed externals over plain `attach`: when the binary crashes or is killed, the daemon automatically restarts it within ~2 seconds via its health-check timer.

examples.title: Full Lifecycle: Add, Stop, Start, Remove
examples.summary: Demonstrates the complete lifecycle of a managed external runtime. Unlike plain `attach` (where stop just forgets the process), managed runtimes can be stopped and restarted like native socketley runtimes.

examples.title: Managed Chat Server (Wrapper API)
examples.summary: Demonstrates a managed external using the socketley::server wrapper. The wrapper handles io_uring, signal handling, and the event loop automatically — much simpler than raw POSIX sockets.

examples.title: Managed Counter Server (Wrapper API)
examples.summary: Demonstrates a managed external using the socketley::server wrapper with per-connection metadata (set_data / get_data). Each message gets a per-connection sequence number in the reply.

examples.title: Managed Chat Server (Wrapper API)
examples.summary: A multi-client chat server using the socketley::server wrapper. Messages from any client are broadcast to every client, the sender included.

examples.title: Managed Connection Counter (Wrapper API)
examples.summary: A simple server using the socketley::server wrapper that tracks connection count and replies to each message with a per-connection message counter.

examples.title: Minimal Managed External Service
examples.summary: A standalone echo server built with the C++ SDK (attach.h). When registered via `socketley add`, the daemon manages its full lifecycle: fork+exec on start, auto-restart on crash, re-launch on daemon boot.

examples.title: An MCP server an AI client asks about a shop's orders
examples.summary: printf 'claude %s\nops %s admin\n' "$(openssl rand -hex 16)" "$(openssl rand -hex 16)" > /etc/socketley/mcp.keys socketley create mcp shop -p 9600 --keys /etc/socketley/mcp.keys \ --lua examples/mcp/shop.lua --tools daemon --instructions "Ask about the shop's orders." -s claude mcp add --transport http shop http://127.0.0.1:9600/mcp \ --header "Authorization: Bearer <claude's secret>"

examples.title: An MQTT broker for devices, apps and browsers
examples.summary: Passwords in a file of its own, rules for who reads and writes what, a WebSocket port for browsers, and sessions kept across restarts. Then the sensors' readings handed to a cache's stream, beside the subscribers.

examples.title: A game server whose moves reach players through a broker
examples.summary: socketley create mqtt games --anonymous --persistent on -s socketley create server referee -p 9000 --lua examples/mqtt/game-moves.lua -s mosquitto_sub -i alice -c -q 1 -t 'game/42/#' -v # a player's session echo 'move 42 e2e4' | nc -q2 localhost 9000 # the referee takes a move

examples.title: A handler states what it answers; the gateway enforces it
examples.summary: This script runs on the SERVER, not on the proxy. That is the whole idea.

examples.title: Filters that run before the proxy picks a backend
examples.summary: on_route() answers "where does this request go". Authentication, per-user rate limiting and header rewriting are not that question, and putting them inside on_route() means they run once a backend has already been chosen for the request. A rejection at that point has already cost the connection it exists to prevent.

examples.title: Dynamic Backend Discovery with Groups
examples.summary: Demonstrates using groups for dynamic proxy backend discovery. Tag servers with -g <group>, then use @group as a proxy backend. The proxy discovers running group members at connection time.

examples.title: Basic HTTP Reverse Proxy

Using Runtime Names as Backends

examples.title: One proxy, N worker processes
examples.summary: A runtime is one process and therefore one event loop on one core. --shards gives a single proxy N processes that share its listening socket through SO_REUSEPORT, and the kernel hands each incoming connection to one of them. It is the only way one runtime uses more than one core.

examples.title: Raw TCP Proxy

examples.title: A proxy that terminates TLS, and one that dials it
Proxy to a backend over AF_UNIX, not loopback TCP
examples.summary: A sidecar proxy and the process it fronts run on the same host, and loopback TCP charges that pair for a whole stack - handshake, sequence numbers, checksums, windows - on a connection that never sees a wire.

examples.title: IP allowlist using on_auth + self.peer_ip
examples.summary: Rejects any client whose IP does not start with the allowed prefix. Rejected clients are disconnected before on_connect fires.

examples.title: First-message token authentication using self.disconnect
examples.summary: Clients must send the secret token as their first message. Authenticated clients get broadcast access; others are dropped.

examples.title: http-dashboard.lua
examples.summary: Serves a static HTML dashboard via --http and handles WebSocket messages.

examples.title: Sending a body larger than the write-queue bound, without losing the client
examples.summary: A write is queued rather than performed, and the queue has a hard bound: fill it and the runtime closes the connection. So a loop that sends a large body as fast as it can loses the client partway through, however fast the machine.

examples.title: Answering with a generated body larger than memory
examples.summary: on_http_request has to RETURN its body, so an answer this server generates rather than reads from disk had to fit in memory first. A file of any size was already served by the splice path; a generated one of any size was not expressible at all -- an export assembled from a cache, a CSV of ten million rows, anything transcoded.

examples.title: Receiving a request body larger than memory, by not holding it
examples.summary: A server without on_http_body waits for the whole body to arrive and answers 413 past --read-buffer. Defining this callback is the opt-in for the other behaviour: the bytes are handed over as they arrive and erased behind them, so the body's size stops being the server's business.

examples.title: Per-client rate limiting using self.disconnect + on_tick

examples.title: One server, N worker processes

It is the only way one runtime uses more than one core.

examples.title: A server listener that terminates TLS
examples.summary: A server runtime encrypts its own listening port. The handshake and the record layer run on the same io_uring event loop as everything else -- OpenSSL sits behind a memory BIO pair and never touches a socket -- and everything above the record layer sees plaintext. That last part is what makes this useful: protocol auto-detection still works, so the one listener serves https:// and wss:// as well a

examples.title: Socketley SDK — a daemon of your own, carrying a runtime type of your own
examples.summary: This one binary is BOTH halves. It serves the control socket the ordinary `socketley` CLI dials, so `socketley ls`, `create`, `stats` and `--lua` all drive it with nothing added; and the supervisor execs this same binary with `proxy-worker` to serve each runtime, which daemon_start() dispatches.

examples.summary: The daemon learns its name and its flags from kvdb.toml and never loads a line of this file; it forks and execs this binary like any other worker. include <socketley/worker.h>

examples.title: chatroom — a terminal chat client over WebSocket.
examples.summary: Built on the cross-platform ws_client.h, so the same file compiles on Linux, Windows and macOS with nothing but the one header. It connects to chatd's port with a real RFC 6455 handshake — the server speaks TCP and WebSocket on the same listener and decodes frames before the room logic sees them, which is what makes this client and a bare `nc` equal citizens in the same room.

examples.title: chatroom — a chat service with rooms, presence and WebSocket clients.
examples.summary: One server wrapper, but the whole surface of it: multicast groups as rooms, per-connection data as presence, the tick as a janitor, and the listener's dual protocol — the same port speaks newline-framed TCP (nc) and WebSocket (a browser, or the cross-platform ws_client.h; see chat_cli.cpp). Frames are decoded before on_message fires, so the room logic never knows which transport a member arrived o

examples.title: edge — the application server behind the gateway.
examples.summary: It listens on an AF_UNIX socket, not a port: the only thing that should reach it is the gateway in front of it. A filesystem node is off the network, and one in a 0700 directory -- not /tmp, as this demo uses for brevity -- keeps other users out too. This is the `--listen unix:` feature through the SDK's unix-path constructor.

examples.title: edge — a TLS-terminating gateway in front of a unix-socket application.
examples.summary: The public face of the pair: TLS on the listener, HTTP awareness for per-request routing, the sidecar mesh defaults (TCP health checks, circuit breaker, retries, drain), and a backend that is a filesystem node rather than a port. Adding a second backend("...") is a one-line scale-out; the strategy then load-balances across them, and health checks eject the dead.

examples.title: jobqueue — a working job queue service in one process.
jobqueue — a worker draining the queue jobd serves.
examples.summary: Deliberately built on the CROSS-PLATFORM header: cache_client.h is the same file on Linux, Windows and macOS, so this worker compiles unchanged on all three and needs nothing from the repo but that one header. A worker fleet on a different OS than the queue is the normal case, not the exotic one.
